masters.notes: Systematized monastic rules, established Shi surname convention, created first catalogue of Chinese Buddhist scriptures.
Fifth Patriarch. Presided over the famous poetry contest between Shenxiu and Huineng at East Mountain (Dongshan).
Founded the radical Baotang school in Sichuan, rejecting all external forms. Teachings recorded in the Lidai fabao ji.
Prominent student of Mazu who served as abbot of Zhangjing monastery in Chang'an.

Early Silla monk who studied under Xitang Zhizang in Tang China and returned to establish the Silsangsan school, one of the Nine Mountain Schools of Korean Seon. His transmission is attested in Korean stele inscriptions and the Zutangji.
Doheon's direct Seon teacher. Known only from the Jijeungdaesa stele at Bongamsa (893 CE, by Choe Chiwon). Transmitted the Beomnang-Daoxin lineage to Doheon, founder of the Huiyangsan school.

Founder of the Linji school. Asked Huangbo three times about the essence of Buddhism and was beaten each time; enlightened after visiting Gaoan Dayu. Known for radical pedagogy: shouts (喝), blows, and paradoxical statements. Developed 'four shouts' and 'four positions of host and guest' frameworks. His recorded sayings (臨濟錄) compiled by Sansheng Huiran are foundational to the koan tradition.
His assembly called 'the dead tree hall' — monks sat in continuous meditation.

Korean Seon monk and master geomancer (pungsu) who profoundly shaped the political geography of Korea. Trained in both Seon meditation and Chinese geomantic arts (fengshui), he applied topographical analysis to temple and capital siting. His prophecies regarding the decline of Silla and the rise of a new dynasty at Songak (modern Kaesong) were later credited with guiding Wang Geon's founding of the Goryeo dynasty (918). He founded or restored numerous temples based on geomantic principles. Though his geomantic legacy sometimes overshadows his Buddhist teaching, he was recognized as a legitimate Seon master. Attested in Goryeo-era hagiographies: credited with prophecies that legitimized the Goryeo founding, with his geomantic writings preserved in the Doseon bigi.
Dharma heir of Yunju Daoying alongside Ieom. One of the Four Fearless Masters of Haedong. Stele preserved in CBETA B31n0170.

Heir of Xuefeng Yicun. In 908, Min kingdom ruler Wang Shenzhi appointed him to supervise the reconstruction of Yongquan Temple on Gushan (Drum Mountain) in Fuzhou, where he served as abbot and established a lasting Chan lineage in Fujian.
Known for the 'three pounds of hemp' koan.
Founded the Huanglong branch. Famous for his 'Three Barriers' test.

Direct disciple of Furong Daokai. His line carried Caodong transmission northward into Jin territory, eventually reaching Wansong Xingxiu via four generations — a separate branch from the southern Danxia Zichun line.
Leading Caodong master. Advocate of silent illumination (mozhao) Chan. Compiled the Book of Equanimity.
Caodong master; teacher of Xueyan Huiman. Appears in standard Caodong lineage charts between Lingyan Sengbao and Xueyan Huiman. Specific dates not preserved.
3rd patriarch of Suseonsa/Songgwangsa. Led the community for ~18 years after Hyesim's death.
Most celebrated Yuan-dynasty master. Declined imperial appointments. Strong ties with Korean monks and extensive international connections.

Royal preceptor and chief advisor to Yi Seonggye (King Taejo), the founder of the Joseon dynasty (1392). Muhak's most famous contribution was selecting the site of the new capital at Hanyang (modern Seoul) using geomantic principles, a decision that shaped the political geography of Korea. As Naong's dharma heir, he carried the unified Seon lineage into the new dynasty and served as a bridge between the Goryeo Buddhist establishment and the Joseon court, even as Neo-Confucian officials increasingly marginalized Buddhism. He designed the layout of key Seoul temples including Hoeryongsa. Attested in Joseon-era court records: his role in the capital selection and his advisory relationship with King Taejo are documented in the Joseon wangjo sillok (Annals of the Joseon Dynasty).
Ming dynasty Chan master who pioneered 7-day meditation retreats. Teacher of Hanshan Deqing, one of the Four Great Monks of the Ming.
Disciple of Hanshan Deqing. Tonsure master of Ouyi Zhixu at Yunqi Temple.
Major post-Hyujeong figure. Led reconstruction of Hwaeomsa (1630-1636). Extended the Buhyu lineage into mid-Joseon.
Shaolin Monastery Caodong transmission. Link figure between Xueting Fuyu and the late Ming Caodong revival.

Late 18th-early 19th century Seon master. The 73rd Korean patriarch. One of the few masters in the intermediate chain with attested dates (1738-1823). Teacher of Manhwa Boseon, who in turn taught Gyeongheo.

One of Xuedou Chongxian's most important dharma heirs. He taught at Tianyi Monastery in Zhejiang and continued Xuedou's literary-poetic Chan. Through his student Huilin Zongben, who became abbot of the imperially sponsored Xiangguo Monastery in Kaifeng, his branch maintained a significant Yunmen institutional presence into the late 11th century.

Best known for the Kalpa Fire koan (BCR 29, BOS 30): 'When the great fire at the end of the kalpa destroys the universe, is this destroyed or not?' — 'Destroyed.' Touzi Datong called him 'the Ancient Buddha of West River.' Lived for over ten years in a hollow tree on Mt. Dasui in Sichuan, then ran a tea stall by the road. Also studied with Dongshan Liangjie and Yunyan Tansheng.

Linji master, dharma heir of Poshan Haiming, abbot of Huayan and Bao'en. His incense-offering recalls that he 'got it in the ranks of war' (兵戈隊裏得來) — he came to the dharma through the Ming–Qing collapse. He died in 1701 aged seventy-three, leaving an unusually large number of heirs, more than thirty of whom the lamps name.

Caodong master, of the Li family of Macheng in Hubei. As a child he would leap for joy at the sight of a monk; he left home at seven and took the full precepts at nineteen under Fumu of Shifeng, then studied the sutras and treatises. He went down to Jinling and called on Lang Zhangren, and then to Yuanjie Jingying at Yunyan, where he had an insight into the 'three not-thats' huatou and received the entrustment. He was abbot of Longhua on Bingshan at Huzhou and of Yunfeng at Hengzhou. He wrote the Fahua jing shoushou, notes on the Chanlin baoxun, and a record of sayings. After his death his body is said not to have decayed, the hair and beard continuing to grow.

links.label: DILA Authority A010055 (his teacher 元潔淨瑩)

masters.notes: Caodong master, of the Feng family of Jianyang in Fujian, born in 1577. He was tonsured in 1604 under Likong at Huxiaoyan, and became a dharma heir of Wuming Huijing of Shouchang. He was abbot of Dongyuan at Jianning in the Wuyi mountains, and is styled in his own stupa inscription 'first-generation Chan patriarch of Wuyi'. He died in 1630 aged fifty-four. His stele places him second, after Boshan Yuanlai, among the men who carried Shouchang's revived Caodong line forward.
Linji master, from Anlu in Chu, dharma heir of Muchen Daomin. He was abbot of Longya at Tanzhou, and died in 1676 aged fifty-seven.

Linji master, dharma heir of Lingji Xingguan. A preface to his own record of sayings calls him 'my dharma-brother Zuliang, who awakened and verified in his prime, entering in person the room of the old man Lingji at Yangfen.' He left a record of sayings in two fascicles.

links.label: DILA Authority A004078 (his teacher 靈機行觀)

masters.notes: Caodong master of the Shouchang line, of the Hu family of Nancheng in Jianchang. In his own account of conduct, dictated at Longhu monastery in Xincheng, he says: 'this mountain monk is named Yuanmi, styled Jianru, and also Quran; a son of the Hu family of Nancheng in Jianchang. My father was named Fu, my mother of the Ning clan.' He was born on the third day of the twelfth month of 1579. Taken as a boy by his father to Baofang, he met the monk Wuming Huijing and was won over by him; he returned alone the next morning to ask for instruction, and Huijing gave him a verse and told him to work at it day and night. At twenty-one he gave up meat and wine and asked to be tonsured, but Huijing refused while his parents lived, so he went to Fuzhou and took the robe from the dharma master Kai of Jinshan. He returned to Baofang as fire-keeper. Huijing, looking into the stove, said: 'if you want the rice cooked, you must turn your body in the flames and see the wall.' He took up the phrase, and after seven or eight days, standing behind the hall at the third watch, body and mind fell still. He died in 1649, aged seventy-one.

Caodong master of Baoxianglin at Nanhai in Guangdong, lay name Zhang Mingda, of Longjiang in Shunde; his father was Yinliang and his mother of the Deng clan. His mother, having repeatedly borne children who did not live, prayed to Guanyin and conceived him. At seventeen he took the robe at Dinghu and was given the name Kaixiong. He became the dharma heir of Zaishan Hongzan. The Dinghushan gazetteer's life of him — under his sobriquet Shijian, 'Stone Arrow' — records that when the venerable Zaiweng came to his village he went to call on him, their question and answer matched, and he went straight home, took leave of his parents, and left to study with him. His record of sayings assembles the comments-on-the-ancients of two hundred Caodong monks. He died in 1676 aged forty-three.

Linji master, dharma heir of Poshan Haiming, and a great teacher in his own right — the lamps count many heirs, of whom Chisong Daoling carried the line into Guizhou. In his own account of conduct he says he was a son of the Wang family of Tongchuan prefecture in Sichuan; he brooded daily on impermanence, suffering and emptiness, felt at twenty-five that he had wasted his life, and could not get his family's leave to go, until he took up a pair of shears and made to cut off his hair, and so broke out of the cage. He was tonsured by Master Jiankong. Reading the Heart Sutra at 'the five aggregates are empty', doubt broke open in him. He read Hanshan's expedient words on Zhaozhou's dog, and knew that what he had was only 'use on the road' and not the house itself. Hearing that a great teacher had appeared at Liangshan — 'the venerable Poshan is truly an eye for men and gods' — he went to him, was given the dog-and-Buddha-nature huatou, took the full precepts, and was sent off with three fascicles of the record of sayings. He was abbot of Baizhang in Sichuan and of Sanmei at Shiqian in Guizhou, and died in 1672 aged seventy.

Yuan and early-Ming master, fifty-third patriarch of Jingshan. Song Lian's stupa inscription opens: 'the master's name was Zhiji, styled Yizhong, a son of the Gu family of Wu county in Suzhou; his father was Maoqing, his mother of the Zhou clan.' He entered the Haiyun cloister as a boy, advancing in the Buddhist books and the Confucian classics together. He went to Jianye and saw Guangzhi Xin at the great Longxiang monastery, who — with the leading literary men of the age — was so struck by his gifts that they vied to praise him. But a fellow-monk rebuked him: 'with talent as sharp as this, do you not think to shoulder the great Dharma, and are content to be a slave to poetry?' He could not answer. He went back to Haiyun with a boulder in his chest, and for more than a month did not close his eyes — until he saw an autumn leaf blow down into the courtyard and suddenly awoke. Unwilling to trust himself without testing, he took his staff to Shuangjing and called on Jizhao Duan — Yuansou Xingduan — who had long marked him as a vessel of the dharma, questioned him, and found him answering as a falcon drops through the autumn sky. He was made attendant, then keeper of the library. He came out at Longjiao in 1342, moved to Puci, was installed at Jingci by the Left Chancellor in 1358, and rose to Jingshan. He died in 1378, aged sixty-eight.

A NUN, and one of the very few women of the Ming–Qing with a record of sayings in the Jiaxing canon. Lay surname Jin, lay name Jin Shuxiu; her dharma name was Xuanzong and her style Baochi. Widowed, she took the robe, and became the dharma heir of Tuiweng Hongchu, thirty-third generation of Linji. She was first abbess of Miaozhan at Jiahe, then of Nanxun at Yanguan, and afterwards at Lingyan. Her record of sayings runs to two fascicles.

Founder-abbot of Qianling at Guiyang and the man who planted the Linji line in Guizhou. In the account of his course, dictated in 1682, he says: 'I am a son of the Han family, born on the twenty-fourth day of the fourth month of 1634; our ancestral home is Changsha, but we lived at Tongchuan in Shu. My father was named Liang, my mother of the Xie clan.' His father died when he was six; his mother and elder brother raised him, and war drove the family into Guizhou. At fifteen he fled into the Nanwang mountains with a companion, living on grass and wood and reciting the Buddha's name until he was thin as a stick. He studied under Jiufeng Lingyao, took Baiyun Xishi as his tonsure master, and afterwards, at Zunyi, called on the master who would become his own. The master asked where he was from. 'Tongchuan.' 'Then you are from my own district' — and the two shouted at each other, and the master beat him out of the room. The next day the master read his verse and asked, 'is this awakening, or is it learning?' 'Do not rub your eyes and make flowers in the air.' He bowed; the master gave him a nudge and said, 'take good care of yourself,' and later handed over the whisk with a verse: 'go deep into hiding, and the dragons and gods will push you out.' In 1667 he was asked to head the Shoushi Chan cloister in the provincial capital, sealed himself in a cell there for a thousand days, and on coming out was asked to found Qianling. He taught for more than thirty years.

Linji master of the Song who carried the school to Japan. From western Shu, he left home at Jiangshan, then went to Wuzhun Shifan at Jingshan and laboured under him for several years; in 1235 Shifan sent him on to Chijue Daochong. He first held the Lingyan Guangfu cloister at Xiangshan in Qingyuan. In 1260 he was invited to Japan and became the second abbot of Kenchō-ji at Kamakura, where he taught the regent Hōjō Tokiyori. He returned to China in 1265 and spent his last years at Longxiang on Jiangxinshan in Wenzhou, dying on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month of 1276 at seventy-eight. Posthumously titled Chan Master Zongjue. The Japanese know him as Gottan Funei.

Linji master of the Qingshan (磬山) line, of the Wang family of Wuyuan in Xin'an. He was the dharma heir of Tongshou, and so a grand-heir of Tianyin Yuanxiu. He was abbot of Shending at Changsha, and died in 1654 aged forty-eight.

Linji master, dharma heir of Poshan Haiming. In his own account of conduct he says: 'I am a man of Yiliang county in Yunnan; my father's surname was Gu, my mother of the Shi clan. The family was poor and I did not read as a boy. At fourteen I left home, tonsured by the old master Shunyu at the Zhulin monastery on Zhuzishan.' At seventeen he was at Yuntai in southern Yunnan; at nineteen the thought of death and impermanence stirred in him. A travelling monk from Jizu gave him Zhaozhou's dog, and he worked at it for five years without an opening, then set it down and went off to recite the Buddha's name. Later Chan master Jifan drew him out — 'you say there is nothing to be done, but there is plainly one thing unfinished in your breast' — and struck him across the face, saying that to press a question to the point where nothing can be done is the point where strength comes, as a soldier who has lost his sword rides bare-handed at the enemy and takes his weapon from him and kills with it. At that he saw where old Zhaozhou had put his hand, and without so much as a bow he slapped his teacher across the mouth and pushed him out of the door, and Jifan shook himself and went off laughing. He became abbot of Kaifeng (Nanyun cloister) at Hengzhou. His heirs carried the line into Yunnan.

Linji master, of the Nie family of Huai'an, abbot of Xuefeng at Fuzhou. He was the dharma heir of Jue'an Kexiang, on whose death he wrote: 'In the autumn of the gengyin year my late master, the venerable Jue'an, passed away at Censhan in Hangzhou; on hearing the news of his death I made this.' He also mourned Xueyan Zuqin of Yangshan. He died about 1334.

links.label: DILA Authority A003948 (his teacher 絕岸可湘)

masters.notes: Linji master of Tui'an at Jiaxing, of the Jin family of Xiushui; his father was styled Chengdan and his mother of the Tang clan. In his own account of conduct, given at the Layman Pang's tea-offering on the eighth day of the twelfth month of 1669, he says he was born on the twenty-seventh day of the fourth month of 1622; both parents died early and his grandfather raised him. As a boy he dreamt Guanyin laid a hand on his head, and thereafter held to her name. At sixteen, his grandfather ill and wanting the marriage completed, he refused; his grandfather died sitting, his grandmother followed, and after the burials he left. He was tonsured at twenty at the Dongta Chan monastery by the old master Juera. In 1643 the great master Xuejiao held the retreat, and asked him sweeping the floor, 'why did you leave home?' 'My parents died early; I fear birth and death.' 'Then why not investigate the one that has no birth and death?' — and struck him. Cutting firewood one day, a hare broke cover, he dropped the knife, and awoke. He later called on Gunan Muyun, on Fu, and on Yu, and at last on the old man Yongzheng in his retreat cell — Yichu Wuyuan — who became his master and gave him the name Tui'an. He died in 1677.

links.label: DILA Authority A010711 (his teacher 一初悟元)

masters.notes: Linji master, styled Banshui, of the Yu family of Ba county (Chongqing), abbot of Sanfeng there. He was the dharma heir of Dahou Yinchuan, himself a disciple of Poshan Haiming. He died on the second day of the seventh month of 1691.

links.label: DILA Authority A026228 (his teacher 大吼印傳)

masters.notes: Linji master of the early Yuan, of the Wang family of Changxi in Fuzhou; his grandfather Yikui was county sheriff of Gutian and his father Liangfu magistrate of Huangyan. At seven he loved to read Buddhist books, and his father, seeing he was no ordinary child, had him leave home at Xuefeng in the prefecture. Six months later he went out over the Feiyuan ridge to Fazang at Yixing, and was ordained by Chan master Yifeng Qi; at fifteen he took the head-shaving and the full precepts, and travelled to all quarters. Passing Ayuwang he called on Chan master Jichuang Zhao, entered his room and matched him, and was made incense-attendant and then keeper of the library. He came out at Shouguo in Siming, moved to Kaishou, and afterwards was installed at Daochang in Huzhou, where he built the great Buddha hall and the Guanyin repository and had the canon copied. His fame reached the imperial court, which granted him a gold-brocade robe and the title Chan Master Fohai Xingkong. He died on the third day of the sixth month of 1301, aged sixty-three, having kept forty-eight summers and ordained more than two hundred and fifty disciples.

links.label: DILA Authority A009669 (his teacher 寂窗有照)

masters.notes: Dharma heir of Hanyue Fazang (1574–1635) of Sanfeng, thirty-fifth generation below Nanyue; abbot of Lingyan at Suzhou, and known as Jiqi ('the one who takes up the succession') and Tuiweng. He edited and prefaced his teacher's sixteen-juan record, having been charged with the task by Hanyue himself six months before his death — 'he put it into my unworthy hands to compile', he writes, adding that twenty-seven years later he still shrank from committing it to print. He was the chief figure of the Sanfeng branch after Hanyue, defending it through the Wudeng yantong controversy, and a great teacher of nuns: the Jiaxing catalogue records at least three abbesses as his heirs (寶持玄總, 靈瑞祖揆玄符, and others). He was born on the eighth of the second month of 1605 and died on the twenty-seventh of the ninth month of 1672, aged 67.

Linji master, dharma heir of Songyuan Chongyue (who as abbot of Lingyin is also styled Lingyin Chongyue). In 1201 he answered the call to Yunju on Mount Lu, and shortly afterwards was appointed by edict to Jinshan. He compiled his master's record of sayings in two fascicles.

From Tongchuan in western Shu (surname Zhang, mother Liu), born at noon on the 22nd of the 6th month of 1610. Tonsured at five at Qinglian monastery after an illness, he saw lights on Emei at seven and carried the doubt from then on; at twenty-one, in 1630 at Bao'en in Jinling, the blaze of the pagoda's light broke it open. He met Linye Tongqi in 1643 and received his charge in 1644. He held Xianglin at Taicang, Caoxi at Pinghu, and Qianfo and Yuanning in the capital. He died in the small hours of the 23rd of the 11th month of 1666, aged 57, and was interred west of the Xianglin hall; sixteen heirs, of whom Shipu Chaozhi succeeded him.

Linji master and the Qing restorer of Lingyin monastery at Hangzhou. His disciple Jiexian's account of conduct opens: 'the master's name was Hongli, his style Jude; he was born of the Zhang family of Kuaiji — a great clan of Yuezhou, descended from Shu, truly the posterity of Master Ziyan.' He was tonsured at the Baohua hermitage on Putuo by Zhongya, and became the dharma heir of Hanyue Fazang. He rebuilt Lingyin — the greatest of the five mountains of Zhejiang — and Wu Weiye's stupa inscription for him is titled 'for the great venerable Jude who rebuilt Lingyin'. He died on the nineteenth day of the tenth month of 1667, aged sixty-eight.

Linji master of the Song, lay surname Yao. He left home at nineteen and worked hard at the Tiantai teaching, but felt he could not efface his own traces, and so went round the noted teachers seeking the Chan dharma; coming at last to Longmen he awakened outright, presented a verse to Foyan Qingyuan, and received his seal. He went to Lushan and sat without food inside a withered tree at Tong'an, to the wonder of all; before long he moved to Nanyue, where he would ride out on a tiger, so that Confucians and Buddhists alike bowed in his dust and the fourfold assembly called him the tiger-tamer. He ended as abbot on Mount Huanglong in Longxing, Jiangxi. He died in 1149, aged sixty-six.

Ming Linji master, dharma heir of Wanfeng Shiwei (1303–1381) and second abbot of Sheng'en monastery on Mount Dengwei at Suzhou, where he cast the great bell and built its tower in 1388. Dragons and elephants came out of his gate, and the age called him the Sheng'en Patriarch. After his death his stupa was raised beside Wanfeng's. His surname is not recorded, and his record of sayings and his stupa inscription are both lost.

Caodong master and abbot of Shaolin, of the Huang family (one account says Wang), from Jinxian in Jiangxi. As a boy he was moved by watching a play, and went off to Funiushan to be tonsured by Tanran Ping; he later went south to Wansong at Jingshan, knocked at the door of Dafang Lian, and studied under Xiaoshan Zongshu, whose heir he became. In the autumn of 1574 he took charge of the Shaolin cloister. He died on the twenty-seventh day of the fourth month of 1585. He is the dharma-brother of Yunkong (Linshan) Changzhong, through whom the roster's own Wuming Huijing branch descends — the two trunks confirm each other.

Song Linji master of Gushan at Fuzhou, a son of the Wu family of Min county. He took the robe in his twentieth year, and hearing that there was a transmission outside the teachings went to Lan'an Dingxu at Yunmen, whose heir he became — eighteenth generation below Dajian. He lived first at Qianyuan, moved to Huangbo, and afterwards held Gushan at Fuzhou. He left a fascicle of essential sayings. His dharma heirs were Jingci Wuming and Yi'an Fajian. He died in 1173.
Fourth Patriarch. First to establish a settled monastic community for Chan practice at Mount Shuangfeng.
Championed Huineng as true Sixth Patriarch against the Northern school. His polemical efforts established Southern school dominance.

Established the first independent Chan monastic code (百丈清規), revolutionizing Chan communal life. Famous for 'a day without work is a day without food' (一日不作一日不食). Subject of the wild fox koan. His monastic regulations became the model for all later Chan/Zen monasteries.
Appears in several encounter dialogues including a well-known exchange with Nanquan.
One of the greatest Tang poets and devoted lay Buddhist. Famous exchange with Bird's Nest Daolin.

Silla monk who traveled to Tang China and received dharma transmission from Xitang Zhizang (Mazu lineage). Returned to found the Dongni-san school, one of the Nine Mountain Schools. Teacher of Doseon.
Co-founder of the Guiyang school. Known for circular figures in teaching.
Awakened by sound of a pebble striking bamboo after burning his notes.
Called out to himself daily 'Master! Be alert! Don't be deceived!'
Heir of Xuefeng Yicun with five dharma successors. Best known for the 'voice of the raindrops' exchange, preserved as Book of Serenity case 46. Also appears in Blue Cliff Record cases 16, 23, and 46.

Third patriarch of the Fayan school and author of the Zongjing Lu (宗鏡錄, Record of the Mirror of the School) in 100 fascicles, one of the most comprehensive Chan works ever composed. Student of Tiantai Deshao. Served as abbot of Yongming Monastery in Hangzhou.
Yunmen school master at Kaixian Temple on Mount Lushan. Teacher of Foyin Liaoyuan.
Fellow student of Yuanwu Keqin under Wuzu Fayan. His sub-lineage led to Wumen Huikai.

Born in Anchang, Sichuan. Dharma brother of Hongzhi Zhengjue under Danxia Zichun. Key figure in the Caodong revival during the Southern Song. Abbot of Changlu and Tiantong monasteries. His emphasis on silent illumination (mozhao) drew Dahui Zonggao's famous critiques. 10th patriarch of the Caodong lineage; his line leads through Tiantong Zongjue to Tiantong Rujing and eventually to Dogen, founder of Japanese Soto Zen.
Caodong master at Mount Xuedou. Teacher of Tiantong Rujing.

Influential Caodong master active during the late Jin dynasty and early Mongol period. Compiler of the Book of Serenity (從容錄, Congrong Lu, 1224), his prose commentary on Hongzhi Zhengjue's 100 verse-comments on old cases, composed at the urging of his lay disciple Yelü Chucai. Self-styled 'Old Man of Ten Thousand Pines' (萬松老人). Abbot of Bao'en Temple in Yanjing from 1197 until his death. His lineage became the dominant Chinese Caodong transmission through his disciple Xueting Fuyu at Shaolin.
10th National Teacher of Suseonsa. Bridges into the 14th century.

The most important institutional figure in Korean Seon history, credited with unifying the Nine Mountains Seon schools into a single Jogye Order. He traveled to Yuan China and received dharma transmission from the hermit-poet Shiwu Qinggong (Stone House) on Tianmu mountain, returning with Shiwu's robe (cassock) and staff as physical proof of transmission. As Royal Teacher (wangsa) under King Gongmin, he reorganized Korean Seon, ending centuries of fragmentation among rival mountain schools. His unification established the institutional framework that persists in Korean Buddhism today. Though Ahn (2019) has questioned the later Joseon-era lineage claims connecting Hyujeong back through Taego, Taego's own Chinese transmission is well documented. Attested in UNDV 2011 conference paper: confirms the Shiwu transmission with physical evidence including the cassock and cane still preserved.
Shaolin Monastery abbot (1557-1566). Sent warrior monks against Japanese pirates. Key bridge figure connecting Yuan-era Shaolin Caodong to the late Ming revival.
68th Caodong patriarch. Founded the Shouchang sublineage. Revived work-ethic monastic practice. Promoted Dahui's kanhua Chan within Caodong.
Brought Shouchang Caodong to Fujian. Restored Gushan Yongquan Monastery (1634). Over 100 volumes of writings. Called 'the last successful Caodong Chan master.'
Chan teacher of the Yongzheng Emperor before his enthronement. Died on Mount Lu; the emperor issued a special edict honoring his death.
Transmission link in the Pyeonyang lineage. The 71st Korean patriarch. No independent biographical sources survive. Known only from Joseon-era lineage charts.

Dharma heir of Wuzhun Shifan representing a second major branch of the Wuzhun lineage, distinct from the Xueyan Zuqin branch that produced Gaofeng and Zhongfeng. Through his student Gulin Qingmao, he produced a major branch of the Yuan-period Linji transmission.

First Hongzhou school master to teach in the Tang capital Chang'an. Won an imperial debate in 796 at the Linde Hall, expelling Northern Chan rivals and opening the capital to the southern school. Taught Emperors Dezong and Shunzong. Author of the Zuochan ming (Inscription on Sitting Meditation). Born in Quzhou (Zhejiang), surname Xu, reportedly of Korean ancestry. Posthumous title: Huijue Dashi.

Of the Yao clan of Cixi, Siming — a leading family. He worked at Confucian studies from nine and was writing well at thirteen. At eighteen an illness taught him the body is a cangue, and he began testing himself against Dahui's recorded sayings; the phrase about Mt. Sumeru gave him his first opening. He then went round Yunmen, Zhenji, Longmen, Li'an and Yufeng as a LAYMAN, and at Jinsu took a beating from Miyun Yuanwu, who named him Sheng. Only in 1644, when the dynasty fell and his mother died, did he shave his head; he then climbed Jingshan to Feiyin Tongrong, who 'undid the jewel in his topknot and gave it to him.' He was installed at Xianjing (1655), Housheng at Hou-shan (1657), and finally at West Lake. He died at the hour of wei on the 6th of the 5th month of 1668, aged 70, with 24 years in robes; his disciples built his stupa on the north face of Leifeng. Four dharma heirs and one nun.

A NUN. Chief disciple of the nun-master Qiyuan Xinggang at the Fushi (Crouching Lion) convent in Jiaxing, and named among her dharma heirs in the account of her death. Qiyuan was a Jiaxing woman of the Hu clan, widowed young, who kept her chastity, left her household for the dharma, and drew a following 'like clouds'; both women left recorded sayings. Yikui Chaochen succeeded her at Fushi — a nun-to-nun transmission, which is what makes her worth the chart.

Of the Liu clan of Lianjiang, Fuzhou. At thirteen he took instruction from Yuexi; later he went to Huyan Jingfu at Lingyin, who gave him the dog-and-buddha-nature word to work on. In time he presented a verse and Huyan nodded, made him incense-attendant and then keeper of the canon, and his name spread. He taught at Biyun in Changzhou (1295), Dianshan in Songjiang, Nanchan in Tongzhou, Heshan in Huzhou (1322), Daochang (1329), and in 1333 took the abbacy of Ayuwang in Siming as its 58th master. The imperial preceptor gave him a gold-bordered robe and the title Buddha-Mind Universal Mirror. In the Zhizheng era he was ordered to hold the great Water-and-Land rite at Jinshan and to ascend the seat. In old age he lived in a hermitage he called Pine-and-Moon, and styled himself the Old Man of Pine and Moon. He wrote his verse and went; the relics from his cremation were past counting.

Caodong master, dharma heir of Mianshi Jingyun of Huguo monastery on Mt. Tiantai — himself an heir of Ruibai Mingxue. He had earlier sat with Miyun Yuanwu at Tiantong and with Ermi at Dongshan. One night, sparring with Ermi, the master called for his attendant, who fumbled the lamp and put it out. 'And the fire?' snapped Ermi. 'It's right here,' said the attendant — and Zhijing suddenly saw the point. He held Jiezhu monastery at Jishan, Yuzhi hermitage at Wujiang, and Luohan monastery at Lichuan. His recorded sayings run to six fascicles.

Of the Li clan of Luzhou; his mother was a Zhao. He was born at noon on the 10th of the 6th month of 1598 — the night before, his father saw the room fill with sunlight. His father died when he was one. At seven, seeing a shadow move at the window, he was seized with the question of where a man's shadow goes when he dies, and brooded for a fortnight until his mother scolded him for going soft in the head. He left home at fifteen, went the round of the lecture-halls at twenty-five, and at thirty-five came to Poshan Haiming at Shuanggui — 'I am gnawed by birth and death; instruct me.' Poshan: 'You are a lecturer. The sutras are full of expedients — do you need mine?' He worked seven months, went blind from sleeplessness, was told by Xiangya to go to bed, and woke at the sound of the wooden board with a boulder rolled off him. He served Poshan ten years as prior before being sealed, and held Yunfeng at Fangshan, Panlong at Jiang'an and Kaiyuan at Nanxi. Died 1669, aged 72, with 37 years in robes; six dharma heirs.

names: 佛海普印廣慈圓悟大禪師
masters.notes: Of the Huang clan of Duchang, Nankang (Jiangxi), born on the first of the 10th month of 1275. At nine he wanted to leave home and his mother refused; he went days without eating until the relatives talked her round, and he was placed with Yushan Zhen at Yunju — his master for life. Tonsured at eleven or twelve and fully ordained, he travelled: two summers at Jiangshan, then Tianxi, where he heard the Lotus expounded and grasped it at once, and the lecturer called him 'a man come back'. In Wu he met Tieshan Qiong and Mengshan Deyi; Mengshan asked where he was from, then 'did you come by boat or by land?' — 'Neither road,' he said. Mengshan spread both hands; he stared straight at him — and they lived together at Xiuxiu hermitage. He later served as prior under Huyan Jingfu at Jingshan, and became abbot of Jiangshan in Nanjing, where the Prince of Liang's dealings with him over the monastery's rebuilding after the fire won him the title Great Chan Master Fohai Puyin Guangci Yuanwu. He died aged 74 (1348), with 56 years in robes; his disciples laid him in the Immovable Stupa at Longpan hermitage, and Jingshan divided the relics to a second stupa below Lingxiao peak.

Of the Yu clan of Hezhou, Chongqing; his mother was a Xun. Born on the 7th of the 8th month of 1610. At eight his father took him to Taikong at Madangshan in his home county and left him there. In 1635 he left Sichuan, called first on Sheng of Tiantong, and then went to old master Lin of Tongxuan — Linye Tongqi — and 'penetrated the deep principle utterly, and so received the dharma as his true heir.' That same year he made a hut on Huading in Tiantai, and afterwards held Guanghua, Luohan (1648), Ciji (1649), Fahai (1650), Yuelin (1651), Longyuan (1654) and Furong at Jingxi (1656). In the third month of 1661 he sickened; on the 27th of the twelfth he bathed, settled the affairs of the house, wrote instructions for the community charging his monks to forget the body and spread the dharma, then wrote his verse, threw down the brush — 'even this smells of the world' — and died. Thirty-three dharma heirs; aged 53, 34 years in robes.

Of the Zeng clan of Luzhou. Dharma heir of Erdu Daotai. He held Guanyin cloister at Xianren-shan in Linshui, Taiping monastery on Mt. Wanfeng in Dazhu, Xinglong in Wanxian, and Huiling at Shehong. His recorded sayings run to two fascicles; his heirs were Tianran and Shuiying. He also tonsured Chunbei Guangde, another master in this batch.

Of the Yang clan of Xingan, Linjiang. Born on the 20th of the 12th month of 1246 (early 1247). A son of a Pure Land household, he sang hymns with his mother as soon as he could speak; he entered Xiangshi cloister at Jianxing monastery at seven and was tonsured at nineteen under a Xianchun edict. He studied first with the monk Zhining, then went to XUEYAN ZUQIN and got the dharma from him, holding the first seat in the Assembled Clouds hall. In 1280 he attended Xueyan to the imperial audience and was given a robe. He held Muping ten years and Huili nineteen; in 1296 he was granted the title Great Chan Master Puzhao, with a gold-bordered kasaya, and Goryeo sent him robes, a gold-lettered sutra and jade. Monks came from Yunnan in the far west to Liao in the east; when the gruel ran short he would pawn things rather than stop teaching. In 1309 the Bureau of Buddhist Affairs installed him at Jianfu in Rao. He died sitting, having bathed, on the 16th of the 6th month of 1312, aged 67, with 48 years in robes.

Of the Wang clan of Xichong, Shunqing (Sichuan). His father, childless in middle age, prayed for two sons — one for the ancestors, one for the Buddha — and got them; his mother dreamed of a monk in a patched robe asking a night's lodging, and on the day of the birth three old monks came to the house and said, 'Your noble son is born just as the sun rises in the east — call him Hongxian (Rising Splendour).' Sent at eight to Shoufan at Guifeng cloister, he would only sit cross-legged and would not study, and people called him 'the daft monk'. He set out at sixteen, buried his teacher and then his mother, and went the whole round: Cao'an Wutai at Tongchuan, Hanpu, full ordination at Minzhong monastery in Shenyang (1650), then Ruo'an at Jiashan, Qi at Xuedou, Lin at Bao'en. Under Jue at Lingyin, working on 'hidden deep in the valley, unashamed before the order of monks', on the third day at midnight he suddenly heard music from Feilai Peak — and the whole knot in his chest fell away. He then went to Jiahe, met Zixian Jue, and received the entrustment. He held Guangsheng at Mt. Huo, the Lion, Prince and Lingyan cloisters at Fenyang, Qianming at Linfen and Puji at Daxie.

Of the Li clan of Fengdu in eastern Shu. Orphaned of both parents at six. Tonsured in middle life under Huanzhu Ming, he took full ordination under Erdu Daotai and inherited his dharma. He carried the line into Chu (Hubei), where he founded and rebuilt: Yuexia cloister at Huangling in Yiling (1665), and Dabei monastery on Mt. Foxing at Zigui. His stele says those who came to take refuge with him were 'not fewer than 1,250' — the number of the Buddha's own assembly. His heirs were Yuechuang Zhishen, Fachuang Zhiyuan and Juechuang Zhihong.

Of the Ge clan of Ninghai, Taizhou. He went to Wuzhun Shifan and got the point. He held Xingsheng at Liuhong in Jiaxing, Nengren at Mt. Yan in Wenzhou, Huiyun at Jiuyan in Yue, Guang'en at Huguo on Tiantai, Yanfu at Chong'en in Lin'an, and Longxiang at Jiangxin in Wenzhou. In 1272 he took Xuefeng, held it ten years, then resigned and retired to Baoshou monastery in Hangzhou. He died in 1290, aged 85. His disciple Miao'en gathered his essentials into the Jue'an Kexiang chanshi yulu.

Of the Mao clan of Jiangjin, Chongqing; his mother was a Tao, who conceived after dreaming a monk gave her a peach to eat, and they called him Yingseng ('answering the monk'). Born at the hour of wei on the 20th of the 7th month of 1614. At sixteen the Diamond Sutra raised his doubt; he went with his mother to Baoding and a monk told him he was too young — go recite the Buddha's name. He read on, dreamed strangely, and the doubt ate into him: 'Far from all inverted dream-thinking — then where does THIS dream come from?' He was tonsured after an illness, went to Poxue at Chongqing, then to Guiyuan, who set him on 'the ten thousand dharmas return to one — where does the one return to?' Three years he was wood and stone, walking without knowing he walked. At the fourth watch one night mind and object both fell away. He came to Zhangxue Tongzui in the winter of 1649 and was sealed. In 1653 he opened Shibao cloister in Yunnan, and later Jingyin, Nanming, Longquan and Yuquan in Guizhou. The Yongli emperor of the Southern Ming sought his teaching, asked him for a verse, gave him the dharma name Zhenfo ('True Buddha') and a robe. He died on the 22nd of the last month of winter, 1666/7, aged 53, with 37 years in robes.

Dharma heir of Jie'an Wujin at Jinming monastery in Jiaxing, and abbot of Santa (Three Pagodas) in the same prefecture. Of Huizhou, a descendant of the Duke of Mu, and a serving officer before he took the robe. He died in 1669. Only the first character of his dharma name, 法, survives.

Of the Lu clan of Hengxi, Yinxian; born on the 10th of the 6th month of 1201. He was tonsured and ordained under Beihai Xin at Daochang-shan in Zha. He first went to Wuzhun Shifan at Ayuwang, who made him keeper of the inner records — he would not take it, and left to follow Shitian at Jingci. He then studied under BEIJIAN JUJIAN at Jingci and got the point, and was put in charge of the writings. He held Faxiang in Hangzhou, Xianci, Xiangtian Xingjiao, Zhimen, Jiaozhong Baoguo, and in 1263 became the 46th abbot of Ayuwang in Mingzhou. He died on the 17th of the 6th month of 1268, aged 68. A noted literary monk of the late Southern Song; his 物初賸語 runs to 25 fascicles. His dharma heir was Huiji Yuanxi — also in this batch.

A Sichuanese; dharma heir of Zhuanyu Guanheng. He held Baolian monastery on Mt. Yue in Fengxin (1651), Xiaseng monastery on Mt. Longmen in Jing'an (1653), Tong'an monastery on Mt. Fengqi in Jianchang, Nankang — which he opened in the winter of 1662 and which was rebuilt splendidly under him — then Qinghua monastery in the south city of Beijing (1672). In 1674 he lodged at Tianning in Jiaxing to cut the blocks of his teacher's recorded sayings, and in 1676 took Lengyan monastery. Twelve fascicles of his recorded sayings survive, plus two from Lengyan.

Of the Shi clan of Fuling in eastern Shu. Tonsured as a boy by the elder Jichu, he studied the Mahayana sutras and treatises under the dharma-master Boshui. Having met Xiangya and learned that there was such a thing as this matter, he saw that the words of the teachings were not the last word, and went up to Dongshan at Sinan in Qianzhong to Yingxiu Wu, to knock directly at the Linji doctrine. He vowed not to sleep; sitting in the still of the night, it was as if someone clapped a hand, and the sweat ran off him. Later he challenged the master in the hall — 'Above, no buddhahood to attain; below, no beings to save: whose realm is that? Say it plainly.' Yingxiu: 'Seen from high, not enough; levelled from low, more than enough.' 'A thousand differences,' said Xingjiong, 'and not one outside this.' 'Do not misidentify it.' He shouted. 'And where does THAT shout land?' 'It stands right here in the open.' 'So it is YOU,' said Yingxiu, 'who has said it plainly.' He served as rector under Yingxiu at Longshan in Chenzhou, and Yingxiu handed him the true line of Caoxi. He held Puti at Lizhou, Taihe at Yuanzhou, and finally rebuilt Pufeng in Chenzhou — founded in the Song and ruined by war — bringing it back in under three years. He died in 1668 and was interred to the left of Pufeng.

links.label: DILA Authority A026271 (his teacher 真悟)

masters.notes: A LAYMAN of Wushang, born on the 8th of the 5th month of 497. He married Liu Miaoguang at sixteen and had two sons, Pujian and Pucheng. At twenty-four the ascetic Songtoutuo woke him up; he built a hut under the twin trees at Songshan, practised austerities seven years, and penetrated the Surangama. In 535 he was commanded to expound the sutra in the Chongyun Hall of Emperor Wu of Liang. As the Liang fell to the Chen and war spread he gathered a great following and had his disciples burn fingers and arms in offering. He wrote the Xinwang ming and the Huanyuan shi. With Baozhi of Jinling he is called one of the Two Great Beings of the Liang. He died on the 24th of the 4th month of 569.

A Ming jinshi who refused to serve the Qing and took the robe instead. He was an old acquaintance of Kong Youde, the Qing Prince Dingnan, who — the Xinxu gaoseng zhuan says — thought highly of his integrity and issued the order for a monastery to be built for him on Mount Qi above Hengyang. That was Renrui monastery, which he founded and where he lived out his life; it held over a thousand mu of temple land. He was a Caodong master. His recorded sayings survive only as quotations in others' collections. His heir was Wenmu Nian, who received the dharma from him in 1658.

Of the Tang clan of Yuzhang (Nanchang); born 1238. He was tonsured by Ming of Mingjue cloister at Xishan. Hearing that Wuchu Daguan was teaching at Yuji he went and attached himself to him, staying at his side; afterwards he called on Dongsou Ying at Nanping, who made him recorder. In 1296 he came out at Baizhang and stayed twelve years; in the Zhida era he moved to Jingci for seven, then to Jingshan as its 46th abbot, and in old age to Yangshan. He bore the title Chan Master Fozhi. He died on the 17th of the intercalary 8th month of 1319, aged 82, and was interred at Xiyin at Jingci. His heirs included Xiaoyin Daxin, Meiwu Nianchang and Shishi Zuying.

Of Jingjiang; abbot of Tianning monastery in Yangzhou. The county gazetteer says he was born strange-minded: at ten he told his father he wanted to be a monk and was refused; married at seventeen, he shared a room with his wife for three years without ever undressing; at twenty he cut his hair for good. He entered Chongsheng in his own county, found the monks there worth nothing, and went on to Guangxiao in Hangzhou. He became the FIRST of the dharma heirs of Jude Hongli, the great restorer of Lingyin and Jingshan. He taught women as well as men: the nun Shangrong of Nianhua hermitage in Jiangdu and the nun Qilian of Guidi hermitage in Suzhou both came to him at Tianning and were sealed by him. He died on the 27th of the first month of 1666, aged 62. His teacher outlived him and came back to Tianning to close his stupa.

Of the Gong clan of Jianyang. Sharp from the start and never able to stomach meat. At seventeen he heard the Surangama and was moved, and took the robe at Zhiti. At twenty-six he went with Zhangren about Fengshan, Luoshan and Xuansha for two years, and knowing there was a matter under his own feet, crossed into Zhejiang and spent years with Zhenji. Then he came to Wuyi Yuanlai at Boshan, and at Shao hermitage, hearing a cock beat its wings and crow, he broke through at a stroke. He opened the dharma at Yingshan in 1646 and afterwards held Boshan itself, Gaoquan and Puning. He died on the 20th of the 6th month of 1670, aged 79, with 62 years in robes. His heirs included Suru Honghan, Zhizhi Hongnan, Yuanzuo Hongyu and Yisheng Hongxi.

Of the Xu clan of Yinxian, Mingzhou; born 1226. At thirteen he was tonsured and took the precepts under Beijian Jujian; at fourteen he climbed Jingshan and saw WUZHUN SHIFAN. At seventeen he took up the dog-and-buddha-nature word and did not leave the monks' hall for five years, until one night the sounding-board rang outside the head-seat's quarters and he saw his own matter. He afterwards went round Shixi Yue, Yanxi Wen, Xutang Zhiyu and Wuchu Daguan. In 1269 he opened the dharma at Zhenru monastery in Taizhou. In 1279, as the Mongols overran the south, the Japanese regent Hojo Tokimune invited him to head Kencho-ji in Kamakura; he went, and in 1282 founded Engaku-ji. He was Tokimune's spiritual adviser through the Mongol invasions. He died in Japan on the 3rd of the 9th month of 1286, aged 61, with 49 years in robes, and was posthumously titled National Teacher Bukko.

Of the Xie clan of Yongquan, Xingguo (Hubei); born on the 12th of the 10th month of 1626. In 1645, aged twenty, unwilling to stay a householder, he shaved his head at Bao'en monastery and went north among the lecture-halls. In 1650 he came south again over the matter of birth and death, and one day after the meal, looking into his original face, he split it open at a stroke: 'The face is wholly shown, it was never covered up — how many times did I fold my hands and ask in the hall? What I see now is not another's seeing; a lifetime's ease, and the bones gone cool.' He went to Feiyin Tongrong at Jingshan, who shouted him down and named and ordained him; he called on Yulin Tongxiu, Wanru Tongwei and Muchen Daomin; and then he came to DUGUAN XINGJING at Wuxing, who sealed him. From 1658 he opened Tiefo at Jing, restored Tianwang (1661), took Dizang at Yangzhou (1662), Tianwang again (1665), rebuilt Huanglong at Ezhou (1668), went to Qixian at Hanyang (1670), and took Guanghui at Jinsu (1676). Five seats, four of them rebuilt from ruin. He died in 1687; eleven dharma heirs.

Ming Chan master; dharma heir of Motang Xuan. His pupil Fazhou Daoji of Tianning in Jiaxing — who came to him from Dongchan, attended him morning and night, and was awakened by the sound of a chime ringing out from the Buddha-hall as he walked in the cloister, whereupon Ji'an sealed him — carried the line on. Only the single dharma character 祚 survives of his name.

Of the Li clan of Yibin (Bodao); his father and grandfather had been Brahmins for three generations. Eight monks are said to have come to the house at his birth, one of them saying the child was an arhat of the Eight Treasures come back. He was a Confucian first and a Buddhist after. He attended Yueming Lianchi at Zhaoyang for years and was tonsured and fully ordained under him in 1613; then he left for a solitary mountain and worked three years without letting his side touch the mat. Returning at the end of his term, he asked the old master, 'After all — how does it show itself?' — and Yueming reached out and clapped a hand over his mouth, and he opened wide. He crossed to Wu, into Fujian, through Guangdong, opened the dharma at Xiaoxiang Hudong, and came back to Shu to teach at Juyun in Zhongzhou, where he revived the Juyun branch of Linji in Sichuan and preached the unity of the three teachings. He wrote in plain language on purpose — his Three-Character Classic of Buddhism apes the Confucian primer to teach Buddhist history and the eight schools. Thirty years out in the world, five seats. On the last day of the 7th month of 1639 he took the brush and wrote: 'Beaten three thousand at dawn, eight hundred at dusk — to see Juyun, blood from the eyebrows.' He sat until noon, gave two great shouts, and died, aged 58.

A master of the line running from Dahui Zonggao down to the Juyun branch in Sichuan. He inherited from Jingci Ming, and his own heir was Fadu Ci. Only the single dharma character 益 survives of his name; nothing else about his life is recorded.
Founder of the Niutou (Oxhead) school. Studied under the Fourth Patriarch Daoxin but developed a distinct teaching emphasizing emptiness.

Korean prince of the Silla royal house who became one of the most influential Chan teachers in eighth-century Sichuan. Ordained under Zizhou Chuji (a disciple of Zhishen in the Hongren/East Mountain line), he built a massive congregation in Chengdu around his 'three phrases' (wunian, moyi, mowang) teaching of no-thought, no-recollection, and no-delusion. His liturgical innovations blending Chan with Vinaya confession rites shaped a distinct Sichuan Chan tradition. Buswell (1989) argues he was an early formative influence on the young Mazu Daoyi before Mazu's move east. His legacy was continued by Baotang Wuzhu, though the Baotang school radicalized his teachings. Attested in Lidai fabao ji (c. 774) and Zutangji (952): both record his teaching career in Sichuan, his royal Silla origins, and his three-phrase doctrine.
One of Mazu's three great disciples alongside Baizhang and Nanquan.
Fourth generation Heze lineage. Teacher of Guifeng Zongmi.

Teacher of Linji and one of the most important Tang Chan masters. Born in Fuzhou, Fujian. Teaching centered on 'one mind' (一心): all beings possess this one mind which is the Buddha. His teachings recorded by lay student Pei Xiu in the Chuanxin Fayao (傳心法要) and Wanling Lu (宛陵錄). Named thirteen successors.
Originally a Diamond Sutra scholar. Famous for 'Thirty blows whether you can speak or not.'
Let out a great shout at moment of death during Huang Chao rebellion.
Initially Linji's student, later studied under Jiashan of the Shitou lineage.
Known for the 'bowl' koan.

Heir of Yangshan Huiji, taught at the South Pagoda (Nanta) on Mount Yangshan in Jiangxi. Transmitted the Guiyang lineage to Bajiao Huiqing, a Korean monk who traveled to China seeking instruction, keeping the school alive for one more generation.

From Mianzhu in Sichuan. Served as Yunmen Wenyan's attendant for eighteen years; Yunmen's only teaching method was to call his name and shout 'What is this?' Together with Mingjiao, he recorded Yunmen's sayings in writing. Later transmitted the lineage to Zhimen Guangzuo. Appears in Blue Cliff Record case 17.
Received Linji transmission from Shexian Guisheng. Accepted Dayang Jingxuan’s Caodong materials and passed them to Touzi Yiqing, saving the Caodong school from extinction.
Huanglong branch master. Enlightened by a thunderclap after working on Huitang’s fist koan. Teacher of Kongshi Daoren.
Yangqi branch master. Link between Kaifu Daoning and Laona Zuzheng in the chain to Wumen Huikai.

Female Chan practitioner born into a scholar's family; her father refused to let her ordain, so she practiced as a laywoman under the name Kongshi ('Empty Room'). She attained deep awakening under Sixin Wuxin of the Huanglong branch; contemporaries Yuanwu Keqin and Foyan Qingyuan praised her realization. She opened a bathhouse near her teacher's monastery with the inscription: 'Nothing exists, not even dirt, so what are you bathing?'
One of the most eminent Southern Song Chan masters. Dharma heir of Po'an Zuxian. His portrait, held in Japan, is designated a national treasure.

Yuan dynasty Linji master, dharma heir of Xueyan Zuqin and dharma brother of Gaofeng Yuanmiao. Teacher of both Shiwu Qinggong and Pingshan Chulin, making him the indirect ancestor of all late-Goryeo Korean Seon. Active at Xifeng Temple (Jianyang) and Daochang Mountain Wanshou Temple (Huzhou). Attested in DILA Authority Database (A021593).
Convergence point where Taego and Naong lineages merge. Also studied under Naong. Critical link to Hyujeong's lineage, though Ahn (2019) notes this chain is a 17th-century construction.
Produced the two greatest 16th-century Seon teachers: Hyujeong (Seosan) and Buhyu Seonsu. Korean Seon traces through him.
One of the 'four great monks'. Prolific writer, exiled to Guangdong. His autobiography is a classic.
Founded the Caodong Tianjie lineage at Nanjing. Ming loyalist. Innovative synthesis of Chan and Confucian traditions.

Major 18th-century figure. Authored Seonmun ojonggangyo (Essentials of the Five Schools of Seon), which systematized Korean Seon doctrine. Was exiled after a controversy. The Jogye Order's kanhwa Seon tradition traces through him.

Transmission link in the Pyeonyang lineage. The 72nd Korean patriarch. According to Han Yongun's 'Brief Chronology,' Gyeongheo 'personally received the dharma inheritance from Yongam Seunim,' suggesting Yongam was still alive when Gyeongheo began his training, though the direct teacher-student relationship was with Manhwa Boseon.

Northern Song Yunmen master who maintained the lineage between Xuedou Chongxian and the school's late Northern Song figures. His role was crucial in keeping the Yunmen transmission alive during a period when the Linji school was rapidly becoming dominant. He transmitted the Yunmen dharma to Cishou Huaishen.

Dharma heir of Baizhang Huaihai and dharma brother of Guishan Lingyou. Nicknamed 'Lazy An' (懶安) for his unhurried manner. After Guishan Lingyou's death in 853, was invited to assume the abbacy at Mt. Gui. Famous for the 'water buffalo' metaphor: 'I am like a water buffalo — if someone calls me a water buffalo, I am a water buffalo.' Teacher of Dasui Fazhen.

Of Quxian in Shunqing, western Shu; his father was a Li (李), his mother a He (何). He was sent as a boy to Shuiyue hermitage in his own village and ordained under Liudu; he took full precepts at twenty. Hearing the Lotus line 'whether sitting or walking, banish sleep and always collect the mind', he had an opening. He was beaten out of the hall by Sheme Shepu, then went to Mt. Huangbo and put a question to Xiangya Xingting, who told him he deserved thirty blows — at which his doubt fell away. He served Xingting six years and received the transmission. He lived through the sack of Sichuan by Zhang Xianzhong's armies, and taught on regardless. He held Sansheng, Wudeng, Yungui in Guizhou, Qingliang and Changshou at Anshun, and Zhonghe at Yongning. Going down to Chu, he stopped three years at Chongfu on the Zi river, then in the spring of 1664 entered the derelict Xifeng monastery and rebuilt it entire in ten years; he also moved his master Xingting's stupa to Youyang and reburied it behind the monastery. He died on the twenty-ninth of the fifth month of 1673, aged 61, with 42 years in robes.

Of the Zhou (周) family of Longxi in Fujian; his mother was a Weng. He would not eat meat as a child. A monk brought a copy of Feiyin Tongrong's recorded sayings to his study and he read it as if it were treasure. He was tonsured by the aged Huitan of Jiuyun monastery at Jinpu, who set out to walk him to the mainland masters and died at an inn on the road; Xingguan wept and carried the body to its stupa. He then met Miyun Yuanwu at Tiantong, who drove a staff into his chest and called him a dead man, and took his full precepts that winter. In 1634 he followed Feiyin Tongrong to Jinsu, sat night after night on the dharma-hall steps, and one night in a thunderstorm the word 'no' fell away and mountains, rivers and earth froze into one piece. Feiyin later approved him, made him head monk, told him 'your verses on the old cases are much like Baiyun Duan's — you are a phoenix feather of the Jinsu gate', and sent him to the old temple site below Mt. Xiangfeng. He founded Xiangfeng (Zifu) there in 1644 out of nothing, and later held Fuyan. He refused to let his words be published — the sayings that survive were gathered by his students after his death. He died on 8 November 1681, aged 66, with 49 years in robes.

Of Ninghai in Taizhou, a descendant of the Song chancellor Ye Mengding; a dharma heir of Zhuyuan Miaodao (1257-1345). He was abbot of Zituo (Guangdu monastery on Mt. Zituo, Taizhou), of Yanqing in Qingyuan, and of Tiantong. He and Shuzhong Wuyun (恕中無慍, 'Kongshi') were dharma-brothers under Zhuyuan and were spoken of together as the two great Yuan-dynasty masters out of Taizhou. His heir was Dai'an Puzhuang, sixtieth abbot of Jingshan. His dates are not recorded. His dharma name is written both 惟一 and 唯一.

Of the Chen (陳) family of Piling (Changzhou), born on the twenty-second of the first month of 1604. In the autumn of 1625 he entered Changsheng hermitage in Jingjiang county and took the robe from the Chan master Duzhi; a month later he went to Miyun Yuanwu at Jinsu and worked under him for seven years. In the spring of 1631 he went with Miyun to Ayuwang, and at the words 'the flesh of the self is not used up' he saw into his own matter. He held nine seats in all and swore never to hand the dharma on lightly to anyone. He died at Mt. Qingyun on the eighth of the tenth month of 1648, aged 45, with 23 years in robes and 16 years teaching; his stupa was raised at Xitang on Mt. Gonggong in Qianzhou.

Of the Feng (馮) family of Hejiang county, Luzhou, in southern Shu; a Confucian household. He first studied the doctrinal teachings, then said 'yellow leaves may quiet a crying child, but they mislead the infant who would leave the world', and set out to find a master. Passing Xinglong monastery in Wanxian he met Chuiwan Guangzhen (吹萬廣真) and was hammered by him; he followed Guangzhen to Juyun monastery in Zhongzhou and served as his attendant for years, not lying down to sleep. When Guangzhen died and TIEBI HUIJI took the seat, Dengbing served Tiebi as he had served Guangzhen, broke through under Tiebi's staff, and was sealed with a verse on the tenth of the sixth month of 1651. He held Xianglu monastery at Shisi, then was invited to Fancun in Zhongzhou, where in the middle of the wars he cleared the thorns himself and built the monastery he named Qingyun ('Auspicious Cloud'). He travelled ten thousand li to sweep Dahui's stupa at Shuangjing in Zhejiang, and came back grieving that its dharma-seat stood empty. He died on the eighteenth of the sixth month of 1680, aged 70, with 53 years in robes; his bones were buried inside his teacher's stupa on Gaofeng.

Of the Yuan (袁) family of Xianju in Taizhou, a Confucian household; born on the twelfth of the eighth month of 1347. At eight he entered the village school and could recite what he heard once; at twelve he asked to leave home and would not be dissuaded. An uncle who had become a monk took him to Ningbo, where Zuo'an Liang of Tiantong took him in; he was tonsured and took full precepts the following year. Serving Zuo'an brought him no opening, so he went to Tianning in the prefectural city, where LIAOTANG WEIYI was posing the 'broken sand-basin' case. Liaotang asked what he had come for; he said 'precisely because the matter of birth and death is urgent'; Liaotang told him to go and sit. One day Liaotang raised the cypress-tree-in-the-garden case, Puzhuang started to open his mouth, Liaotang slapped him across it — and he had his opening. In 1377 the throne ordered the monks of the empire to study the Heart, Lankavatara and Diamond sutras, and he was invited to lecture on them at Jinshan. He opened the hall at Beichan in Fuzhou in 1379 — and at that opening he burned the incense of gratitude for LIAOTANG. He rebuilt Yunju from ruins in five years. In 1393 he was summoned as one of the eminent monks of the realm, and that autumn was sent to Lushan to perform the imperial sacrifice; he was made sixtieth abbot of Jingshan. He died at Jingshan on the twenty-third of the tenth month of 1403, aged 58, with 45 years in robes.

Of Tongzhou; abbot of the Wuwei ('Fearless') hall at Guoqing monastery on Mt. Tiantai. He was a long-standing attendant of Sanfeng Fazang, and stood at Fazang's deathbed among the twenty-five who received his final words. The dharma he received, however, came from Fazang's heir TUIWENG HONGCHU (Jiqi Hongchu): Hongchu's own recorded sayings, the Nanyue Jiqi heshang yulu in ten fascicles, carry on EVERY volume the byline 'compiled by his dharma-heir disciple JIJI' (嗣法門人濟璣等編). His recorded sayings survive as the Xieyun Ji chanshi Guoqing Wuwei tang yulu.

Of the Lu (魯) family of Yuechi county, Shunqing prefecture, northern Sichuan; his mother was a Zhou. Born on the eighth of the twelfth month of 1633 (癸酉腊八, = January 1634). His father took him at four to read at Yashan monastery in the county, and he wept whenever he heard the monks chanting the Huayan. In 1642 the rebels overran the region; in 1643 both his parents died within days of each other at Hutou monastery; in 1644 he was carried off by the rebels and dragged through seven of their camps. In 1652 he heard that 'the Old Man' — Sanshan Denglai — had settled at Gaoliang in Zhongnan, and was brought to him by the garrison commander of Shibao and the layman Yuan Baoshan. Denglai received him gladly, tonsured him, and set him the huatou 'who is it that recites the Buddha's name?'. He served as attendant, deputy prior and then prior through nine monasteries. In 1663 he went with Denglai to found Gaofeng; when Denglai left for Tanhua, the building of Gaofeng was left in Xingchong's hands, and he finished it in 1666. Denglai named him among the heirs charged to go out and teach. He was abbot of Baoji monastery in Wanxian.

Of the Lin (林) family of Yueqing in Wenzhou; a dharma heir of Hengchuan Rugong, of the Songyuan branch of Yangqi Linji. He studied under Jianweng Jing of Xuedou in Mingzhou, Shilin Gong of Nanping and Jue'an Zhen of Chengtian. He was abbot of Baoning at Jinling (Nanjing) under the Yuan. His heirs included Liao'an Qingyu, Zhongmou Liangyou and the Japanese monks Jikusen Bonsen (竺仙梵僊) and Sekishitsu Zenkyu (石室善玖); Jikusen carried his line to Japan, where the Kurin (古林) school became one of the twenty-four schools of Japanese Zen. Born 1262, died 1329.

Of the Zhao (趙) family of Wujiang in Suzhou prefecture; his given name was originally Yu (庾). His forebears held office; his father died when he was a child and his uncle, a censor, raised him — and, being drawn to Buddhism himself, passed on to the boy whatever he found in the old lamp records. Xingtao passed the provincial examination young and took the jinshi in his prime, the leading man of his district. He served as magistrate of Ouning in Fujian and was being promoted when the dynasty fell; he shaved his head and hid at Wuyi. He went to Guoqing to find TUIWENG HONGCHU (called 大山儲 in the inscription) and missed him twice. He then took the robe from Baoen Xian (浮石通賢) at Wujiang, trained under him for two years without opening, and broke through at a winter retreat at Haimen; Xian approved him and he took the full precepts. When Hongchu returned to Lingyan, Xingtao carried incense to him and questioned him closely; under Hongchu's answers on Linji's three kinds of student he saw clear through, offered a verse, and HONGCHU SEALED HIM WITH A VERSE OF HIS OWN. Hongchu then said: 'You are a man of Wu; you came to the way by way of office. Guoqing is my old house — Hanshan, Shide and Fenggan left their traces there. I hand it to you.' He entered Guoqing in the autumn of 1650. He died on the twenty-fifth of the seventh month of 1652.

Of Zhongzhou in Sichuan. He belonged to the Juyun (聚雲) house and was a disciple of ER'AN DENGSONG (耳菴燈嵩), who had received the robe and bowl from 'Patriarch Three-Slaps' (三巴掌 = Tiemei Huili). Sanshan Denglai, at whose assembly Yumei was a fellow-student, pointed him out and said 'this is Brother Er'an's lion cub'. He was received as abbot of Tianning Chan monastery on Mt. Wufeng in Zhongzhou on the eighteenth of the ninth month of 1669, and he refers to his late master throughout as 'the old abbot of Tianning'. His recorded sayings in one fascicle survive.

Of the Luo (羅) family of Pengchi in Pengzhou, Sichuan. As a small boy he heaped up mud and sand into the shape of stupas; when the monk Zudeng of Anguo monastery on Mt. Yuzhang came to the house he pressed his palms together, and Zudeng laid a hand on his head and asked whether he would follow him. He was tonsured at nineteen. Zudeng taught him the pratyutpanna nianfo samadhi, which did not suit him; he went to the lecture halls of Chengdu and studied the Nature treatises, then said 'is scholastic learning the final dharma? — I have tasted enough', and went south out of the Three Gorges. He saw Huai'an Zhao at Zhaojue, Zhewong Ruyan at Jingshan, and followed Gaoyuan Zuquan to Ruiyan in Taizhou. Zuquan could not open him and at last said 'my devices are exhausted and you will not look — the connection is not here; go and see Xuedou', and Liaohui went. THE MAN THEN HOLDING THE SEAT AT XUEDOU WAS FOJIAN WUZHUN SHIFAN. He was abbot of Dinghui, then Nengren in Dongjia, Donglin in Jiangzhou and Tiantong in Mingzhou, retiring at last to Huanzhi hermitage. He died on the twenty-second of the third month of 1262, aged 65.

Of the Zeng (曾) family of Dianjiang in Sichuan; his lay name was Zeng Bubo. He held a Confucian degree and sat the examinations repeatedly without success. A monk brought him Chuiwan Guangzhen's Gu yin wang zhuan; he read it over and over 'as if drunk, as if waking', then got hold of the records of Tiebi Huiji and of Master Bazhang, and 'the mind-flower opened'. He swore to himself: 'one day I shall be a child of the Juyun house.' His mother died when he was twenty-six and his father three years later; within two months of the funeral the country rose in revolt, he hid for six months, his wife died of illness, and he gave his two sons to his elder brother and took the robe from the two masters Nan and Zhe of Mt. Diaoyan. Sheltering from the war at Dongming monastery in Zhongzhou he wrote to TIEBI HUIJI and got a reply; he went into the mountains to him. He entered the hall on the twenty-sixth of the eleventh month of 1648 and broke through in 1649; he formally received Tiebi's dharma in 1654. He was abbot of Chongsheng and Xinglong in Sichuan, of Tianning in Zhejiang, and founded Gaofeng Kaixi in Zhongzhou. He wrote the Wujia zongzhi zuanyao (五家宗旨纂要), a manual of the doctrines of the five houses. He died on the eighteenth of the seventh month of 1685.

Of Yinjiang in Sinan, Guizhou; his father was a Yang, his mother a Lu. Born on the twenty-third of the eighth month of 1640. He was betrothed at thirteen, lost his father at twenty-seven, and took the precepts of abstinence at twenty-nine. He liked the Ox-herding verses, and found his way in on hearing someone read the Mencius line 'the nature of a sheep is like the nature of an ox; the nature of an ox is like the nature of a man'. Two years later he left home against his mother's wishes and was ordained by MINSHU; Minshu died within the year, and after helping raise his stupa Daole went on to SHENGKE DEYU of Huayan. Shengke beat him at their first interview until his head bled — 'and then I began to know what hurt'. Shengke offered him a verse of transmission in the spring of 1676 and he DECLINED IT. He went back to Guizhou to see his mother, held Longshan monastery for three years, retreated to Mt. Gaotun through the fighting, buried his mother, and in 1684 came out of Shu to Zunyi, where he was kept at Yuquan monastery. In the spring of 1685, hearing that Shengke had left his monastery and was staying at Fangshan in Luzhou, he went to attend him again — and this time the old master tested him with the dead phrase, the live phrase and the neither-dead-nor-alive phrase, and sealed him with a verse, a staff and a whisk. He was abbot of Huayan in western Shu.

Lay surname Tao (陶), of Taihe in Ji'an; a dharma heir of Xiaoweng Miaokan (1177-1248), nineteenth generation below Huineng. He came out as abbot of Jianfu monastery in Raozhou in the sixth month of 1227, moved to Kaixian on Lushan, and returned to Jianfu in 1229. He wrote the accounts-of-conduct (行狀) of his own teacher Xiaoweng and of Chijue Daochong — the two are quoted as authorities on monastic layout in later handbooks. His heir was Yusou Chengjian. He died in 1271, aged 59. His dharma name is written both 道燦 and 道璨.

Of Xin'an; lay surname Bao (鮑). His father Bao Qinjiao was a prefectural student; his mother dreamed of a tablet reading 'Hall of Accumulated Good' before she conceived. Born on the twenty-fourth of the tenth month of 1623. He failed the examinations at eighteen, and at nineteen left his parents for Jinling, met a monk on the road who urged him to practise, and was tonsured at Yixing. At twenty he took the full precepts from Zhuanyu Guanheng at Qingliang monastery in the capital. He heard friends talk of the Chan gate, read the Changuan cejin, threw over doctrinal study and went to Lingao at Yaofeng in Suzhou, then to Shiyu Mingfang at Dongta monastery in Jiaxing, where — after a fortnight with an unbreakable doubt-mass and a night without sleep — the great drum sounded at dawn in the Buddha hall and his chest fell open. THE HEAD MONK OF THAT ASSEMBLY WAS HIS OWN MASTER-TO-BE, JIE'AN [WUJIN]. He went on to Feiyin Tongrong at Jinsu and traded pushes with him on the abbot's steps. His transmission, however, came from JIE'AN WUJIN (介菴悟進) of Jinming monastery in Jiaxing, and he says so from the seat, at the opening of the hall, in the reverential form. He was abbot at Huanglian and at Qizhou. He belongs to the DUANQIAO (斷橋) branch of Linji — a rare surviving line outside the Miyun Yuanwu mainstream — and calls his master the thirty-first generation of it.

Lay surname Chen (陳), of Nanchang; a dharma heir of Huiji Yuanxi (1238-1319), twenty-first generation below Huineng. He left home at Shuilu cloister, first called on Yishan of Kaixian, then went to Huiji Yuanxi. In 1328 the Yuan emperor Wenzong turned his former princely residence at Jinling into the monastery Longxiang Jiqing and ordered Daxin to open it — one of the most powerful monastic offices of the age; he was made Grand Master of the Palace (太中大夫) and titled Chan Master Guangzhi Quanwu. Under Emperor Shundi he was commanded to revise the Baizhang Rules (敕修百丈清規). His heirs included Zongle and Zhengzu. He died in 1344, aged 61, with 46 years in robes.

Of the Wang (王) family of Gaoliang in Kuizhou (Liangshan, Sichuan); a dharma heir of Poshan Haiming (1597-1666). His recorded sayings in three fascicles survive. His own heir Miyin Zhenchuan burns the transmission incense for him at every hall-opening as 'the thirty-second generation of orthodox Linji' — which fixes Lingyin's place in the line exactly, since Poshan is the thirty-first.
Southern Song Caodong master; a dharma heir of Donggu Miaoguang. Nothing more is recorded of him.

Lay surname Yang (楊), of Baodi (near Tianjin); born on the fifteenth of the ninth month of 1614. Abbot of the Zhengfa monastery at Guzhongpan on Mt. Pan (Jizhou, near Tianjin). He said from the seat in old age 'this old monk has been in the world seventy-five years'. His recorded sayings in four fascicles survive, cut by his disciple Langkong Shun. He is the heir of DABO XINGQIAN, whom he names in his transmission incense as 'the thirty-sixth generation of the orthodox line of Caoxi'.
Abbot of Dongta monastery in Jiaxing; a dharma heir of Baofang Jin. Nothing further is recorded.

Of Zhongzhou in Sichuan; lay surname Wan (萬). He wanted to leave the world as a child and got his parents' leave; he left home at sixteen and at twenty-two took the precepts from XIANGYA XINGTING, whom he attended for three years. He then travelled to seek the way, went to Shuanggui and met POSHAN HAIMING, submitted to him and took the disciple's place, and shirked no labour; in time he was made prior. He was invited to Bazhou and preached at Zhongfeng and Jingci. He is described as unbending to the last and never willing to borrow another man's authority. On the sixteenth of the fourth month of 1669 he sat down in the hall at Shigu monastery in his own prefecture after the morning gruel, put out his right foot, said 'Do you understand? I am going; the whole ten-direction world is just THIS', spoke a verse, and died — aged 47, with 25 years in robes. Five heirs, among them Lüluo Hengxiu, raised his stupa to the left of Shigu monastery.

Of the Zhang (張) family of Sixian ward, Jiaxing; born 1487. He never went to the village school, yet his reasoning was mature from childhood. At eighteen something struck him and he asked his parents to let him leave home; they refused, so he sat day and night and would do no work. Three years later he slipped into Tianning monastery as a postulant. He was tonsured at Dongchan under Ang, and it was Ang's dharma-uncle JI'AN ZUO — a son of Motang Xuan — whom he served in earnest. Walking in the cloister one day he heard the chime struck in the Buddha hall and broke open; he went straight to the abbot's room, and Ji'an, seeing him come, laughed and said 'you have been robbed'. 'The thief is taken.' 'Where is the loot?' He shook out his sitting-cloth: 'A mess, a mess.' Ji'an approved him. He was head monk at Jueweng monastery in Chang'an at twenty-eight, and the old masters of Hangzhou could not stand against him in the hall. He was abbot of some twenty houses in turn, among them Anyin at Jinling (from the Jiajing era, at the invitation of the eunuch Zhang Yong) and Tianning at Jiaxing, where he died. He is described as unhurried and courteous, exact in his discipline in the smallest things, sharing every gift equally with the community, never soliciting patronage, and — after the Japanese pirate raids drove soldiers into his hall — living wholly without restraint, laughing, scolding, and unreadable. He died in the autumn of 1560, aged 74, with 52 summers. He counted himself the twenty-sixth generation from Linji. This is the man Yungu Fahui actually studied under.

Of the Yang (楊) family of Tangxian; abbot of Dajue monastery in Beijing — hence the epithets 大覺 and 清涼 in the incense formulas of his heirs. A dharma heir of Huanxiu Changrun. He came south to Yue (Zhejiang) in 1591, and it was at Zhifengtu that Zhanran Yuancheng met him. Born 1552/3, died 1594/5.

Southern Song Linji master, styled Huiweng (晦翁), sobriquet Zhenlan ('truly idle'); of Fuzhou. A dharma heir of Mu'an Anyong (d. 1173), nineteenth generation below Huineng. He was abbot of Chongfu monastery in Quanzhou and of Jingci in Hangzhou. He compiled the LIANDENG HUIYAO (聯燈會要) in thirty fascicles — one of the five great lamp records — writing its preface in the Qianguang hall in 1183 and putting it to the block.
Directed one of the most prolific translation bureaus in Buddhist history. His translations shaped the vocabulary of East Asian Buddhism.
Nun mentioned in the Platform Sutra who could recite the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. Huineng reportedly explained its meaning to her.
Appointed National Teacher by two Tang emperors. Known for 'the National Teacher calls three times' koan.
Hongzhou school master at Xingshan Temple in Chang’an. Teacher of the poet Bai Juyi, who wrote his memorial inscription in 819.

One of Mazu's 'three great disciples'. Often called 'Old Teacher Wang' (王老師). After enlightenment under Mazu, retreated to Mount Nanquan for 30 years. Famous for killing the cat (南泉斬貓) and 'ordinary mind is the Way' (平常心是道). Had seventeen dharma heirs.
Co-founder of the Guiyang school, earliest of the Five Houses.
Known for 'The entire ten-direction world is the eye of the monk.'
Critical link in the survival of the Linji school through the Five Dynasties.
Compiler/editor of the Linji Lu (Record of Linji). Known for sharp exchanges.

From Nancheng in Fuzhou (Jiangxi). Ordained at fourteen, studied eight years under Dongshan Liangjie, and also visited Linji and Cuiwei Wuxue. Later became abbot of Miaoji Temple on Mount Longya near Changsha. Posthumous title: Great Master Zhengkong. Appears in Blue Cliff Record case 20.

Founder of the Yunmen school. Born 864 in Jiaxing. Enlightened when Muzhou slammed the gate on his leg. Established Yunmen Monastery on Yunmen Mountain in Guangdong with 500+ monks. Known for terse, one-word answers: 'A dried shit-stick.' Famous for 'every day is a good day.' His mummified body was preserved.
Preserved the Linji transmission through the difficult Five Dynasties period.
Key transmitter in the Yangqi branch.
Teacher of Hongzhi Zhengjue. Key figure in the Caodong revival.
Initially studied Yunmen, received Caodong transmission from Zhenxie Qingliao. Abbot of Tiantong monastery. Teacher of Xuedou Zhijian.
Caodong Chan master at Daming Temple in Cizhou. Direct teacher of Wansong Xingxiu; granted him his definitive awakening and dharma transmission.

Compiler of the Wumenguan (無門關, Gateless Barrier), the most widely studied koan collection. Attained awakening after six years of working on Zhaozhou's 'No'. The Wumenguan's 48 cases with verse commentary became central to Linji-lineage koan training.
Yuan dynasty Linji master at Lingyin Temple, Hangzhou. Teacher of Chushi Fanqi.

Naong Hyegeun's primary dharma heir and the master who rebuilt Songgwangsa, the 'Sangha Jewel Temple' originally established by Jinul. During the late Goryeo and early Joseon transition, he preserved the Seon monastic community through a period of political upheaval and growing anti-Buddhist sentiment from Neo-Confucian reformers. His reconstruction of Songgwangsa ensured the physical and institutional survival of the Jinul-Hyesim legacy. He maintained the unified Jogye lineage established by Taego Bou, transmitting it into the fifteenth century. Attested in Songgwangsa temple records: his rebuilding efforts and dharma lineage from Naong are preserved in monastery inscriptions and chronicles.
Ming dynasty Chan elder at Fatong Temple in Beijing. Teacher of Zibo Zhenke for nine years.
69th Caodong patriarch. Also called Boshan. Author of Canxue zhijin (Exhortation on Great Doubt), a classic on huatou practice.
