Second abbot of Huangbo monastery after Miyun. Published the controversial Wudeng yantong (1654) asserting Linji orthodoxy. CBETA: J26nB178.

Third-generation Shaolin Caodong master (after Xueting Fuyu and Lingyin Wentai). Served as abbot of Shaolin Monastery during the late Yuan dynasty, maintaining the Caodong transmission that Xueting Fuyu had restored there.

The 74th Korean patriarch. Lecturer on Buddhist doctrine at Donghaksa Monastery on Gyeryongsan Mountain near Daejeon. Took in the teenage Gyeongheo after Venerable Gyeheo left the order, teaching him the doctrinal curriculum. Gyeongheo later told followers to honor Manhwa as the one 'from whom I received the work of the dharma.'

Originally from Longcheng in Qinzhou (present-day Tianshui, Gansu). Entered monastic life at age three at Yingqian Monastery on Mount Maiji. After serving as abbot at several monasteries including Qixian on Mount Lu and Changlu Chongfu, he was appointed the first abbot of Fayun Monastery in the capital Kaifeng by Emperor Shenzong in 1084, receiving the honorific "Yuantong." Closely connected with Song literati including Su Shi, Huang Tingjian, Wang Anshi, and the painter Li Gonglin.

Japanese Rinzai master, a son of the retired Emperor Go-Saga. On the twenty-sixth of the ninth month of 1281 he went to Kenchō-ji at Kofukusan and received from Mugaku Sogen the kesa that had come down from Enshō (Lanxi Daolong), carried it back to his temple and had the drum sounded to announce it to the assembly. He was the first abbot of Un'gan-ji in Shimotsuke (下野州東山雲巖禪寺). Posthumously Bukkoku Zenji (佛國禪師) and Bukkoku Ōgu Kōsai Kokushi. He died in 1316, aged 76. His heir Musō Soseki became the most influential Zen figure of the Muromachi period.

Linji master of the far southwest, thirty-sixth generation below Nanyue. Dharma name Falin 發林, sobriquet Hengxiu(lin) of Lüluo. Born on the twenty-third of the seventh month of 1626. He was the heir of Yunhuan Chen (雲幻印宸, 1623–1669), who was himself an heir of Poshan Haiming — so he stands two steps below Poshan. He preached in the Sanba and Liuzhao country (Sichuan/Yunnan-Guizhou). He wrote the 行狀 for Jinping Poshi Zhuo, and he edited his own teacher's recorded sayings.

Linji master of the capital. Dharma name Chaozi 超自, sobriquet Heyi 何一. He received the charge of Xingkong 性空 — one of the twenty-two heirs of Feiyin Tongrong, who alone crossed the Yangtze with a single bottle and bowl to carry Chan into Hebei, where the prefectures of central China and Qi-Qing turned to him. Heyi lived at Chongning hermitage in the western suburbs of the capital, sealed in retreat reading the canon for years, with hundreds coming daily to question him. He preached under princely patronage.

names: 松江府華亭松隱唯菴德然禪師
masters.notes: Of the Zhang 張 family of Huating (Songjiang). At seven he recited the Lotus Sutra at Tianlong monastery in Hangzhou and was tonsured young under Wuyong Gui. He first saw Shiwu Qinggong, then heard Qianyan Yuanchang expound and broke through. Shiwu told him his affinity lay in Wusong and wrote out the two characters 松隱 for him; he returned home, built a hut south of Guohui and named it Songyin, hanging Shiwu's writing as its plaque, and did not cross its threshold for three years. He wrote out the Huayan Sutra in his own blood. When Qianyan died the assembly asked him to succeed to the seat. Summoned in the early Hongwu era as a man of the Way, he soon returned home ill. He built a seven-storey pagoda to house the blood-written sutra. He took leave of the assembly and died calmly on the fourteenth of the fourth month of 1388.

Of the Li 李 family, originally of Xuzhou prefecture in Sichuan, settled at Anshun in Guizhou. Born on the twenty-eighth of the sixth month of 1625. Dharma heir of Lingyin Yinwen, he became abbot of Shengjue monastery on Mount Guangfu. Thirty-sixth generation below Nanyue.

Lay surname Chen, of Xianyou in Xinghua (Fujian); sobriquet Yisou. As a child he was tonsured by Donglin of Mt Lian. Grown, he called on Chaozong Shilin and others, who set him on the koan 'the ten thousand dharmas return to one'. He then went to Feiyin at Jinsu, and one night, hearing the bell, had an opening. He went again to Wanru Tongwei at Longchi and received the dharma. He was abbot of Tongtian Chan monastery in Fujian. He died on 12/3 of 1669, aged 54, with 40 dharma-years; his stupa is on the eastern slope of Mt Lian. He left a fascicle of recorded sayings and a collection of poems, the Jipiao ji. His heir was Danya Chaoyuan.

Of the Shi 施 family of Xiushui in Jiahe (Jiaxing). Born on the eighteenth of the tenth month of 1491. As a layman he was called Jingzhai, married, and had a son and a daughter; kindly by nature, he gave himself to the inner books and longed for the way of the patriarchs, travelling with his friend Jizhou Fazhou for eight years before returning home to press the enquiry alone. When Yeweng Xiao — a fourteenth-generation descendant of Huqiu Shaolong and heir of Baofang Jin — was staying at Dongta monastery, he went to call on him, and every view he presented was swept away, until all he had prided himself on was gone. One day Yeweng said 'I have a word for you', and only laughed when asked; when Rukong at last made the full disciple's obeisance and begged, Yeweng gave it. He died on the sixth of the eighth month of 1580, aged 90.

Of the Gaoyang 高陽 family of Suzhou, thirty-second generation of the Linji house; also styled Ou'an. Born on the thirteenth of the first month of 1621, after his mother dreamed a strange dream. Quick as a child and fond of sitting alone, he recited the Cundi dharani daily and would set out food and bow to any travelling monk who came. At fifteen he wanted to leave home and nearly starved himself when his parents refused. He met Jie'an (Wuji n) — 'question and answer between them mixed like water and milk' — and received the charge and attended him. He returned to Ou'an, made an image of Guanyin, built a meditation hall, and copied out the Huayan, Surangama and Amitabha sutras entire. Worn out, he withdrew to a thatched hut outside the East Gate and there, taking up the brush, wrote 'All my life solitary, I kept the gate and held to plainness; though my way was cool, I trust the blaze of those who come after', gave a shout, threw down the brush and died — the hour of yin on the seventeenth of the seventh month of 1677, aged 57, with 34 years in robes.

Of the Zhang 張 family of Putian in Xinghua (Fujian); a licentiate before he ordained. Born on the eleventh of the eleventh month of 1630. Dharma heir of Yisou Xinggao (1616–1669), thirty-sixth generation below Nanyue. He held the seat at Tongtian for a year in obedience to his grandmaster's wishes. He died in the hour of chou on the eighteenth of the fourth month of 1698, aged 69, with 36 years in robes; his stupa stands on the right slope below Daibei hermitage.

Name Daodu, sobriquet Zongbao, also styled Kongyin; a son of the Lu clan of Nanhai in Guangdong. At three his mother carried him upstairs and he watched a spider spinning its web, staring a long while, until grief and joy came over him together. At six he lost his father. He got hold of the Platform Sutra — AND COULD NOT READ. He carried it in his sleeve and bowed earnestly to Guanyin; one night he prostrated until he collapsed exhausted, and woke feeling as though he hung in space, sweat soaking his back; he lit a lamp, took out the sutra, guessed at a character, asked someone — and was right, and thereafter read whole lines at a glance. At fourteen, sitting under a tree, HIS CHEST SPLIT LIKE A CLEFT BAMBOO. At sixteen he took a knife to a boulder, bowed to the Buddhas of the ten directions, SHAVED HIS OWN HEAD, built a hut on Mt Long and lived alone for more than ten years. He served his mother with total devotion — when she was ill he carried spring-water twenty li a day on his shoulder — and when she died he kept vigil at her grave three months. AT TWENTY-NINE he went to Boshan, to WUYI YUANLAI, who had been asking every monk from Guangdong: 'Why does Zongbao not come? Can the Way be reached without coming to Boshan?' Boshan called him into the abbot's room and they talked the night through; he gave him his name and his full ordination. Boshan died five months later. He held Luofu, Xichan at Fuzhou, Changqing, and Haichuang at Guangzhou, and his whole-body stupa stands south of West Creek at Huashou Terrace on Mt Luofu. He died in 1661, aged 62, with 33 summers. 'Only two men,' says his heir, 'personally received his seal.'

Of the Pan 潘 family of Shanghai; also called Daoxiong. Born on the third of the fifth month of 1632. Dharma heir of Zhu'an Zhenyan — 'the true son of Zhu'an, whose tallying with him was deepest' — he opened the dharma at Lianhua monastery at Wumen (Suzhou), where his eye of the way was clear and his forging of students exacting. His record was edited by his own disciples and prefaced in 1673 by Luo Zhenxing, who wrote that he was fit to revive the way of Cheqi and Jinming and shed light on Duanqiao.

Linji master of Xiangyan, thirty-seventh generation below Nanyue. Dharma heir of Xianglin Zhen (象林本真, 1620–1691). He re-cut and reissued his teacher's recorded sayings and also re-edited the collected writings of Zhengjue Runguang Ze — the acts of a literary executor to his own line. His own 語錄 carries a 行實.

Of the Zhu 朱 family of Linhai in Taizhou; styled Liao'an, sobriquet Nantang, later 'the old man left over from Nantang'. Orphaned at nine, he went with an uncle to Mount Shuangjing as a novice; at sixteen he passed the sutra examination under Huyan Fu and was ordained. He studied under Gulin Qingmao and became his heir, and also visited Dongyu Hai and Dongzhou Yong. He went out to Kaifu at Lishui in 1329, moved to Benjue at Jiaxing in 1333 and sat there ten years, was granted the title Ciyun Puji Chanshi by the Imperial Preceptor, and in 1345 took Lingyan at Wuzhong. His calligraphy was famous, and his letters reached Japan, where they are treasured as bokuseki. He died on the twenty-fifth of the eighth month of 1367, aged 76; when the body was burned, red and white lights circled the coffin, and the skull, tongue and teeth did not burn.

Lay name Xu Ji'en (also Xu Shichen) of Qiantang. He passed the mingjing examination and lived as a scholar, only ordaining at about forty-six. Caodong heir of Sanyi Mingyu (1599–1665), himself an heir of Zhanran Yuancheng; thirty-seventh generation below Qingyuan. He was abbot of Ciyun, Fanshou and Xiansheng. A prolific writer, he left the Xuefo kaoxun, the Qiyuan zhitong (a Chan reading of the Zhuangzi) and Yuejing shi'er zhong, besides his eighteen-juan record — a scholar's bibliography as much as a monk's. He was born on the fourth of the tenth month of 1615 and died on the twenty-fourth of the ninth month of 1684, aged 70.

From Wanxian in eastern Shu (Sichuan). Abbot of the Huangling Chan cloister. Dharma heir of Chunbei Guangde, thirty-eighth generation below Nanyue — the last generation recorded in the Jiaxing canon's Linji sequence. He co-edited his teacher's recorded sayings.

Linji master of the Yangqi line, tenth generation. His dharma name is never given — the record calls him only 'the venerable Yuejian'. He followed Xiyan Liaohui, abbot of Tiantong, for six years. On the third day of the third month of 1264 he was invited from the head-seat quarters at Jianfu in Raozhou to take Ehu Renshou monastery in Xinzhou; he later held Tianning and Jianfu in Raozhou, and Jianfu a second time. At the anniversary of Xiyan's death he offered incense year after year with fierce, mocking affection: 'he is a man of the Penglai mountains — only Penglai incense will do to offer him.' His record was edited by his heir Miaoyin and prefaced in 1284.

Of the He 何 family of Tongchuan in Chengdu. Dharma name Chaochuan 超船, sobriquet Zizhou. Born in the hour of chen on the sixteenth of the third month of 1619. Dharma heir of Eryin Mi, thirty-sixth generation below Nanyue. He was abbot at Tanxi in Xiangyang and at Lumen. Zhang Lian, who wrote the preface to his record, describes climbing Lianhua peak in 1642 to see Eryin at Lianxin hermitage and talking with him till dawn — 'truly kin in the dharma across the generations'.

names: 盛京奉天般若古林禪師
masters.notes: Of the Li 李 family of Changsha in Huguang. Tonsured on Mount Emei at six, he served twelve years at Shuanggui — Poshan Haiming's monastery — before his own awakening. Dharma heir of Yusong Chuanyi. He carried the Linji line to Shengjing/Fengtian (Mukden), the northernmost Chan seat in this batch: at his installation a monk asked 'whose tune do you sing, whose house do you succeed?' and he answered 'not before Maitreya, not after Sakyamuni' — and when the monk pressed, 'then you got the seal at Emei and now spread it wide beyond the passes', he said 'you flatter me to death'. Born 1623; he sat down and died in the night of the sixteenth of the eleventh month of 1695, aged 73.

Of the Peng 彭 family of Meishan; his clan-ancestor was Xiatang Huiyuan, the Chan master who answered Xiaozong on the dharma and was titled Fohai. Quick as a child — he knew to bow to monks and images at three or four — he begged his parents' leave at sixteen and went to Zhiming at Fabao cloister on Mount Shilong in Danling; he was tonsured and fully ordained at twenty-two. Travelling south through Hunan he visited the patriarchs' traces, and while living near Shishuang he walked the hundred and twenty li to bow at Daowu's stupa on every new and full moon, never stopping even in old age; one night in a thunderstorm the stupa was said to have moved to meet him, and it is called the Thunder-moved Stupa to this day. He went on to Wuyong Quan at Tiantong and Kongsou Yin at Maofeng, and finally, hearing of the renown of Po'an at Qionglong in Wu, went and stayed — Po'an knew him at once for a vessel of the dharma. He was abbot of Lingyin. He died on the eleventh of the first month of 1245, aged 75.

Styled Shunfu; his mother was of the He 賀 family. Born in the hour of chen on the ninth of the tenth month of 1612. Dharma heir of Yuanhu Miaoyong, thirty-fourth generation below Nanyue. He wrote and prefaced his own ten-juan record, to which a 源流頌 (verses on the lineage) is appended — a man keenly conscious of his own succession. He was a prolific teacher: the Jiaxing catalogue lists at least seven masters as 嗣介庵進, including Zhu'an Zhenyan, Shanduo Zhenzai, Daxiao and the layman Lu Ying. He died on the twenty-third of the ninth month of 1673, aged 62, with 37 years in robes.

Linji master of Langpan in YUNNAN — one of the very few Chan seats that far southwest. Dharma heir of Poshan Haiming. The 五燈全書 preserves his teaching: 'Shitou said, a needle cannot pierce it. Yaoshan said, flowers grow on stone. Here at Langpan it is not so — it is like standing in a thicket of a hundred flowers: whose nose has no fragrance in it?' His heir Banshui Yuan of Sanfeng carried the line on.

The great Chan patriarch of Lingnan. Born in the hour of hai on the fourteenth of the tenth month of 1608; styled Lizhong. In 1642, at the invitation of Chen Zizhuang and others, he opened the dharma at Helin and the Chan wind rose again in Guangdong, which had been in decline since the Yuan. Dharma heir of Zongbao Daodu, whose 行狀 he wrote as 嗣法門人. He was abbot of Haiyun, Haichuang and Huashou, and founded Biechuan monastery on Danxia; he was a noted calligrapher. Though a monk, he held up loyalty, filiality, integrity and honour to his students, and when the Ming fell, scholars, officials and loyalist remnants took refuge with him in their thousands — many of his disciples, as his modern chronicler observes, 'had somewhere to flee to and something they meant to do', and their taking of the robe was not their first intent. He died in the hour of you on the twenty-seventh of the eighth month of 1685, aged 78.

Of the Pan 潘 family of Huaining in Shuzhou. Caodong master of Huguo monastery on Tiantai. Dharma heir of Ruibai Mingxue. His teaching in the 五燈全書: asked to set aside the wondrous mind of nirvana and simply declare the treasury of the true dharma eye, he said 'auspicious vapour fills the courtyard'; asked then what the wondrous mind of nirvana might be, he said 'lucky clouds cupping the sun'.

Yunmen-house master of Beichan at Changning in Hengzhou (Tanzhou). Dharma heir of Fuyan Liangya. Asked at his installation 'whose tune do you sing, whose house do you succeed?', he answered 'the peaks of Zhibo stand fair, their fame carried beyond the seas' — and when the monk said 'in days past you got the seal from Fuyan in person; today you convert the lost here', he replied 'you have had your fill of the monastery, at least'. The 續傳燈錄 records seven dharma heirs for him, among them Fachang Yiyu and Xinghua Shaoxian.

Of the Wang 王 family, originally of Huguang; his father was a tax officer at Danyang and the family settled there. His mother dreamed a monk entered the door carrying a bundle. At seven he dreamed he sat in a crowd waving a whisk and expounding; his mother said 'that is how monks preach — one day you shall leave home'. At fourteen he was tonsured under Zhanran at Miaojue monastery, who asked him 'what have you come for?' — 'to become a Buddha', he said, and Zhanran marvelled. When Zhanran was transferred to Shushan he went to Songyin, teaching at Yunjian, and vowed in a small hermitage not to return until he had penetrated; after six days in samadhi he raised his head, saw a pine, and broke open. Thereafter he never slept, sitting like an iron banner — whence 'Chan of the iron spine'. At Xuanmu he met Guolin, who fitted him like needle to mustard-seed and then pointed him to BAOZANG CHI — the master under whom, after being scolded ('the dharma is like a great ocean, deeper the further in — why moor here?'), he broke through to the source of the dharma on the second night and received the charge. In 1404 he climbed Tianmu for a thousand-day retreat; in 1408 he came to Anxi, found the peaks fine, and stayed. He sat in retreat there more than thirty years, never leaving the mountain, and from 1427 built out the monastery — Dongming — until hundreds lived there. He died on the twenty-seventh of the sixth month of 1441, aged 70.

Of Baixiang county, Zhaozhou, in the north — surname Li. Tall, with silkworm brows and a beard curled like a snail-shell; he had been a glazier's craftsman. Tonsured in middle age by Wujin of Tiantai, he could not read a word and spent sixteen years wandering the mountains at practice. In 1633 he went to Emei to feed the monks, met bandits who killed his companions, and escaped alone. Sent on to Chuiwan Guangzhen at Zhongzhou, he was recognised at sight — 'one of ours has come' — and set to sweeping the hall. When Tiebi asked why he did not take the proper road, he answered: 'I'm a northerner, I don't know one character; you're a man of letters, my work isn't yours.' Chuiwan gave him 'the ten thousand dharmas return to one', and after twenty-five sessions he broke through, laughing, and named himself 'the Three-Slaps monk'. He opened the hall four times, passed his robe to Er'an, and died in 1650 aged 65.

Of the Lin 林 family of his own prefecture (Fuzhou). He took the jinshi examinations young and had a name as a scholar. At twenty-five, reading the Sutra of Bequeathed Teachings, he said 'I was nearly ruined by the Confucian cap' and wanted to leave home; his mother resisted, as his marriage was already fixed, and he broke it off with a verse — 'peach red and apricot pale, I hand them all to the spring wind; green bamboo and yellow flower shall be my companions in the Way from here on.' He was ordained under Baoshou Le, travelled Hunan with a single staff, called on every notable master, found the dharma had no different flavours, and came home to build a hut. He was awakened under Dahui Zonggao and became his heir. He was abbot of Xichan on Mount Yi in Fuzhou. He died on the fifteenth of the seventh month of 1153, aged 62, with 37 years in robes.
Author of the Zhao Lun, the first mature synthesis of Madhyamaka thought in Chinese.
Student of the Fifth Patriarch Hongren. Settled in Zizhou, Sichuan. Empress Wu Zetian gave him a patriarchal robe. Died in seated meditation at age 94. Transmitted to Chuji.

Early Korean Seon figure (704-779). First studied under Beomnang at Mt. Hogeo, then traveled to Tang China and received transmission from Chigong (a Korean disciple of Puji of the Northern School). Bridges the Beomnang lineage with the Northern School tradition. Attested in the Jijeungdaesa stele (893 CE, composed by Choe Chiwon).

masters.notes: Dharma heir of Shitou Xiqian. Named after Mount Wuxie where he resided.
Featured in the 'condolence call' koan (Blue Cliff Record, Case 55).
Formidable laywoman nicknamed 'Iron Grindstone' for her relentless debating style. One of few women in the lamp records.

Silla monk who studied under Nanquan Puyuan in Tang China. Founded the Sajasan school, one of the Nine Mountain Schools of Korean Seon. His transmission from Nanquan places him in the Mazu Daoyi lineage.

A dharma heir of Linji Yixuan who held Baoshou cloister in Zhenzhou. The lamp records group him with Xinghua Cunjiang, Sansheng Huiran, Dajue and Guanxi Zhixian — Linji's inner circle. Zhaozhou came to see him and he sat with his back turned; his exchange with the tinker Hu ('Can you nail down empty space?' — 'Then smash it open for me, Reverend!' — and Baoshou hit him) is among the best-known Linji-school encounters. His heir was Xiyuan Siming; a second-generation Baoshou, whose name is lost, succeeded him.

From Fuzhou. First studied under Deshan Xuanjian alongside Yantou and Xuefeng, then became a dharma heir of Dongshan Liangjie. Achieved great enlightenment at age twenty-seven and became abbot of Mount Qin. Known for the 'one arrow piercing three barriers' exchange.
After Shishuang's death, challenged the assembly about understanding the late master.
'If you have a staff, I will give you a staff; if not, I will take it away.'
Linji master. Student of Shoushan Xingnian. Teacher of Fushan Fayuan, through whom the Caodong lineage was preserved.
Received Caodong transmission via proxy through Fushan Fayuan. Saved the Caodong lineage from extinction.
Principal reviver of the Caodong school. Refused an imperial purple robe, preferring imprisonment.
Systematized kanhua (keyword investigation) Chan. Most influential Chan master of the Southern Song.
Founded the Songyuan sub-lineage. His two main dharma heirs Po'an Zuxian and Yunan Puyan produced the lineages of Wuzhun Shifan and Xutang Zhiyu respectively.
Late Song Linji master whose recorded sayings became profoundly influential in the later Linji tradition. Dharma heir of Yunan Puyan (not Wuzhun Shifan as sometimes misattributed).

Yuan dynasty Linji Chan master, dharma heir of Gaofeng Yuanmiao. Significant for Korean Seon history as the Chinese teacher who transmitted to both Taego Bou and Baegun Gyeonghan, linking Korean Seon to mainstream Chinese Linji lineage. Also received teaching from Ji'an Zongxin, a dharma brother of Gaofeng.
Also known as Hamheo Deuktong. Wrote Hyeonjeong non defending Buddhism against Neo-Confucian attacks. Commentaries on Diamond Sutra and Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment. No known dharma heirs.
Ming dynasty Linji master. Teacher of Yunqi Zhuhong. His teaching featured the stick and thunderous shout.
Clashed with his teacher over Linji's teaching, splitting the late Ming Linji revival.

Fourth-generation Shaolin Caodong master, dharma heir of Huanyuan Fuyu. Served as abbot of Shaolin Monastery during the mid-Yuan dynasty, continuing the Caodong lineage that would persist at Shaolin into the Ming.
Carried the Pyeonyang lineage into mid-17th century. Important link figure in the main trunk of Korean Seon.

The 75th Korean patriarch and the reviver of Korean Seon. Born Song Donguk (宋東旭) in Jeonju. Entered monastic life around age 9 under Venerable Gyeheo at Cheonggyesa, then studied under Manhwa at Donghaksa. Attained enlightenment in 1879 after encountering plague victims, which drove him from sutra study to intensive meditation. On November 15, 1887, achieved great awakening. Revived kanhwa Seon (hwadu meditation) and taught at Beomeosa, Haeinsa, and Songgwangsa. In 1905, at age 59, abruptly left the sangha and wandered incognito in northern Korea, reportedly living as a layperson teaching Confucian classics until his death in 1912 at Gapsan. His four great disciples -- Suwol (1855-1928), Hyewol (1861-1937), Mangong (1871-1946), and Hanam (1876-1951) -- became the pillars of 20th-century Korean Buddhism.

Also known as Yuanzhao Zongben. Dharma heir of Tianyi Yihuai who first taught at Ruiguang Monastery in Suzhou, then served as abbot of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou where over a thousand disciples gathered. Later served at imperially sponsored monasteries in the Northern Song capital Kaifeng, including Huilin Monastery. Together with his student Shanben, they were known as "Big and Little Ben." He was one of the most prestigious Buddhist monks of his generation.

A Changshu man of the Zhang clan, tonsured under Poshan Dongwen. He first studied with Boshan (Wuyi Yuanlai), then met Miyun Yuanwu at Jinsu and became his heir — the thirty-first generation of Linji. He was abbot of Gunan at Meili (hence 'the Reverend of Gunan'), then Qizhen at Siming, Meixi at Jiahe, Jile at Xinghua, and finally TIANTONG, retiring to Helin at Jingkou. A calligrapher and poet, he left the Qihui yulu and the Lanzhai bieji, and had ten dharma heirs. He died in 1671.

Youngest son of the Jiang clan of Qiyang in southern Hunan; his father was named Chunlong, his mother of the Li clan. He was born in 1633. He never studied as a boy, and about the age of twelve both his parents died; he was tonsured at Tianquan in 1644. In 1653, when the country had quietened, he took leave of his master and travelled to the lecture-halls. He entered QISHAN for the summer retreat in 1654 and was fully ordained that winter under LANFANG, a thirtieth-generation Caodong master at Renrui monastery on Qishan in Hengzhou. During work-practice a monk asked, 'Mountains, rivers and the great earth fully reveal the Dharma-King's body; before us they are vivid and clear — what then is the Dharma-King's body?' and the master answered 'Revealed.' Hearing it from the side, Wenmu Nian suddenly awoke. He later presided at a 'new Danxia'.

A son of the Lü clan of southern Hunan, born about 1631. Born into civil war, he was TAKEN CAPTIVE AND CARRIED INTO GUIZHOU and pressed into an army camp; at Changshou hermitage in Anshun he heard the Reverend Yunfu give a dharma-talk and conceived the wish to leave the world. When the dynasty's forces retook Yunnan and Guizhou his unit scattered, and he fled to Longtan monastery at Annan and was tonsured under the elder Wuxia. Hearing that SHANQUAN DAWEI was teaching at Wanshou monastery in Longchang, he went and received full ordination; Shanquan took him for a vessel at first sight. He followed Shanquan to Songkui and, while attending him in a discussion of the Surangama, awoke at the passage where the Buddha raises his golden arm. Shanquan deeply approved him. He never left him again, staying at Songkui for over twenty years; when Shanquan died in 1684 the assembly asked him to succeed, and he rebuilt Songkui. He died in the winter of 1697, aged 67, with 40 years in robes, having told his disciples: 'When I am gone, do not trouble with pyre and expense — bury me whole.'

A son of the Zhao clan, his family from Hulin (Hangzhou) and settled at Danghu. His father was old and childless and prayed for a son; the family declined after his birth. He began school at six under the name Chongguang, but the household grew poor and by seven he was working for a living. At thirteen he gave up meat; at nineteen, when his parents moved to marry him off, he said 'if I do not go now, I shall never get free,' and fled to Putuo, where he was tonsured under Shaozong. He received the novice precepts from the great Yunqi Zhuhong. He studied for years at Jinsu under MIYUN YUANWU, followed him to Fujian, later sealed himself in retreat at Wuyuan, and became Miyun's heir the following year. He was abbot of Qinglian in Zhejiang and of BAO'EN monastery at Wujiang in Suzhou. He died in 1667, aged 75.

Born 1610 in Chongqing department, Chengdu, Sichuan, of the Hu clan; his mother dreamt of a foreign monk carrying a lotus-torch. He was tonsured at nine at Zhongfeng monastery in Guan county and served ten years, and at twenty went to Emei for full ordination. He left Sichuan in 1638 and travelled south, reaching Miyun Yuanwu at Tiantong in the winter of 1639; in 1642 he returned to Sichuan and met POSHAN HAIMING, who struck him across the head so hard that blood ran down his face — 'Do you understand?' — and everything that had blocked him melted at once. Poshan sent him on to Xiangya. At about forty, judging that his learning was thinning as his years grew, he abandoned everything and practised as one dead; sitting one night, he heard the door creak and 'the burden fell away.' He then went to DANGSHAN YUAN at Lumen in Xiangzhou, who tallied with him 'as needle to mustard-seed' and entrusted him with the true dharma eye. He presided over four monasteries — Shuangchi, Baishui, Baoshan and finally Huanglong on Mt Baizhang, Xiangyang, which he took in 1657 — for more than twenty years.

Born 1638, 10th month, 2nd day. The father was Hu Yingrong, style Chunyu, the mother of the Hong clan; both were charitable people who kept a lifelong vegetarian fast, gave coffins to the poor for years and fed monks beyond counting. Before the birth the mother dreamt that an old monk with bare head and bare feet, carrying a gourd and a staff, came begging food and lodging, and was taken in. From eleven, when the mother died, the wish to leave the world took hold — but the father cursed and forbade it, and FIFTY YEARS WERE SPENT IN THE DUST, grieving night and day at not being able to go forth. In 1690 the household was abandoned at last for a hermitage; the children brought in relatives to prevent it, swearing they would fight to the death anyone who tonsured 'our mother' — so the ordination was performed with a knife, on the self. In the second month of that year came a dream of a great white ox on a mountain, which lowered its head to be mounted and flew up; the Reverend Zongyuan of Shanguang heard the dream and cried, 'Your master has come!' — for the water-buffalo is Guishan's koan, and the Reverend of Guishan had arrived at his hermitage the day before. That was GUMEI DINGLIE, thirty-fourth-generation Linji master of Great Mt Gui in Tanzhou.

Born 1595 in Hezhou, Chongqing prefecture, Sichuan, of the Cai clan; his mother was of the Yu clan. As an infant he would retch at the smell of chicken and refuse unclean food; a physiognomist warned that he should not marry, and at ten he was sent to Jinzhong monastery in his own village and given to his uncle Daoran. He went south at seventeen (or nineteen) and spent fourteen years in the lecture-halls. In 1627 he settled at Danghu, expounded the Surangama, and sealed himself in to read the canon — but within six months nearly died of dysentery, and realising that 'a lifetime of learning is not the final matter' resolved to break out and find a teacher. A friend sent him MIYUN YUANWU'S RECORDED SAYINGS; reading the verse 'before a single thought arises — look at what it is like,' doubt seized him and he forgot food and sleep. Two more years brought nothing. Then, walking absently, HE MISSED HIS FOOTING AND FELL FROM A TOWER — and in the instant of falling, 'as one wakes from a dream,' he understood. He trained under Miyun at Tiantong and became his heir; he was abbot of Tongxuan, Qizhen and finally TIANTONG. He died in 1652, aged 58.

Born 1614 in Zi county, Chengdu, Sichuan; his father was Zhou Chaofu, his mother of the Rao clan, a family of the Embroidered-Uniform Guard. He was a child when the She chieftain's rebellion broke out in 1621; his father, telling him that 'because the world is not level there are wars and killings,' let him go, and he was placed at Jiulong monastery in Fushun county under Xingtian. He was taught by his father and his master for twelve years, until both died in the spring of 1633 — whereupon, reflecting that 'yesterday's is gone by this morning, and the morning's gone by evening,' he went to the elder Yinxin at Fujia hermitage. He became the heir of QIRAN CHAOZHI. He was abbot of Xilai monastery at Anlu in Hubei from 1657, and in 1680 succeeded his own master at Huanglong on Mt Baizhang, Xiangyang.

A WOMAN — a Chan nun. From Jingmen, of Guandong ancestry, long resident in the capital. Her father was Zhou Zhixiang, who followed the founding emperor on campaign and distinguished himself repeatedly, declined office, and retired to farming and study; her mother was of the Niu clan. The parents were over fifty and childless, and prayed to the three bodhisattvas for an heir. WHEN SHE CAME OF MARRIAGEABLE AGE HER PARENTS FORCED HER TO MARRY OUT — but she was chaste by nature, coveted neither pleasure nor wealth, vowed a lifelong fast before the embroidered Buddha, and set her will on the white robe; she was tonsured under the Reverend Buren. She then investigated Chan for more than twenty years, visiting teachers who pressed her hard, until the obstruction broke. She received the seal from her master GULÜ [FAN], and came forth as abbess of Yong'an and Hong'en. Her realisation, she said, came at Wutai and in Liaoxi; she met tigers, wolves and bandits without fear, and faced fire, flood, sword and famine as things of no weight. Imperial kinsfolk and officials were moved to build monasteries for her, and she was called 'the Ferry of Compassion'.

A Xiushui man of Jiaxing, of the Zhang clan; on the night of his birth his mother dreamt of a rooster flying from a bridge into the sky, and he was named 'Bridge.' As a boy he built shrines of tile and stone, set Buddha-images on them, and made the other children bow. HE MARRIED AND HAD A SON — and when the boy was four he was still sighing 'the dust of the world sticks fast; how shall I get out?' His schoolmaster Fang Yanshan pointed him to the sutras and then to the man himself: 'Wuqu, the old man of your own prefecture, is a descendant of Linji, THE DIRECT TRANSMISSION OF CHAN MASTER YEWENG XIAO — a genuine man of the Way. Knock on his door and he will make much of you.' He went; Wuqu said 'I have waited a long time for you.' His mother would not let him leave home, so he practised while feeding her, and only after her death was he tonsured. When he set out to build a hermitage on Jingshan, Wuqu told him: 'YOUR AFFINITY LIES BY THE WATER' — and he settled at Cart Creek (Chexi) for over twenty years. He compiled his master's recorded sayings, and in 1610 was asked to lead the Chan retreat at Jingshan. He died in 1612, aged 72. His heir Nanming Huiguang carried the line on.

Dharma heir of Xiuye Minglin, and thus the fourth in the Sichuan line Dangshan Yuan → Qiran Chaozhi → Xiuye Minglin → Zhitan Zuizheng. He was resident at the Huanglong hall on Mt Baizhang, Xiangyang, which his master had taken over in 1680. His recorded sayings survive in one juan, taken down by Shangneng and Shangying.

A son of the Zhuang clan of Taixing in Weiyang (Yangzhou); his father's style was Chengzhi, his mother of the Ma clan, a house that had served the Three Jewels for generations. THERE WERE EIGHTEEN CHILDREN AND HE WAS THE LAST. In the cradle he would put his palms together at a Buddha-image and retch at the smell of wine or fish. At nine his brothers, sisters, nephews and nieces all died one after another; at eleven he lost his father, the family estate emptied and the gate went quiet — and the wish to leave the world stirred. But his mother was old, and he laboured to feed her and never failed in his duty, giving away what was left over and never thinking of marriage — until his mother arranged a match in secret and forced him to wed. His hunger for the Way only grew, and he strayed into a heterodox sect and even led it, before turning back: 'This is not the true gate to the Way — how can I go on thinking myself right?' At the Lantern Festival he went into the city to see the lamps, saw a notice for a Chan retreat at Juehua hermitage, and thought: 'Here is a gate of Chan; the road of practice is not lost after all.' He carried incense to Juehua and met ZHULANG. 'Layman, where do you come from, and what for?' — 'I have come to ask for teaching. But I do not know whether a householder may practise Chan.' Zhulang laughed: 'CAN YOU EAT AT HOME?' — 'I eat.' — 'IF YOU CAN EAT, YOU CAN DO CHAN.' He later held the Huayan hall at Longshan in Fenyang, Shanxi.

A Kunshan man of the Li clan, tonsured at Shaolong cloister under Zhixing. He met XINGZHONG ZHIREN at Yunding and received transmission from him. He was abbot in turn of Pumen, Lingyan and Wanshou in Suzhou, and finally of JINGSHAN. Summoned to the capital in the early Yongle era, he took part in the compilation of the Yongle Encyclopaedia. He was himself a lamp-historian: he compiled the Zengji xu chuandeng lu in six juan, besides his own recorded sayings in two juan, for which Yao Guangxiao — the 'Black-Robed Chancellor' of the Yongle court — wrote the preface. He died in 1418, aged 74, with 67 years in robes. His heir was Cuifeng Zongmi.

A monk of Yuezhang cloister in Suzhou and a dharma heir of Tuiweng Hongchu (Jiqi/Lingyan Hongchu), and thus of the Sanfeng line: Hanyue Fazang → Hongchu → Neishao Zhizhong. At his opening of the dharma hall he burned incense first for Sakyamuni, then for Mahakasyapa and down through the line to Fazang, and finally for his own master, 'Old Reverend Lingyan, thirty-second generation of the orthodox Linji line, formerly resident at Guoqing on Tiantai.'

Born 1625 in his home prefecture, of the Cheng clan. He was tonsured at fifteen under a clansman-monk, Xiaosong, and studied the doctrinal texts with him for years; then, hearing of the teaching-wind of the Old Man of Hengshan, he went and took refuge with him. At the first knock he set to work hard on the matter, morning and evening without let, and the old man valued him and named him Lingyi. HE PRACTISED BITTERLY FOR OVER TWENTY YEARS. One day he presented a verse, and the old man said: 'Today at last I know I have not deceived you' — and handed over the responsory verses, staff and whisk that had come down from GRAND-MASTER TIE, renaming him Zhuofeng. When Hengshan travelled to Jiangnan he took charge of Qingyun; he opened the dharma at Qingyun monastery in Zhongzhou in 1680, on the forty-ninth day after his master's death. When Hengshan died his burden grew heavier still. In the autumn of 1685 the man who had promised to help him died; within ten days Zhuofeng too fell ill, and as he lay dying he took brush and paper, wrote a few lines, threw down the brush and stared, as though something were still unsettled.

A Meizhou man of western Shu (Sichuan), of the Wang clan, and a dharma heir of YANSHI SHANKAI of Jinshan. He was abbot in turn of Bao'en, Nengren and Jiangshan Taiping-Xingguo in Jiankang, then Huqiu at Pingjiang, then Lingyin, and finally JINGSHAN — its thirty-sixth abbot. Emperor Lizong wrote out four characters for him, 'Shixi, robe-transmitting,' and titled him Chan Master Fohai. He died on the ninth day of the sixth month, 1254.

A Caodong master, dharma heir of Sanyi Mingyu, and thus in the line of Zhanran Yuancheng. He entered Qichang monastery at Qianxi on the eighth day of the twelfth month, 1676. His recorded sayings were edited by his disciples Zhizhi and Zhiyuan.

A NUN — the second abbess of the Fushi ('Lion-Subduing') convent at Meixi, succeeding her teacher QIYUAN XINGGANG. On Xinggang's death in 1654 the leadership was given jointly to her and to her dharma-sister Yichuan Chaolang; when Yichuan died, Yigong was left in sole charge. Her recorded sayings survive in one juan, taken down by Mingyuan, with a preface by Gao Yiyong and a colophon by her dharma-sister Yikui Chaochen. She stands in the Linji line Miyun Yuanwu → Shiche Tongcheng → Qiyuan Xinggang → Yigong Chaoke.

masters.notes: A Yuan-dynasty Linji master, dharma heir of DONGYAN JINGRI (1221-1308), and the eighteenth-generation descendant of Linji. He was abbot of Baosheng at Qingyuan from 1299, of Dingshui Chan monastery from 1313, and of TIANTONG from 1329. He died in 1357. His recorded sayings were compiled by ten of his dharma heirs, among them Zhenru Wenqi and Wuzuo Wenshu; the preface is by Xingzhong Zhiren.

Name Yunfen, style Yuzhao, sobriquet Xiaotang. Of the Wu clan of Jingling; his father Yan was a district licentiate and his mother, of the Xu clan, was widowed early and kept a lifelong fast, reciting the Lotus daily — the boy would stand beside her with folded hands and listen, and vowed to become a monk to repay her. His mother assented; his clan did not, and forced him to marry. AT TWENTY HIS WIFE DIED and he was free at last. He was tonsured under the Dharma Master Xuancui at Liantai monastery in Yingzhou and took full precepts from the Vinaya master Sanmei. In the chaos of the dynastic collapse he hid on Mt Yuquan in Jingnan and studied the sutras three years, until a passage in the Lotus — the great white ox, 'stout and strong, its pace level, swift as the wind' — stuck in him. An elder told him: 'Master the whole canon and you are still caught in the fish-trap. If the sage's mind is not penetrated, you will not escape birth and death. Chan flourishes in the south. What is a pair of straw sandals to you?' He set out — and at his own gate found his mother dying, and stayed to nurse her and bury her before going. He met TUIWENG [HONGCHU] on the road in the spring of 1650. On New Year's Day 1651, during an intensive seven-day retreat, he came forward and bowed; Tuiweng struck him; he made to speak and Tuiweng struck him again: 'Are you trying to make Buddhism out of it?' — and at that word he was through. He offered Li Bai's poem as his verse of attainment, and Tuiweng laughed: 'I rejoice with you. Today you have reached your home village.' He held Qianming on Lushan from 1657, then Chicheng, Guangxian, Tongquan, Zizhi and Dongyan, and finally revived HONGSHAN BAOTONG BAOGUO monastery at Ezhu at the governor's request. When a monastery's officers proved unruly he simply shook out his robe and left: 'I have cut open my belly and gouged out my heart for them morning and evening and cannot alter their habits. I am ashamed of my thin virtue. I dare not learn to be a viper clinging to its den.'

Abbot of Tianyuan monastery at Nanpu (Wanxian, Sichuan) and a dharma heir of MINSHU RUXIANG, who was himself an heir of Poshan Haiming. He had at least two dharma heirs of his own, Huanzhu Ming and Chunbei De, both of the thirty-seventh generation.

A man of Minxian in Fuzhou, of the Deng clan. When KUCHAN ZIJING was teaching at Yishan he went to see him. One day Kuchan asked: 'Since once seeing the peach blossom, right up to now he has never doubted — where is it that he does not doubt?' The master ROARED WITH LAUGHTER AND WALKED STRAIGHT OUT, and Kuchan deeply approved him. When Kuchan moved to Lingyin, he served as inner secretary; he went home to see his aged mother. He became abbot of the King Asoka (Yuwang) monastery at Qingyuan (Ningbo).

A Wuning man of the Chen clan. He became a full monk at seventeen and went to Chan master An of Yan'en, who sent him on to HUITANG ZUXIN at Mt Huanglong. There he kept the assembly's hours but his questions and answers came to nothing — until, having been reading Xuansha's sayings, he grew tired and took a walk; walking fast, HE WALKED OUT OF HIS SANDAL, and stooping to pick it up, HE HAD A GREAT AWAKENING. For ten years he refused abbacies; he finally took Taiping at Shuzhou, then HUANGLONG itself. He was a celebrated letter-writer and a friend of the poet Huang Tingjian and the philosopher Cheng Yi. He died in 1117 and was titled Chan Master Foshou.

Abbot of Longshan at Chenzhou and a dharma heir of MINSHU RUXIANG, who was himself an heir of Poshan Haiming. He was a prolific teacher: the lamp lists five heirs under his name — Bailu Tianchang Hui, Pufeng Changming Jiong, Longshan Liurun Gao, Yunqi Dadu Ding, and Yuanling Zhiding.

A man of Changshu (Haiyu) in Suzhou, of the Qian clan. He came to WANFENG SHIWEI and asked after the real meaning, and awakened under Wanfeng's staff; he served as HEAD MONK (首座) in Wanfeng's assembly and taught from a divided seat. Wanfeng sent him a verse of entrustment — 'Tortoise-hair I hand over to my children and grandchildren; rabbit-horns I pick up and ask the ford of…' — and Shen Guan, the vice-prefect of Hai'an, who studied under him and later composed WANFENG'S OWN STUPA INSCRIPTION, wrote in it that he had 'long studied at the seat of Reverend Haizhou, the master's DHARMA-HEIR DISCIPLE.' When Wanfeng died in 1381 Puci helped compile the recorded sayings, sought the prefaces, and set up the stone of the stupa inscription. Much later, in 1441, he succeeded to the ABBACY of Dongming as its second-generation abbot. He died in 1450, ninety-six years old and seventy-four years a monk.

A man of Yingshan in Shunqing prefecture, northern Sichuan, of the Luo clan — a family of scholars in which 'every gate had passed the examinations.' He was born imposing in appearance and unusual in frame. At eight he lost his father and kept the fast with his mother; that same evening a yellow dragon dozens of yards long was seen soaring over his head to the clouds, and when he pointed his brother said: 'A dragon.' He became the chief dharma heir of CHUIWAN GUANGZHEN, and on Chuiwan's death in 1639 SUCCEEDED HIM AS ABBOT of Juyun monastery — the man through whom the Sichuan Juyun line continues. He was later abbot of Dizang, Yinweng, QINGZHONG, Yunyan, Baosheng and Zhiping. He died in 1668, aged 66.

The twenty-fifth generation of Linji, resident on Mount Tianmu. He came to consult YIFENG NING of Dagang, the twenty-fourth generation, who esteemed him as a vessel of the dharma and conferred a verse on him: 'Patriarch after patriarch has no dharma to hand on; every man has it of himself. You receive the dharma of no-handing-on — quickly now, pass it to those who come after.' Ascending the hall, he said: 'Holding up a flower and smiling — that is growing a branch off the side of the trunk. Facing a wall and settling the mind — that is painting legs on a snake. Here with me there is no Chan to practise and no Way to study; I simply make each one of you into a buddha and a patriarch straight off. Do you trust that far?' Then, after a long silence, he slapped his knee: 'The sword is named Juque; the jade comes out of Kungang.' His heir was Yeweng Zhenxiao, and through Yeweng the line runs to Wuqu Rukong and Wuhuan Xingchong.
Founder of Donglin Temple on Mount Lu. First patriarch of Chinese Pure Land Buddhism.
Foremost disciple of the Fifth Patriarch in the traditional account. Leader of the Northern school emphasizing gradual cultivation.

One of the most influential Tang dynasty Chan masters. Born 709 in Sichuan. Founded the Hongzhou school, producing 139 dharma heirs. Known for 'this mind is Buddha' (即心是佛) and 'ordinary mind is the Way' (平常心是道). Pioneer of unconventional teaching methods including shouts and blows.
Author of the Essentials of Sudden Enlightenment. Mazu called him the 'Great Pearl'.
Awakened by Mazu's 'This very mind is Buddha.' Became a recluse on Damei mountain.
The 'Boat Monk' who spent decades ferrying passengers. After transmitting to Jiashan, he capsized his boat and drowned.

Co-founder of the Caodong school. Born 807 in Kuaiji (Shaoxing, Zhejiang). Created the Five Ranks (五位偏正) teaching and the Jewel Mirror Samadhi (寶鏡三昧). Enlightened upon seeing his reflection crossing a stream. Had 26 dharma heirs.

Silla monk of royal Jinhan lineage who studied under Mayu Baoche in Tang China. Founded the Seongju-san school, one of the Nine Mountain Schools. One of the longest-lived of the Nine Mountain founders.
Co-founder of the Caodong school. Systematized Dongshan's Five Ranks teaching.

Heir of Xuefeng Yicun and close dharma brother of Changqing Huileng, with whom he appears in paired dialogues. Produced twenty-six dharma heirs, making him one of Xuefeng's most prolific successors. Appears in Blue Cliff Record cases 8, 22, 23, 76, 91, 95 and Book of Serenity case 71.
Founder of the Fayan school, last of the Five Houses. Emphasized integration of doctrinal study with Chan.
Caodong lineage patriarch. Teacher of Dayang Jingxuan, the last living Caodong lineage holder.
Huanglong branch master at Donglin Temple on Mount Lu. Teacher of the poet Su Shi.
Dharma brother of Yuanwu Keqin. Subtle, penetrating teaching style.
Key link in the Huqiu lineage.

Founder of the Jogye Order, the dominant school of Korean Buddhism. Uniquely among Chan/Seon masters, Jinul achieved three distinct awakenings entirely through reading texts rather than through face-to-face transmission: first from the Platform Sutra, then from Li Tongxuan's commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra, and finally from Dahui Zonggao's letters on hwadu (huatou) practice. He synthesized 'sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation' (dono jeomsu) as the normative Seon path, harmonizing Seon meditation with Hwaom (Huayan) doctrinal study. He revitalized Korean Buddhism from his base at Songgwangsa, which he rebuilt as a 'community of the Samgha jewel.' Attested in Buswell (1991), The Korean Approach to Zen: the definitive English-language study of his thought and legacy.
4th National Teacher of Suseonsa. Named Royal Teacher (Wangsa) in 1259.
Founded Shizi Lin (Lion Grove Garden) in Suzhou. Combined Chan with Pure Land.
Obscure transmission link in the Taego-to-Hyujeong chain. First documented in a 1625 source. Poorly attested.
67th Caodong patriarch. Studied at Shaolin under Xiaoshan, then retreated to Bingshan for 20 years.
Dharma brother of Miyun Yuanwu under Huanyou. Founded a separate Linji branch. Teacher of the imperial Chan line.
Revived Chan in southwest China (Sichuan). Called 'Little Shakyamuni.' Founded Shuanggui Temple (1653). Had 87 dharma heirs.
Yuan-Ming transition. Shaolin Caodong transmission. Dates approximate.

Originally from Weinan in Huazhou (present-day Hua County, Henan). First studied under Qingfeng, then continued under Fayan Wenyi. His enlightenment came through the famous "fire boy seeking fire" exchange: after Qingfeng told him the fire boy comes seeking fire, Fayan rejected his intellectual understanding, and when he returned to ask again, he achieved deep awakening. He served as abbot of Baoen Monastery in Jinling (modern Nanjing), capital of the Southern Tang kingdom.

A Qing Caodong master of Guyu, abbot of Xiangtian in Yue, and an heir of Shiyu Mingfang. His four-fascicle recorded sayings survive. He appears in his teacher Shiyu's record attending him in his last illness, asking the old question 'there is one who is not sick — who is he?' His own heir was Daxiu Jingzhu of Nanhua at Caoxi.

From Langzhong (surname Yang, mother Xu), born on the 15th day of the 6th month of 1626. Orphaned at sixteen when his district was overrun, he fled to Hanmian, saw the slaughter, and took tonsure. Hearing that Zhangxue Tongzui was teaching at Jingming, he went to him; Zhangxue asked if he could read, he said no, and was sent into the hall — where one night at the sounding of the watch 'a thunderclap in empty space' shattered the lump in his chest. He followed Zhangxue east to Tiantong and back, served him some twenty years, and was charged by him with the Caotang seat. He was still alive in 1686, aged 61.

From Zhongnan in western Shu (surname Li), tonsured at nineteen under Daxiu Xian and trained in Yogacara and the Lankavatara under the treatise-master Gaoyuan Yu. Illness at Diaoyucheng convinced him that doctrine was not enough and he turned to Chan. When Poshan Haiming returned from Tiantong to Sichuan and was installed at Taiping in Liangshan, he went to him; after several rebuffs, the sight of a collapsing mound of earth broke him open 'like the bottom falling out of a bucket.' He received Poshan's dharma in 1643, held seven monasteries across Guizhou, and died on the 15th of the 8th month of 1678, aged 69, with forty-three dharma-heirs.

A Qing Caodong master and heir of Xiangtian Jinian Jingxian, whose recorded sayings he himself edited (fascicles 2 and 3). He held Nanhua at Caoxi, Bailian and Dingyin at Zuili, Miyin in Huzhou and Tianhua at Yuecheng, and left a twelve-fascicle record of his own. He died on the 15th of the 8th month of 1656, aged only 42, with twenty-three years in the robe.

From Zhongzhou (surname Yang), he had his opening on the 'ten thousand dharmas return to one' and went to Wanfeng; he was sealed by Minshu Ruxiang, travelled everywhere, and returned to the gorges to inherit Minshu's dharma in the line of the old man Poshan. He held Sansheng at Neijiang and then went north, being installed by the Prince of Shuncheng at the Zhenru cloister by the White Pagoda. In 1683 he returned to Sichuan to sweep his teacher's stupa at Wanxian. He was still alive at seventy-nine, on pilgrimage to Putuo.

From Neijiang (surname Li, mother Yao), born at midnight on the 15th of the 10th month of 1610. Tonsured in infancy under Qingran of Guzi mountain, he was set going by the Lotus line 'even one raised hand, even one small bow of the head, all complete the Buddha-way' — 'is becoming a Buddha as easy as that?' Hearing that Poshan Haiming had brought the Jinsu robe and bowl into Shu, he came out of his hermitage to him, and after Tiantong, where the sound of the board opened him through, Poshan sealed him. He opened Yumen at Niushan, Jingming at Hanzhong, Caotang at Baoning and rebuilt Zhaojue in Chengdu at seventy-six; he compiled the Jinjiang chandeng. He died on the 26th of the 12th month of 1695 (Jan 1696), aged 86.

An heir of Fogu Xingwen, whose recorded sayings he edited. He succeeded his own teacher in the two seats the latter had founded — Caoxi at Pinghu in Jiaxing (from 1681) and Xianglin at Taicang near Suzhou (from 1682). His own record in two fascicles was compiled by his heir Mingsong. His dates are not recorded.

From Dazhou in Shu (surname Hu), tonsured at thirteen and set on pilgrimage at twenty. He first met Miyun Yuanwu at Jinsu — asked about his face before his parents were born, he took the stick and felt at ease — then Shiche Tongsheng, under whom a 'not mind, not Buddha, not a thing: what is it?' and a thunderous shout stripped him. He finally received the seal from Wanru Tongwei at Longchi in 1652. He held eleven monasteries across the north — Tianjin, Xiongxian, Zhuozhou, Tanzhe in the Western Hills, and Zhongpan on Mount Pan — and died on the 10th of the 8th month of 1673, aged 72; his stupa is under Zigai peak.

From Jintan (surname Chen), tonsured in his twenties under Gaoyuan at Yaojiang and fully ordained under Muchen Daomin at Tiantong. He worked on the koan of Nezha dismembering himself and had an opening, and presented Daomin with fifty-three verses on the Huayan, which Daomin praised. By his own account he followed Daomin through seven monasteries and attended him for thirteen years before receiving the dharma. He then held Dajue at Qingzhou and Jinsu at Jiaxing, and died on the 24th of the 11th month of 1673, aged 54; Lüyan He was among his heirs.

From Tongxiang in Jiaxing (surname Qian, mother Shen), born on the 7th of the 6th month of 1604. A hard boy who learned riding and archery at fourteen and meant to take a commission, he was turned by the sight of slaughter, went vegetarian, and at twenty-nine, on reading the Platform Sutra, abandoned his household and was tonsured at Jingshan under Wuyi. He was struck open by Miyun Yuanwu at Tiantong ('I do not know how to practise either'), was ordained by him in 1634, and after three years of labour broke through on striking a pillar. He was invited out to the Chandeng hermitage at Loujiang in 1669 and died on the 5th of the 2nd month of 1670, aged 67.

From Lingling (surname Jiang), born on the 4th of the 8th month of 1621; illness at thirteen persuaded his father to let him take the robe. He was tonsured by Jianqu at the Dongle hall and wandered to Tiande, Xilian and Luohan; Qiezhuo gave him the name Yiwei. In 1653 he read the recorded sayings of the Old Man of Yishan, was astonished, and brought him to his own hermitage; on the Buddha's enlightenment day of 1657 he received his charge. He held Hongsheng, Shoufo, Shengming, Zhusheng, Baojing and Zuisheng, and died on the 7th of the 9th month of 1684, aged 64; his stupa stands to the right of Benshan monastery at Nanyuan.

A man of Xizhou, a learned scholar before he took the robe, who studied with the living masters Dayang Jingxuan and Liangya of Fuyan on Nanyue. Reading Yunmen's recorded encounters he had a sudden awakening, and settled in the stupa of Chan master Hongjue on Mount Yunju, where students flocked to him and he was known as the Stupa-master Gu. He first preached at Zhishan; in 1037 Fan Zhongyan, governing Poyang, invited him to Jianfu. He died on the 4th day of mid-winter, 1045.

Lay surname Xiong, of Qijiang county in Yu (Chongqing). Born at the zi hour on 21/2 of 1605. At thirty, awake to the emptiness and suffering of body and world, he went to Mt Huayin to venerate Samantabhadra, met the master Changbai, and was tonsured and fully ordained by him. Changbai died six months later and he took over the cloister's affairs, resigning after four years to study in Jiangnan. Invited by Liu Sande of Sichuan to Baiyi pavilion on Mt Hu, he went; he later paid respects to Poshan Haiming, travelled to Emei, and sat in seven monasteries in succession discussing the Surangama, Perfect Enlightenment and Diamond sutras. When the dynasty fell in 1644 he hid in Yelang in Sichuan for eight years. In the 9th month of 1653, hearing that Poshan was at Jincheng temple in Liangshan, he went to him, followed him to Shuanggui, and there - the conditions ripe - became his dharma heir. He soon returned to Yuzhou and held Chongyin, then Zhiping, Shibao, Yuantong, Hongfu and Baolian. He died on 18/9 of 1673, aged 69, with 38 dharma-years.

An heir of Tian'an Bensheng of Jinsu, and thus a grand-heir of Muchen Daomin. He held the Longquan hermitage on Mount Wu in Huzhou, the Shizi Lin at Tiaocheng, and the Dongchan monastery on Mount Long in Anji, and left a seven-fascicle record compiled by Chengchun. Only the first character of his dharma name (He) is preserved; his dates are unrecorded. A preface to his record by the elder Xiaoxi calls him 'a thousand-league colt of our house' and rejoices on behalf of 'my dharma-brother Sheng of Jinsu' — his teacher.

A Yuan Linji monk of Cixi and heir of Liao'an Qingyu, whose recorded sayings he helped edit (fascicle 2). He was installed at Mingyan Dafan on Mount Tiantai in 1357, moved to Longhua Baosheng in Hangzhou in 1364, and in 1374, under the new Ming, took Jinshan Longyou at Zhenjiang. He left a one-fascicle record of his own; his heir was Qingyi. His dates are not recorded.

From Fuqing in Fujian (surname Chen), turned toward the gate by chancing on the Zhengmai in a temple at Wushan, tonsured at nineteen. He worked three years on the character wu without result, changed to 'the ten thousand dharmas return to one' under Wuyi at Gushan, then found real footing under Miyun Yuanwu at Huangbo, was ordained by him, and followed him out of Fujian to Jinsu — where, by his own account, six years of toil left him still unmatched. He was finally sealed by Poshan Haiming, whom he followed into Sichuan and served as western-hall elder. He opened Longpan, Nianhua, Baolin and Lengqie, held Huangbo twice, and died in the 7th month of 1651, aged 54.

From Yongchuan in western Shu (surname Zhang), born on the 30th of the 1st month of 1637; his father carried him into Guizhou. Tonsured at sixteen under Zhiru of Dongshan, he took the ten precepts at twenty and at twenty-one met Lingyin at Diancheng. In the winter of 1661, serving as precentor at Lingyin's retreat at Guanyin monastery in Doubao, he received the dharma on the Buddha's enlightenment day. He taught across Yunnan and Guizhou — Qingyuan, Huaguang, Yuhuang, Dengjue, Yuange, Yuantong — and went up to Tiantong to sweep Miyun's stupa. He died in the 1st month of 1701, aged 63, and his bones were brought back to Dongshan.

From Jiangdu in Weiyang (surname Shi), sent at twelve to the Tianning monastery of his prefecture; he was tonsured by Shaolin Song of Jingci, given the robe by Tieniu Yin of Lingyin, and took Longxi Zuxin of the Dongtang cloister as his teacher of record, serving him five years. Roused one night by the thought that Bodhidharma's heirs had been ordinary men like himself, he set out at dawn and travelled the south, coming at last to Wude Juetong, who was then preaching Songyuan's dharma at Jianfu in Poyang; he followed him to Fuyan and Huazang and was matched to him 'as lodestone to iron.' Coming out at Banshan in Jiankang in the early Chunyou years, he raised the incense as Wude's heir. He held Jinshan, Luyuan, Shushan, Chengtian, Zhong Tianzhu and Lingyin, was summoned to Jingshan in 1277, and died on the 24th of the 4th month of 1280, aged 82.
A Qing Linji monk, recorded only as a disciple of Yuan'an Benliao (遠菴本僼) of Ruiyan and Tiantong. Nothing else about him is preserved: no dates, no seat, no recorded sayings, no stele.

From Kunshan (surname Lu), driven to leave home when his sister-in-law's corpse stirred. Tonsured at twenty-one at Tiantong and ordained three years later, he studied with Muyun Tongmen and then attached himself to Muchen Daomin (Hongjue), from whom he received the dharma after fifteen years of hammering. He was installed at Shending in Tanzhou in 1656, succeeded Daomin in the seat of Tiantong in 1661, and then held Ruiyan (1670), Pingyang (1674) and Baiyun (1679). He died in the 4th month of 1682, aged 61; his heir was Yikui Yuankui.

A Northern Song Linji master, dharma heir of Guyin Yuncong (Guyin Cong). The Xu chuandeng lu files him under 'the heirs of Chan master Guyin Cong' and records his exchanges; Xiyu Jingduan and Cuiyan Xianchou came from his gate. No dates survive.
Compiler of the Blue Cliff Record, the most celebrated koan collection in Chan.

A Southern Song Linji monk and heir of Songyuan Chongyue, twentieth generation from Huineng. He taught at Jianfu in Poyang and then held the Huazang Chan monastery at Changzhou (the Baozhong Xianbao Huazang), later moving to Fuyan and Huazang. It was at Jianfu that Xuzhou Pudu came to him and took his dharma. Only a handful of his sermons survive; his dates are not recorded.

From Lin'an in Hangzhou (surname Ruan), whose family lived at the foot of Mount Tianmu — whence his other name. Tonsured at sixteen by Zhiyue of the Zhenxiang monastery, he went to Hunyuan Tanmi at Jingci without result, then to Foizhao Deguang at Ayuwang, who questioned him on the flag and the wind and approved him. But hearing that Songyuan Chongyue was teaching Ying'an's dharma at Jianfu in Rao — and that in his room he drove monks out with the stick at the first hesitation — Wenli suddenly let go of all he understood, went to him, and 'obtained Songyuan's house-dharma, and so became his heir.' He opened at Huiyun in Lin'an in 1212 and held Guangshou, Nengren, Fuquan, Jingci and finally Tiantong. He was learned in the Yijing and exchanged words with Zhu Xi and Yang Jianhu. He died on the 10th of the 10th month of 1250, aged 84.

A Ming Linji monk of the Qinling mountains, and the recipient of the dharma from Jingshan Huaibao. He is a hinge, not a figure: almost nothing of him survives beyond the fact of the transmission, and he owes his place entirely to the pedigree that runs through him down to Chuiwan Guangzhen and the Juyun house of Sichuan. Chuiwan's own stele concedes that for Tieniu and his heir Yueming, unlike the ten masters above them, 'only the words of their meeting and the verse of entrustment are recorded.'

links.label: DILA Authority A019881 (his teacher 荊山懷寶)

masters.notes: A Ming Linji monk of Hangzhou (surname Qian), who taught at Taigang (Dagang) in Nanjing and was styled Great Master Yuanming Pujue. He stands in the line running from Wuji Mingwu through Yuexi Cheng, and transmitted to Tianmu Baofang Jin of Hangzhou. He died on the 3rd of the 9th month of 1491, cranes circling the hall.
Argued all beings possess buddha-nature. Championed sudden enlightenment, anticipating Chan.

Sixth Patriarch and pivotal figure in Chan history. Born 638 in Xinzhou, Guangdong, to a poor family. Received secret transmission from Hongren after composing a verse demonstrating sudden awakening. His Platform Sutra (六祖壇經) established the 'sudden awakening' teaching. All Chan lineages descend through his five principal dharma heirs. His mummified body is preserved at Nanhua Temple.
Ancestor of the Caodong lineage. Author of the Cantongqi (參同契, Harmony of Difference and Sameness). Along with Mazu, one of the two great branches of Tang Chan.
Third generation Heze lineage. Transmitted to Suizhou Daoyuan.
Resided at Guizong monastery on Mount Lu. Known for dramatic teaching methods.
Famous for answering every question by raising one finger.

Silla monk who received transmission from Zhangjing Huaihui in Tang China. Founded the Bongnimsan school, one of the Nine Mountain Schools of Korean Seon. His lineage traces through the Mazu Daoyi tradition.

Founder of the Sagulsan (Mount Sagul) school, one of the Nine Mountains Seon lineages of Korea. He traveled to Tang China and trained under Yanguan Qi'an, a direct disciple of Mazu Daoyi, practicing for six years before receiving dharma transmission. Returning to Silla, he established Gulsan Monastery as his base and built one of the most active Seon communities of ninth-century Korea. His lineage maintained strong ties with the Mazu school's emphasis on everyday-mind-is-the-Way. He received lavish royal patronage, and his stele inscription is an important source for early Korean Seon. Attested in Zutangji (952): records his awakening under Yanguan Qi'an after six years of practice.
Principal dharma heir of Dongshan. Major monastery on Mount Yunju.
Direct ancestor of the Fayan school. 'What is this?' about a rock triggered Fayan's awakening.

Heir of Xianglin Chengyuan, both from Sichuan. Teacher of Xuedou Chongxian, whom he awakened with two blows of a fly whisk. Xuedou stayed five years and later compiled Zhimen's discourse record. Key link transmitting the Yunmen school to its greatest poet.
Reviver of the Linji school. Pioneered verse commentary on old cases (songgu).
Huanglong branch master. Teacher of lay student Zhang Shangying, the Song chancellor.
High-ranking Song official who became devoted Chan patron. Author of Hufa lun.
One of the most prominent female Chan masters. Known for her sharp repartee.

Dharma heir of Songyuan Chongyue. Teacher of Wuzhun Shifan, through whom his lineage produced Xueyan Zuqin and Gaofeng Yuanmiao. Teacher corrected: the roster had Songyuan Chongyue, who was his dharma-brother, not his master. Both were heirs of Mi'an Xianjie -- attested by two independent lamp records, which place him under a Mi'an Xianjie succession heading.

Most historically consequential heir of Wansong. Appointed by Kublai Khan to restore Shaolin Monastery, where he installed the Caodong lineage as the dominant transmission. Composed the 70-character generation poem still used to name Shaolin monks today, institutionalizing the lineage. Through him, Wansong's line became the 'unbroken' Shaolin Caodong transmission continuing through the centuries.
Yuan dynasty Linji master. Dharma heir of Zhongfeng Mingben. His line continued through Wanfeng Shiwei to the Ming revival.

Early Ming Linji master in the Zhongfeng Mingben line, heir of Wanfeng Shiwei. Active at Baofeng monastery; his transmission continued through Tianqi Benrui and eventually reached Yunqi Zhuhong, the eighth Pure Land patriarch.
One of the 'four great monks' of late Ming. Spearheaded the Jiaxing canon printing project. Died in prison.
Dharma heir of Miyun Yuanwu. Teacher of the eminent nun Qiyuan Xinggang. Used huatou (critical phrase) practice.
Chinese Chan master who emigrated overseas in 1654. Entirely Chinese-trained; his departure was a loss for Chinese Chan. CBETA: J27nB193.

Sixth-generation Shaolin Caodong master, heir of Songting Ziyan. Served as abbot of Shaolin Monastery in the early Ming, maintaining the Caodong transmission through the Yuan-Ming dynastic transition.

Only dharma heir of Yongjue Yuanxian. Established Gushan Yongquan Monastery as a hereditary Caodong dharma-transmission seat. The Gushan Caodong line continued through his successors for 250 years, eventually producing Xuyun.

Second patriarch of the Niutou (Oxhead) school. He trained under Farong at Mount Niutou and formalized the contemplative practices Farong had developed, emphasizing the teaching that all dharmas are empty and that the mind-ground is originally pure. He appears in the Jingde Chuandeng Lu (juan 4).

Of the Chen clan of Ziyang, Chengdu, born on the twenty-fourth day of the first month of 1613. In his own account, a corpse in a stream being eaten by fish turned his mind to impermanence; asked his tutor over the Analects line 'hearing the Way in the morning, one may die at evening' where the Way is when the breath does not return, and got no answer, he shut the book and resolved to leave home, starving himself for days until his parents relented. He was tonsured at Baofeng monastery on Jingju mountain. He called on Xinxuan, Yinxin, Miyun Yuanwu and Wanfeng, then late in life entered Tiantai and attended Linye Tongqi for seven years, receiving the seal. He held ten seats over his life, the longest being the ancient Fengxue monastery in Ruzhou, which he restored. He died at Jinsu cloister in Xincai on the thirteenth day of the fourth month of 1676, aged 64.

Of the Qian clan of Kuaiji, Shaoxing, descended from the royal house of Wu-Yue; born on the twenty-seventh day of the fourth month of 1634. His father, childless at thirty-seven, prayed to Guanyin, and his mother dreamed a Tiantai monk entered the room. Born with his eyes sealed shut for forty days, he was opened (says his own account) after a wandering monk told his parents the child's pure eye simply would not yet look on filth. He was tonsured at twenty-two, ordained four months later, called on Yunyan of Liling and Erzhan of Shishuang, and awakened watching a waterfall fall from the sky on Mount Huangyan. He called on Yulin Tongxiu, Muyun, and Hongjue, and finally received the mind-seal from Yuan'an at Tiantong. He held Yuezhang Shousheng, Yonglong at Jingshan, Shending Zisheng, Ruiyan and Tiantong.

A dharma heir of Bie'an Xingtong. He took the seat at Jiedai monastery in Wenzhou on the fifth day of the fifth month of 1696, and also held Ciyun at Wuxi. His attendants Purun and Faquan recorded his discourse record in three fascicles; Yang Yongjian wrote the preface. Almost nothing else survives: his record is verse and dharma-talk, with no life attached.

Of the Zhang clan of Tongchuan (Sichuan). He studied under Yun'e Xi and received his transmission, then went out as abbot of Fahai monastery in Xichuan. He preached at Funing monastery in Lingxia (Ningxia). His discourse record runs to two fascicles.

Of the Li clan of Neijiang, born on the fifteenth day of the eighth month of 1626. He was tonsured at twenty-three (1648) under Zhangxue Tongzui at Yumen. In 1654 he accompanied Tongzui to pay respects to Poshan Haiming at Shuanggui. He was fully ordained in 1657 under Tongrong at Yaofeng, called on Eryin Xingmi at Longyuan, and returned to Jingming. In 1660 Tongzui handed him the source-scroll and the whisk. From 1670 he held Zhugu Chan cloister, then Zhaojue in Chengdu, Chaoyin, and Bore. He was still alive in 1693, aged 68. He edited his master's discourse record; his own runs to twelve fascicles.

Of the Shen clan of Songzhou; his father was named Lun, his mother of the Ren clan. Born on the eighth day of the fourth month of 1660. His mother dreamed Guanyin told her the child was no householder and must be given a good name. Sent at one year old to Rushan at Miaojue monastery, he was ordained under Shenghui. Reading the Lotus at a donor's request, he stuck on the line 'the father young, the son old', found no one to ask, and left Songzhou for Zhaojue. He served a year under Zhangxue, went home, sealed himself in for three years, and returned to Zhaojue, where Foyuan Chegang now held the seat; after being beaten out of the abbot's room and struck repeatedly on the path, he broke through and received the transmission. He held Zhaojue at Weifeng, Chongshan, Dabei, Wuliang and Fazang. His discourse record runs to six fascicles; his heirs number eighty-three monks and six laymen.

Of the Zhao clan of Mianyang in Chu; his father was named Shijie, his mother of the Du clan, a family in the Confucian line. Orphaned young, he was tonsured at sixteen at the West Chan hall of Donglin monastery in Huang'an, Huangzhou — the very place the Fifth Patriarch first crossed. At eighteen, spurred on by his uncle-in-dharma Tongshan, he broke his ties and set out. He went first to Miyun at Taibai peak, then to Ruigong at Longhua on Mount Bian and Feigong at Jinsu in Wuyuan. Weary of wandering he built a hut at Jiangyin and rested some years, then went to Longchi and met Wanru Tongwei, from whom he received the milk of the dharma. He was made abbot of Ruru hermitage at Jiahe, then Puji cloister in the capital (1656), then restored Haiyun and Baoguo, and ended at Wanshou. He died on the ninth day of the fourth month of 1670, aged 60, in his fifty-third year as a monk, after six great abbacies; ten men received his dharma.

Of the Jiang clan of Tianshui in Qinzhou, born on the third day of the third month of 1647. He lost his mother at three and his father in boyhood, took a wife of the Wang clan at thirteen to eke out a living with his stepmother, and at fifteen left the world for the Haihui hall in his own prefecture under the elder Taixu; his wife died soon after. Fully ordained at eighteen. In 1666 he went south; his master told him 'here we do not know Chan — Zhaojue in western Shu is Yuanwu come again; go and see him.' He went to Zhangxue Tongzui, who slapped him across the face and later set him on the 'original face' case, but after some years he made no headway and left, calling on Changpo, Danzhu and Lianyue with no result. Finally he came to Nouyun at Caotang and received the transmission in 1669. He was abbot at Guhuang and the Dabei cloister in Guanxi.

Of the Xu clan of Fengling in western Shu, a family of Confucian scholars; born on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month of 1638. Precocious — at six he could recite and explain the Confucian classics. At ten he was tonsured alongside Wanfeng Shan and served Qingzhong Tiebi Huiji; the two novices were famous in the assembly for their quick tongues and their verses. Told by Qingzhong to make a verse on a lamp, he answered on the spot: 'Bright as a lightning flash, it can pierce the void; a lamp in time to come — is it bronze, or iron?' He was ordained at Chongsheng, went to Wuyun, and returned to his master, who wrote him a transmission verse. He kept the record-keeper's office and attended Qingzhong for twenty-one years, and on his death succeeded to the seat. He later moved to Fangguang and to Lengyan in Zhejiang. He died on the twelfth day of the third month of 1707, aged 70, and was entombed to the right of Qingzhong's stupa. Thirty-three monks and eighteen laymen received his dharma.

Of the Zheng clan of Yanguan (Haining); his father Qiru, his mother of the Lu clan. Born on the seventh day of the tenth month of 1587. A vegetarian from childhood, he entered Xingshan monastery at twelve under Zhouzhou and was tonsured at seventeen. Troubled by birth-and-death, he went to the old man Wuhuan at Chexi for instruction in practice, then attended Nanming Huiguang at Jingshan. Reading the Brahma-Heaven Sutra he had an insight and offered a verse; Nanming rebuked him, and he stopped writing verses. In the autumn of 1620, Nanming, gravely ill, put Xiangyan's verse to him; twice he moved to open his mouth and twice Nanming shouted him down, and when he nodded, Nanming handed him the transmission verse: 'A dharma neither given nor received, a mind neither given nor received; given to the handless one, it snaps the sinews of empty space.' He held Puming at Yunfeng in Fujian and died on the eleventh day of the tenth month of 1642, aged 56, in his thirty-ninth year as a monk.

Of the Hu clan of Long'an in western Shu. He left home at nineteen and was fully ordained at twenty-two, then walked the Jiangnan circuit, calling at the gates of the great masters and finding an entry at each. In 1667 he visited Shaolin, passed Fengxue, and met Yun'e Xi; the connection took, and he stayed close to him for six years, receiving the seal. In 1672 he entered Qin and opened the dharma at Xingfu Chan monastery in Jingyang, then moved to Guangjiao, Qingfu, Dunhuang and Jinsu. In 1684 he took Xingshan, and in 1688 Fengxue — his master's seat. He left a discourse record and the Qiaokong yixiang, twelve fascicles each.

Of the Xia clan of Fuling, a leading local family. He entered a monastery young and studied for years under Wansong; when Wansong died he went to Tiebi Huiji and received his transmission. He opened the dharma at two places — Huilong in Fu and Tanhua in Zhong — and died at Huilong at the age of fifty, which his stele-writer calls the kindness of dying at home. Disciples in both Fu and Zhong raised stupas for him. His record survives in a single fascicle; the man who wrote his stupa inscription admits he never met him and had not yet read it.

Of the Chang clan of Puzhou in Hedong, Shanxi; his father styled Lushan, his mother of the Zhang clan. In his own words: at sixteen, looking up at the blue sky one summer evening as the sun set, he thought 'the world is so wide — why be penned in here and spoil my good roots?', and resolved to leave home. At twenty he dreamed of a flood on the Yellow River throwing up a flower ten feet high, and a wandering monk who said 'I have come to take you to my home.' He slipped away from his parents, went to Putuo, and was tonsured under Ruxiu. He served in kitchens and gardens, never sparing himself. At twenty-five he came to Miyun Yuanwu at Jinsu and vowed not to leave the hall until he had awakened; Miyun struck him across the head twice and he got nowhere. Seeing a monk reading the Wanfeng Record, he took up 'the ten thousand dharmas return to one — to what does the one return?', swept everything he had learned into the sea, and at twenty-seven put his question to his own master, then West Hall at Jinsu. He rebuilt the ruined Tang seat of Guishan, holding Miyin monastery on Mount Dawei from 1637, and died there in the spring of 1649, aged 50, passing the succession to his disciple Huishan.

Of the Yue clan of Yongfeng village on the north road of Guozhou (Nanchong), born in 1626. His grandfather Menglong took the jinshi and served the Wanli emperor, was frugal and outspoken at court, and was reckoned a famous minister; the family kept to the Confucian line thereafter. As a boy he did not play, and was as grave as a grown man. He read a book once and put it down, yet could give back its sense in a few words that left old scholars straightening their robes. At seventeen he travelled to Mount Emei and was tonsured, and studied under Huijue Zhaoyi.
