He went to Yunnan and Guizhou and met the great master Zhizhi, who was sparing with approval but said only 'just so, just so' to him. Returning to Shu he met Huijue again, who likewise assented and handed him the robe and whisk: 'Take good care of it.' He was abbot at Wanshou in Renhuai, Longzhou in Jiading, Foxing in Ziyang, and finally rebuilt Xiangji at Nanchong. He died on the twenty-third day of the first month of 1667, aged 42.

Of the Liu clan of Leting in Luanzhou. He would not touch meat even in the womb, and was born still and grave. His mother died when he was eleven and his father put him under Xiaokong at Hanjiadao to be tonsured. At eighteen he sealed himself in a retreat and, reciting the Lotus, stuck on the line 'the Buddha's son dwelling in this ground is already the Buddha's own enjoyment', and doubt arose. He went to Panshan and put it to Liaozong Chaojian, who simply hit him; the doubt grew fiercer and he held one phrase waking and sleeping. Watching the mid-autumn moon with the assembly, he drew a circle in the air and offered a verse; Liaozong approved it, gave him the source-record, and made him record-keeper for five years. From 1688 he was abbot of Wanshan in Luanzhou, then Shifo at Gaoshan, Huayan at Shengjing, Dizang at Ningyuan, Chaoyang at Qingshan and Shengyan at Leyi — over twenty years' teaching, a rare northern (Zhili/Liaodong) house.

A Caodong master. The lamps say he was of the Zhang clan of Shangyu in Kuaiji, tonsured as a boy under Chengzhao Daoning, that he called on Zhenxie Qingliao at Changlu at twenty with some result, and then went home to Hongzhi Zhengjue at Tiantong, who acknowledged him as a true son of the inner room. He opened the dharma at Butuo in 1137, then Wanshou, Jixiang and Xuedou; in 1176 he was ordered to take Jingci monastery in Lin'an, and in 1180 retired to Xuedou. His own stupa inscription tells a different story (see below). Thirteen of his heirs are named.

Of the Fan clan of Jiazhou (Jiayang), born 1634. At ten he was tonsured by Huijue Zhaoyi and served him closely; seeing a corpse, he had an insight. He was abbot of Xiangguo monastery in Chongqing (Yuzhou). He edited his master's discourse record in three fascicles; his own runs to one. He died on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month of 1674, aged 40. His heir was Yitang Faxiu of Xiangguo, Chongqing.

Of the Zhuang clan of Jiangdu, Yangzhou; his father Jifang, his mother of the Shi clan, who dreamed an old monk lodged with her before his birth. Born on the seventeenth day of the third month of 1612. He lost his father at thirteen and, wondering where the dead go, resolved to leave home. At twenty he was tonsured at Zhongshan in Jinling; the next year he went to Ruibai Mingxue at Bianshan and asked how to settle birth-and-death. 'Who gives you birth-and-death?' — 'I don't know.' — 'What have you been practising?' — 'Reciting the Buddha's name.' — 'Who recites? And what is the Buddha?' He was left with nothing to say, and the doubt grew. Sitting the summer at Jiezhu, he looked up one night at a man lighting a lamp and broke open. Ruibai tested him hard and beat him repeatedly before acknowledging him. When lineage-forgery was rife, Ruibai had him open the canon and compile the Chuandeng zhenge, fixing the genealogy of the five houses. He opened the dharma at Yanshou in Puqi in 1654 and held Yunyan at Ningzhou, Yaoshan and others. He died on the twenty-fourth day of the intercalary seventh month of 1672, aged 61; forty men received his dharma.

Of the Chen clan of Linhai, Taizhou; his mother of the Lin clan. At seven he entered the village school and never needed a lesson twice. Before he came of age he asked his parents to let him enter the sangha and was tonsured under Jizhao at Jingshan. He called on Lingshi at Jingci and on Yiyuan, then went with Mu'an Cong to Zhuyuan Miaodao at Jianyan monastery on Mount Zituo in Taizhou; barely had he opened his mouth on the 'wu' case when Zhuyuan shouted, and he awakened outright. He was abbot of Lingyan on Mount Xiang and then of Ruiyan in Huangyan. In 1374 a Japanese embassy asked the Ming court to send him to teach in Japan; nearing seventy and ill, he declined. He died on the tenth day of the seventh month of 1386, aged 78, in his fifty-ninth year as a monk, having written: 'Seventy-eight years, no dharma to speak of; the last word — the pillar wags its tongue. Bah!'

Of the Han clan of Yanguan (Haining), born on the thirteenth day of the tenth month of 1576. He resolved on the monastic life as a small child and was tonsured at Xingshan monastery in Zuili under Qinquan. He took the full precepts from the elder Guxin, then went into retreat at the old hermitage of Chexi on Mount Baiyun at Shuangjing and did not go out of doors for three years. One day he picked up a scrap of paper from the ground bearing the line 'Knowing the direction, one knows he has gone; but the one who goes does not arrive at a direction' — and had an insight. He brought it to the old man, who sealed him and made him head monk. He served Chexi at Jingshan for eight years, and the old man gave him the robe and a transmission verse. He then shut himself in a death-retreat at Yongqing monastery at Gaoting for four years. He made three vows: never to take a public seat, never to handle temple business, never to gather disciples. He died sitting, on the twenty-seventh day of the eleventh month of 1620, aged 45, in his twenty-third year as a monk. His heir was Yuanhu Miaoyong.

Of the Long clan of Tongchuan. His father died when he was eleven (or twelve) and he was tonsured under the old man Sanshan Denglai at Gaofeng; fully ordained at twenty-two. He heard Sanshan raise the case of Nanquan's pitcher and goose and had an insight, then worked the 'wu' case for a year until Sanshan raised Baizhang's opening of the fields and, at the words 'he spread his hands', broke through completely and was sealed. When Sanshan died in 1685 he succeeded to his seat. He restored Fayu monastery on Mount Putuo, converting it from a vinaya house to a Chan one — its first Chan abbot — and also held Yongshou at Dongyuan in Wulin. He compiled the Xudeng zhengtong, one of the very lamp records this harvest depends on, and the chronological biography of his own master. He died on the first day of the tenth month of 1717, aged 57, in his forty-fifth year as a monk.

Of the Qu clan of northern Chu (Chenxi); his mother of the Wang clan. Born on the twenty-third day of the ninth month of 1618. From infancy he loved to look at Buddhist images. Coming of age, he heard a monk recite the Lotus line 'if one with wisdom hears it, he can believe and understand', and the wish to leave the world arose. In the collapse of the dynasty he abandoned his home and fled into Guizhou, where he was tonsured at the Guanyin grotto in Anshun by the elder Taixu and took the ten novice precepts; two years later he left for Hanguang and was fully ordained. Set to work on 'the face before your parents were born' he made no progress, and went to Yuechuang Chelu, who hit him twice and told him he was a dullard and to go back to the hall. He vowed to seal himself in until he understood; one night at the fourth watch, heavy with torpor, he fell to the ground and lost all consciousness — and when he came round, his limbs would not move, sweat streamed off him, and the doubt melted like a hundred-catty load set down. He came out and Yuechuang tested him on dozens of cases and confirmed him. He was abbot of Wanshou at Taiping in Annan, Puguang at Songkui, and Puxiang at Ciyun. He died in 1684, aged 67, in his forty-fifth year as a monk.

Of the Wu clan of Poyang. He was received by the monk Zhenchun Mu at Bao'en monastery at five and ordained at seven. The Central Asian monk Kongjian saw him and thought him remarkable, and sent him to Yuansou Xingduan at Jingshan, who made him record-keeper; Yuansou said of him, 'Recorder Ren is a tiger, and winged.' He came out as abbot at Yunding and Chongbao in Yuezhou, and at Huqiu and Wanshou in Suzhou. He was learned in the inner and outer canons and especially deep in the Book of Changes. In the Hongwu era he was summoned to the capital with Chushi Fanqi and Mengtang Tan'e and lodged at Tianjie monastery; his memorial pleased the Ming founder. He spent his last years at the Songlin hermitage. He died on the nineteenth day of the third month of 1382, aged 74, in his sixty-seventh year as a monk. He left the Danju shigao.

Of the Fu (or Chuan) clan of Shangrao, Xinzhou. At eight he became a boy-attendant to the elder Chuan of Jingde monastery, who set him to bow to Guanyin; one night he dreamed the bodhisattva stroked his head, and thereafter books opened themselves to him. Struck by the Platform Sutra's phrase about fire burning the sea-floor, he went to Wuyi Yuanlai at Boshan, who set him on the Boatman Monk's case; he held it walking, standing, sitting and lying, and had an insight in the mill-shed when the millstone's nose pulled loose. He then sealed himself in for six years and reached the source; he wrote the Song of the Snow Barrier, and Wuyi, pleased, opened his door and made him head monk. He took the seat at Yingshan in 1627, and on Wuyi's death in 1631 the assembly pushed him to succeed at Boshan. In 1636 Huqiu and Miaoxing in Hangzhou invited him. Falling ill in autumn 1637 he resigned, sailed south, and reached Yingshan on the first of winter; he died on the eleventh day of the tenth month, aged 53, in his thirty-first summer.

Of the Ge clan of Tanyang. Feeding monks at Jingci in Hangzhou one day, he happened to open the Platform Sutra and it came to him as something long familiar. When Fojian was ordered to take Jingshan, he and Tianjie Ri went together to study there and got the essentials. He then went to Duanqiao Miaolun and worked at it hard, asking for instruction eleven times; sitting bolt upright one evening he suddenly saw the lamplight in front of him and broke open. He came out as abbot of Ruiyan in Taizhou. He died on the seventh day of the first month of the first year of Zhiyuan. His heirs included Wujian Xiandu, Jingtang Gu and Yiyuan Ling.

Of the Chen clan of Shanghai (Yunjian). Tonsured at eighteen under Wuhai Xue and fully ordained at twenty. He called on Gunan Men and Xuedou Yun, then went to Ruo'an Tongwen at Jiashan, served him long, entered the inner chamber and received the transmission. He lived in retreat at Daqian and Puti in Qizhou, then held Li'an monastery at Nanjian in Hangzhou — where over four separate terms he was the fifth and longest-serving abbot — as well as Longyou at Jinshan and Zhulin at Jiashan. He also wrote the Liangzong jueyi in the Linji-Caodong lineage controversy. He died in 1694 aged 71, in his fifty-third year as a monk, and was entombed to the right of Li'an. Thirty men received his dharma.

A monk of Zhugong (Jiangling). He is remembered in a single exchange: coming to Wunian You, he was asked, 'Trekking county to county, roaming prefecture to prefecture — what in the end is it all for?' He said, 'The great matter of birth-and-death. I ask the master to ferry me across.' Wunian said, 'Are you a man of Jingzhou, then?' He stands in the Juyun branch's reconstructed line of Dahui Zonggao, between Wunian You above him and Tieniu Deyuan below.

Abbot of Dagang in Nanjing and of Guang'en monastery in Beijing. In 1452 he was ordered back to Dagang in Nanjing and granted the title Cishan. When Jingcheng, a monk of Puji monastery on Wutai who had worn himself out on the sutras without settling his mind, came to him for confirmation, he put a few questions that Jingcheng could not answer, set him on 'does a dog have buddha-nature', and on his awakening gave him the robe and whisk.

First Patriarch of Chan and traditionally the 28th Indian patriarch. Born as a prince in southern India, possibly of the Pallava dynasty. Arrived in China c. 520, reportedly met Emperor Wu of Liang who asked about the merit of his works; Bodhidharma replied 'no merit.' Settled at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song, where tradition says he sat in wall-gazing meditation (壁觀) for nine years. His teaching emphasized direct transmission outside scriptures. Named Huike his dharma heir after Huike demonstrated wordless understanding.
Author of the Song of Enlightenment (證道歌). Said to have attained awakening in a single night's meeting with Huineng.
Known for 'The mind-moon is solitary and round; its light swallows the ten thousand forms.'
Obscure link figure in the Beomnang-Daoxin lineage. Known only from the Jijeungdaesa stele at Bongamsa (893 CE, by Choe Chiwon). Transmitted the dharma from Sinhaeng to Hyeeun.
Teacher of Deshan. Their encounter with the blown-out candle is one of Chan's most celebrated awakening stories.
Dharma heir of Danxia Tianran.
Slammed the gate on Yunmen's leg, triggering his enlightenment. Called 'Chen the Sandal-Weaver.'
Woman Chan master who defeated seventeen traveling monks in dharma combat.
Dharma heir of Shishuang Qingzhu (807-888). Dates corrected from d.950 to d.903 per lineage chronology.

From Hebei. Taught at the South Hall (Nanyuan) of Baoying Monastery in Ruzhou with an extremely strict, confrontational style. Critical link in the Linji lineage: only through his line (via Fengxue Yanzhao) did Linji's transmission continue.

Direct heir of Yunmen Wenyan, taught at Xinkai Temple in Baling (modern Yueyang, Hunan). Instead of written transmission documents, he used three turning phrases to convey the essence of the Yunmen school. Appears in Blue Cliff Record cases 13 and 100.
Last living Caodong lineage holder. Entrusted lineage to Linji master Fushan Fayuan to preserve the school.

Northern Song Yunmen master who served as abbot at nine major monasteries including Jinshan and Lushan Kaixian. Emperor Shenzong bestowed on him a Goryeo robe, golden bowl, and the title 'Chan Master Foyin.' Close friend and teacher of the poet Su Shi (Su Dongpo), with whom he exchanged the famous 'Eight Winds' letter.

Northern Song Yunmen master who served as abbot of several major monasteries. Renowned poet-monk whose verse explored how nondual insight applies to ethical decision-making in everyday life. His recorded sayings (yulu) circulated widely among Song literati.
Laywoman who achieved awakening. Notable female figure in Song Chan.
Yangqi branch Linji master. Teacher of Wumen Huikai, compiler of the Gateless Barrier. Gave Wumen the koan of Zhaozhou’s ‘No’.

Primary monastic heir of Wansong Xingxiu. Succeeded him as abbot of Bao'en Temple in Yanjing. Compiled two major koan collections — Konggu ji (Empty Valley Collection) on Touzi Yiqing's verses and Xutang ji (Empty Hall Collection) on Danxia Zichun's verses. Invited to the Mongol court in 1268.

Yuan dynasty Linji master, 19th generation (not 18th as sometimes claimed in Korean sources). Dharma brother of Shiwu Qinggong — both studied under Ji'an Zongxin. Gave formal dharma transmission to the Korean monk Naong Hyegeun at Jingci Temple in Hangzhou. Also served as abbot of Lingyin Temple. Authored Jingjuyin (淨居吟), over 200 poems. Attested in DILA Authority Database (A016698).
Transmission link during the darkest period of Joseon Buddhist suppression. Active when monks were banned from cities.

The most revered figure in Joseon-era Korean Buddhism, known both as a profound Seon master and as the warrior-monk who organized Buddhist militia (seungbyeong) to resist the Japanese invasion of 1592 (Imjin War). His treatise Seon'ga gwigam (Mirror for Seon Students) became the standard primer for Korean Seon practice, synthesizing Seon, Gyo (doctrinal study), and Yeombul (Pure Land recitation) into a unified curriculum still used today. At age 73, when the Japanese invasion began, King Seonjo called upon him to rally monks as soldiers; he mobilized thousands across the peninsula. He traced his lineage through Taego Bou to the Chinese Linji school, though Ahn (2019) has challenged the historicity of the intermediate links in this lineage chain. Attested in Jorgensen (2015): provides a full English translation and study of the Seon'ga gwigam.
Central figure of the late Ming Linji revival. Made his line the dominant Chan transmission into the Qing.

names: 寧波府天童山翁道忞禪師
masters.notes: First to succeed Miyun at Tiantong (1642). Summoned to Beijing as Chan teacher to the Shunzhi Emperor. CBETA: J26nB180, J26nB181.

Seventh-generation Shaolin Caodong master, heir of Ningran Liaogai. Served as abbot of Shaolin Monastery in the early-to-mid Ming dynasty, continuing the unbroken Caodong transmission established by Xueting Fuyu.
Based at Longshan Temple in Guangdong. Transmitted Miyun's Linji lineage to the Vietnamese monk Nguyen Thieu, who brought it to Cochinchina in 1665.

Third patriarch of the Niutou school. He resided at Mount Niutou continuing the tradition established by Farong and Zhiyan. Under his stewardship the Niutou community maintained its independence from the northern and southern Chan lineages centered on Hongren's successors.

A nun. Born 1606 in Hengzhou, Huguang, lay surname Liu. She read Tongji's Nanyue Chandeng lu, went to him for instruction, and sat forty-nine days and nights before breaking through; he tonsured and ordained her, she being thirty-four. After his death she went to Muyun at Helin and to Ruoan at Jiashan, and finally to Wanru Tongwei at Longchi, who sealed her. She held Huideng in Suzhou, Pudu at Xinghua, Guofu and Shanhu. Her record runs to four fascicles.

From Yongjia in Wenzhou, lay surname Ye. He was tonsured by Tuiweng Hongchu at Lingyan in Suzhou and later received his dharma. He held Guoqing and Zhenru on Mount Tiantai and Tongxuan, and in 1705 named Bin Yuanzhang to succeed him at Tongxuan. His record runs to eight fascicles; he also left a set of matching-rhyme poems to Hanshan.

'Crazy Ji'. From Linhai in Tiantai, lay surname Li. He was tonsured at eighteen at Lingyin under Xiatang Huiyuan and inherited his dharma. He drank, ate meat and drifted through the markets, and was called Ji the Madman; after Huiyuan died he went to Jingci under Dehui and served as secretary. He died in 1209, aged sixty, after forty-two years in robes. He became, over the following centuries, the most popular saint in Chinese Buddhism.

From Changzhou in old Yu (Sichuan), lay surname Jin, born 1606. Tonsured at Wofo monastery, he was set going by Poshan Haiming, then went to Tianyin at Qingshan, Xuejiao at Jingshan, and finally to Miyun Yuanwu at Tiantong, where he awakened one midnight at the sound of the bell. He spent six years in retreat on Lotus Peak. When Miyun died and Linye Tongqi took the seat at Tongxuan, Linye called him back by verse and gave him the transmission in the winter of 1644. He held Falun, Faxiang, Qizhen, Daming, Fashen, Longyuan and finally Bao'an at Qishan. He died in 1665, aged sixty.

From Yongfeng, lay surname Yu, born 1630. At twenty-one he left the world and became a monk under Xuejian Daofeng at Boshan, who gave him the Chuanzi 'hiding the body' case to work on; he broke through on the Poisao Duo story after a night of hearing ghosts cry. He received Xuejian's transmission in 1668 and held Boshan Nengren in Xinzhou, Gaoquan and Yingshan. He died in 1706, aged seventy-seven, after fifty-four years in robes. His record carries both an account of conduct and a stupa inscription.

From Dazhou in western Shu, lay surname Luo. He heard the Diamond Sutra at seven and was tonsured at eight by the long-browed monk of Lanhua monastery. He went to Wutai in the famine years of the late Ming, then south — to Yunwo, to Gunan Muyun (who gave him 'your face before your parents were born'), to Judé at Tianning, to Xuedou, Yunmen and Tiantong, and finally spent twelve years under Yulin Tongxiu at Bao'en. In 1661 he passed through Yixing, sparred with Eryin Mi, and received a whisk and verse. He held the Shuiyue Chan cloister at Jiangling and Tanhua monastery at Zhijiang, and edited Eryin Mi's record in ten fascicles.

Dharma heir of Yuzhao Yunfen (Xiaotang). He held Xinghua at Nanyun, Pilu at Fangguang, Faxing at Tongquan, and Ciming and Yijiao in Beijing. He was still alive in 1683, aged fifty. He edited his master's record in six fascicles; his own runs to six. One heir is recorded.

Lay surname Li. He was tonsured by Dongxu Xinguang and received the dharma from Guyun Pei. He held Yongzhen at Jianxi, Xiting at Bailu and Caoan at Qingyun, and gave the precepts at Qingyun in Fengcheng, Yuantong in Fuliang and Tianzhu in Chongren. He was still alive in 1737, aged fifty-six. His record runs to six fascicles.

From Wutang, lay surname Ju; fostered into the Zhang family of Danghu. He married and had a son. At twenty-seven a pair of dreams turned him toward leaving home; at thirty-one he abandoned his household and went to East Mountain at Tianmu to be tonsured by Bianzhi of western Shu, who set him on 'your face before your parents were born'. He met Miyun at Tiantong, then attached himself to Linye Tongqi, following him to Guanghua and Tongxuan. Linye gave him the transmission in the spring of 1649. He opened the dharma at Guanghua Chan monastery in Yuhang. Four or more heirs are recorded.

From Xinhua county, Baoqing prefecture (Hunan), lay surname Deng, born 1636. Tonsured at seventeen, he roamed with his master; reading Huangbo's Essentials of Mind set him going. He took the precepts from Qushan and later went to the Venerable Lüluo. He received the transmission from Hengxiu Falin in 1670 and held Mituo, Yuanming and Baojue in Yunnan. He returned to the Lüluo stupa-cloister ill in his last years and died in 1685, aged fifty, after thirty-two years in robes; his stupa stands to the left of the old man's.

From Taizhou, lay surname Yu, born 1630. He went to Tianning in his prefecture, where Jubo Jiheng was carrying on Lingyin's line and 'making the single lamp of Sanfeng burn north of the Yangtze'. He was tonsured at Jingye hermitage and took the precepts from Jiheng; he then went south to Judé at Lingyin, who told him 'your affinity lies at Tianning — go'. He returned, received Jiheng's dharma, and succeeded him. He held Jinghu on Lushan, Qingyun, Falun, Baiyun, Tianning at Yangzhou, Dajue, Jile and Qingliang. He died in 1688, aged fifty-nine.

From Tongcheng, lay surname Yang, born 1584; his father died when he was young and he served his mother. Tonsured at twenty at Julong hermitage on Jiuhua, he was given a verse to hold by Zibo Zhenke, took full precepts at Yunqi in 1608, and in 1610 went to Zhanran Yuancheng at Yunmen Xiansheng monastery in Shaoxing. Yuancheng broke him open — 'the four elements are false, the deluded mind is empty: who is dragging this corpse of yours here?' — and he came through on the seventh night. He succeeded Yuancheng at Yunmen, then moved to Bianshan in Huzhou and finally to Baizhang in Hongdu, nine seats in all. He died in 1641, aged fifty-eight; his whole body was interred in a stupa at Longhua on Bianshan.

From Tongbai in Nanyang, lay surname Gu, born 1610. He asked at ten, hearing a neighbour weep, 'everyone dies — what then?' He married at nineteen and left home anyway, was tonsured at Daolin monastery in 1630 and took full precepts at Baoguo the next year. A monk from the south told him 'you will never settle birth-and-death this way — there is a Chan road', so he went: Jiuhua, the southern sea, Fujian and Yue. He came to Ruibai Mingxue at Bianshan, was struck, and awakened at the sound of the bell during a seven-day sitting. He held Zhaoqing, Longfu, Longhua, Nengren, Yunmen Xiansheng, Foguang, Shanquan and Shanqing. He died in 1665, aged fifty-six. Forty-two heirs are recorded.

From Xi'an in Guizhou, lay surname Zhang. Tonsured at seventeen at Fahai monastery, he met Shanquan Dawei two years later, who set him on 'the ten thousand dharmas return to one'. He took full precepts on Mount Yunjiu, worked with Yuefeng on Tiantai, and returned to Shanquan at Songkui to be sealed. After his master's death he travelled ten years. His dharma-uncle Guyuan put him in at Tianlong; he moved to Songkui and back to Tianlong. Finding that the lamp records held nothing from Guizhou, he collected the recorded sayings of the whole province and compiled the Qiannan huideng lu.

From Zhangzhou, lay surname Lin, born 1005. Ordained at Chongfu in his home prefecture, he travelled widely — Fushan Fayuan, the hermit of Bajiao, Yuantong — and stayed longest with Beichan Zhixian of Tanzhou, under whom he awakened. Late in life he spent three years in the deep ravines of the Western Hills, then took the invitation to Fachang: a few old rooms in Fenning, Hongzhou, where he farmed with hoe and fire and was content. He died in 1081, aged seventy-seven.

From Daizhou (Shanxi), lay surname Bian, born 1608. He would not eat meat as a child and liked to sit still; he was tonsured barely past ten and travelled widely. He took full precepts from Miyun Yuanwu at Tiantong and had his first opening at the sound of a rockfall. He then went to Feiyin Tongrong and received his dharma. In 1661 he was installed at the Xuanfochang at Kunshan near Suzhou at the invitation of the Bordered Yellow Banner general Li and the local gentry; he later held Weimo monastery at Changshu. He died in the winter of 1678, aged seventy-one, after sixty-one years in robes, and his stupa stands at Weimo. Over twenty heirs are recorded.

From Changguo in Ming prefecture, lay surname Li, born 1242. Small of body and fierce of temper. He was tonsured by Zhiweng Deju and went to the bottom of the Caodong teaching under him. He held Shimen at Cixi, Xiangshan, Zhimen and Tianning, and finally Tiantong, where students came from Korea and Japan. He wrote the Baojing sanmei xuanyi. He died in 1324, aged eighty-three, after sixty-five years in robes.

From Lingling in southern Chu, lay surname Tang, born 1625; the youngest of four sons, orphaned early. He slipped away at thirteen to be tonsured by the master Hongren at Dading hermitage, took the seven-piece robe from the Venerable Wuxue the next year, and studied vinaya and the sutras. He found no connection with Shanci Ji at Nanyue; at Xishan he served Suigu Yuan for years and had his opening there, blowing on a dying cooking-fire that flared through the whole hermitage. But it was Baizhang Jingle who gave him the dharma, in 1647, after testing him on the Five Ranks. He opened Yishan in 1655 and moved to Xiangshan in Quanzhou. He died in 1688, aged sixty-three.

Linji master, a man of Nankang; dharma heir of Xuzhou Pudu. He was abbot of Lingyin in the early Yuan, was summoned to an imperial audience, and was granted the title Foguang Haiyin dashi ('Great Master Buddha-Light Ocean-Seal') on returning. His verses are said to have come out of his mouth already finished, as though composed beforehand. He compiled his master's recorded sayings. His heir was Tanfang Shouzhong of Jiangshan (Longxiang), through whom the line continues.

From Dongguan in Kuaiji, lay surname Xia, born 1561. His family was destitute after his parents died and he served as a postal runner; having misdelivered a dispatch and facing arrest, he fled to Yinfeng, who gave him 'who is it that recites the Buddha's name?' — and he had his first opening in three days and nights, aged twenty. Tonsured at Tianhuang, ordained at Yunqi, he sealed himself in retreat at Baolin and broke through on Qianfeng's 'raise one, not two'. Cizhou Fangnian, come south from Beijing, confirmed him. He opened the dharma at Yunmen Guangxiao in 1614, then held Jingshan, Dongta and Yunmen Xiansheng. He died in 1627, aged sixty-six. He revived the Caodong house in Zhejiang; six heirs, including Ruibai Mingxue (also in this batch). He wrote the Kaigu lu and the Zongmen huowen.

From Lishui in Chuzhou, lay surname Wu, born 1304. Tonsured at fifteen at Chanzhi monastery under Kongzhong Jia, he practised sitting so hard he went three years without sleeping through a night. He wandered Fujian and found no one; back home he rebuilt the old Fulin cloister on Mount Baiyun and read the Surangama and the Yuanjue. He got nowhere with Lingshi at Jingci or Duanya at Xifeng — but hearing that Wujian Xiandu was teaching on Huading he went, and 'at one sight cut out his own heart', serving him for years. He returned to Fulin in 1354 and later held Puci, Maoshan and Wufeng. Summoned by the Hongwu emperor in 1369 to the great assembly at Jiangshan, he went. He died in 1370, aged sixty-seven; his cremation yielded five-coloured relics.

From Songling in Wujiang, lay surname Yu, born 1604 into a bookish family — his father owned a cartload of books. Passing a mountain temple at sixteen he saw the Surangama and was troubled by it; he went to Tianyin Yuanxiu at Qingshan, who gave him 'your face before your parents were born'. He was tonsured at twenty-four at Li'an under Foshi, went to Miyun Yuanwu at Jinsu — 'fire-snakes burned my face, my bones and hair went cold' — and returned to Qingshan, where he awakened one night in a gale on the cliff. He held Li'an at Nanjian for ten years, and Zhulin, Longyou and Guloutze. He died in 1655 at Yingtian monastery in Wujiang, aged fifty-two. He compiled the Xudeng cungao. A dharma-brother of Yulin Tongxiu, the Shunzhi emperor's teacher.
From Hanzhou in Shu (Chengdu prefecture); dharma heir of Eryang Yuanqin. He died in 1534. His heir was Jingshan Huaibao of Zhugong.
Second Patriarch. Famous for cutting off his arm to demonstrate sincerity to Bodhidharma.
Received patriarchal robe from Zhishen in 702. Key link in the Sichuan Chan lineage recorded in the Lidai fabao ji.
Student Longtan transmitted line that produced Deshan Xuanjian.
Known for his teaching that the three poisons are themselves the three disciplines.
Dharma heir of Damei Fachang in the Mazu lineage. Teacher of Juzhi, to whom he transmitted the one-finger Chan teaching.
Known for sitting facing the wall when visitors came.
Known for the 'watch the dog!' koan.
Korean monk with the second-longest entry in the Zutangji (952). Studied under Yangshan Huiji of the Guiyang school. Uniquely synthesized Chan with Huayan doctrine.
Community of 1500+ monks. His students founded the Yunmen and Fayan houses.
'Cuiyan's eyebrows' koan — tested whether his teaching had been in error.
Caodong lineage patriarch. Transmitted the Caodong dharma from Tongan Daopi to Liangshan Yuanguan.
His two greatest students founded the Huanglong and Yangqi branches.
Taught Huang Tingjian using the scent of osmanthus.

names: 溫州淨居尼定光大師妙道
masters.notes: Female Chan master of the Southern Song.
Dharma heir of Songyuan Chongyue. Teacher of Xutang Zhiyu.
5th National Teacher of Suseonsa. Studied under Hyesim, Mongyeo, and Honwon.

Ordained at age nine at Tianning Temple in Haiyan, Zhejiang. Studied calligraphy under Zhao Mengfu and became one of the foremost Chan poet-monks of the Yuan dynasty, composing over a hundred Pure Land poems. Yunqi Zhuhong later ranked him first among the most eminent monks of the era.
Mid-Ming Linji master. His heir Wuwen Mingcong continued the lineage.

Hyujeong's foremost disciple, celebrated equally as a Seon master, military commander, and diplomat. During the Imjin War (1592-1598), he led monk-soldiers in combat against the Japanese forces, distinguishing himself at several engagements. After the war, he was sent to Japan as an envoy in 1604 and successfully negotiated the return of approximately 3,500 Korean prisoners of war, a diplomatic feat that made him a national hero. His combination of martial valor and diplomatic skill during Korea's greatest military crisis cemented the image of Buddhist monks as defenders of the nation, counterbalancing the Neo-Confucian narrative that Buddhism was socially useless. Attested in Joseon wangjo sillok and Japanese records: his diplomatic mission to Japan and the repatriation of prisoners are documented in both Korean and Japanese sources.

Founded the Pyeonyang-pa, the dominant branch through which ALL modern Jogye Order lineage traces. War lieutenant during the Imjin War (1592-98). More significant for lineage than his dharma brother Yujeong/Samyeong, who was more famous as diplomat.
Imperial Chan teacher to the Shunzhi Emperor. Titled Yulin Guoshi (National Teacher). Dissuaded the emperor from abdicating to become a monk.
Mid Ming Shaolin Caodong transmission. Teacher of Yuezhou Wenzai.

Chinese monk from Chaozhou, Guangdong who brought Linji Chan to Vietnam in 1665. Founded Thap Thap Di Da Temple and Quoc An Temple in Hue. 33rd generation Linji. Patronized by the Nguyen lords. His lineage (Lam Te) remains one of the largest in Vietnamese Buddhism.

Fourth patriarch of the Niutou school, bridging Huifang and Zhiwei. He maintained the community at Mount Niutou during the period when Shenxiu's Northern school was ascendant. He deepened the school's integration of Madhyamaka emptiness with Chan practice.

Lay surname Chen, of Shimen in Lizhou; styled Fazhu. His parents both died when he was twenty and he gave up his Confucian studies; at twenty-five, feeling he could never repay their kindness, he left the world and was tonsured by Changming Jiong at Mt Qixing in Cili. He worked on the huatou 'the three are-nots' and attended him three years, took full ordination under Yingxiu at Mt Long, then followed Jiong to Mingshan in Yuanzhou and served him seven years more, receiving his seal. He was abbot of Pufeng temple on Mt Tianyun in Chenzhou. He edited his master's recorded sayings and left two fascicles of his own; he had twelve heirs.

Lay surname Lin, of Houguan (Fuzhou). At fifteen his parents put him with his uncle Zhilong at Guangxiao in Wanling; he took the full precepts at eighteen. He called first on Tieniu Yin and travelled widely among the elders, keeping long company with Shaoshi Mu and Wuji Pai. He met Zheweng Ruyan at Tiantong - 'needle and mustard-seed found each other' - but knowing he was not yet settled he went to him again at Shuangjing, and there his lifelong doubt melted at a stroke. From 1228 he held Xiao Jingci, and then Xiangshan, Wanshou, Xuedou, Ayuwang, Jingci, Lingyin and finally Jingshan. In 1261 he was granted the title Fozhi chanshi. He died on 14/6 of 1263, aged 75, with 58 summers. His heir Yunfeng Miaogao carried the line on.

A descendant of the Han grand preceptor Qiao Zhou; his family lived below Mt Yang in Yuechi, Anhan. Born 7/10 of 1605 to Sheng Gong and his wife Yang. He recited the Four Books at five, knew the Spring and Autumn at ten, and after borrowing a Heart Sutra from a monk said 'this is the utmost of sages' and set his mind on leaving the world; at thirteen, about to be betrothed, he saw an old monk sitting under a tree looking like an ancient buddha, and left home. He lectured on the Surangama at twenty-five and drew crowds at Niushan and Huanglong. In 1632 he went to Poshan Haiming at Shuanggui and, after twenty-one days of total impasse, broke through at a shout from Zhu Weitai; Poshan made him head of the western hall. He was caught in the massacres of 1644-45; in the spring of 1645, held in a military camp at Liangshan, he announced 'I have never taken food that was not righteous - and shall I take pleasure in this, among spears?', stopped eating, and on the first day of the third month gave a final address, shouted once, sat upright and died, aged 41.

Lay surname Xu, a man of Jingmen. Abbot of the Neihuguo (Inner Protecting-the-State) monastery in Jingnan, where he opened the canon and took the seat in the 3rd month of 1686 at the invitation of the lay patrons Li Yufan and Lu Diaoyuan. He left four fascicles of recorded sayings, prefaced by three officials of the day.

Lay surname Hou, of Xinning in Kuizhou; styled Zhuanjing (Brick Mirror), sobriquet Shanhui. Tonsured in 1638 by Shipu Zhuo. Wrestling with the Nanquan koan he forgot food and sleep, and then 'the ice broke up' at his teacher's snow-day address, after which his repartee ran free. He called on Wanfeng and Hongjue, and received the seal from Bao'en Tongxian (Fushi). He held Huguo at Pingyue, Wanshou at Xingqing, Sheng'en at Wengan, Changsong at Huangping, and Fuhai at Gaoyou. He died in 1687 and his stupa stands at Yongquan cloister on Tiger Hill, Suzhou.

Lay surname Zhao, of Wuwei prefecture; styled Zisu. He left home at six under Shuijie Quan at Mt Simian, and later lived at Moyun hermitage on Mt Lu'an. At twenty-two he took the full precepts under the elder Yuan of Huishan, then studied vinaya with Jianyue at Huashan and called on Tianzhang of Guangjiao. At thirty-four he came to Wenruo Xingying at Fushan, who made him rector; after a seven-day intensive he broke through the ball of doubt, and became the direct heir of the Fushan elder in the orthodox Linji line. In the 8th month of 1672 he took up residence at the old Panlong monastery on Mt Zhongnan in Huazhou, and gave the ascent-of-the-hall there in 1678. He died 4/11 of 1689, aged 59, leaving twelve heirs.

Lay surname Zhuang, of Quanzhou. He came to the capital as a young man and was ordained at Tianqing temple after passing the sutra examination. He called on Nanchan Qingya at Sanqu, then studied the Huayan deeply under Dinghui Zunshi in Eastern Wu. Hearing that Lingyuan Weiqing had opened the dharma at Taiping, he went; at an evening session Lingyuan's words struck exactly at his illness and he came to himself. He entered his room, and Lingyuan forged him with the wisdom of distinctions and enjoined silence on him - he attended him for ten years. Foj:ian Qin later made him a seating master. He opened the dharma at Ganlu, then Zifu in Luzhou and Tianning in the Eastern Capital (Kaifeng). His conduct was so severe that he was nicknamed 'Iron Face'. He died seated, having taken leave of the assembly, on 27/12 of 1123, aged 59, with 32 summers. He had eight heirs, including Jiechen, who edited his record.

Lay surname Zhang, of Zhongzhou in Chongqing. A dream moved him to seek a master at twelve, but he was not tonsured until twenty. He took the precepts under Xiangya and worked on 'the ten thousand dharmas return to one - what does the one return to?'; one day body, mind and world fell away and everything was vast and empty. He then went to Poshan Haiming at Shuanggui, and afterwards followed Zhangxue Tongzui to Hanzhong, opening the dharma at Jingming; at his master's first discourse his breast opened, and he received the seal and succeeded him in the seat. He held Jingming and Baolin in Hanzhong and Shangshan temple in Yunnan fu. He died in 1694, aged 79. His heir was Feizhi Ming of Jingci in Jiangjin.

Lay surname Liu, of Changshu (Yushan) in Suzhou; styled Tianshu. Born 14/12 of 1632; the night before his birth his mother dreamt of the sun rising in the east. At one year old his left arm withered; an old monk passing by stroked his head and said 'this is a man of the patriarchs' place - the illness is not worth worrying about', so his father named him Liu Zu ('Liu the patriarch'), and he recovered. At fifteen he told his mother he was leaving and went to Maian De at Poshan; he was tonsured at nineteen. In 1651 he paid respects to Muyun Tongmen, and in 1656 took the full precepts under Feiyin Tongrong. Grinding wheat one day he went utterly still, and when a fellow monk pushed his hand and said 'why not put your back into it?', he shoved the millstone forward and broke through completely. When Muyun was about to die in the winter of 1671 he handed him the dharma robe, and Xingzhi succeeded to the seat at Helin. He died in the 10th month of 1680, aged 49; his stupa is in the eastern grove by the Cuckoo Tower at Helin.

Lay surname Yang, of Nanchong in Guocheng. He wanted to leave the world from boyhood but his parents refused, so he took up the Diamond Sutra as his practice. When both parents died in 1648, he was thirty - and he went at once to Fayu and was tonsured. Setting out south to study with Bai Zhai, he met Wuzhu, who set him on the 'ten thousand dharmas' koan; he called on Yunce, and then on Poshan Haiming, from whom he received transmission in 1659. He held Fozi temple on Mt Longyin in Pengxi, Guangde cloister in Suining, and Zifu cloister in Xichong. He had twelve heirs. Neither his death-year nor his full lifespan is known; the one fixed point is that in 1660 he was forty-two.

Lay surname Li, of Sanwu (Sanwu station); styled Biemu, childhood name Shanbao. He would not eat meat even in swaddling clothes, and as a small child, taken to the hermitage by his mother, would kneel with palms joined whenever he heard the sutras chanted. A dream at fifteen settled his resolve; his mother refused him, so he slipped away by night to Fuyuan hermitage and was tonsured by Hongjue. He took the novice precepts at Yishan, was set on 'the original face', and had an opening one day at the cry of a cat. He was fully ordained in 1659, followed Jingting to Yishan the next year, and in 1662 helped found Nanyuan. In conversation with his master one day he was seized with awe; at the fifth watch he heard the bell, the sweat poured off him, and everything he had held dissolved. He received transmission in 1677 and held Hongsheng at Nanyuan (Quanzhou) and Jisheng at Caoshan. Neither his death-year nor his lifespan is known; he was alive in 1697, aged sixty.

Lay surname Zhang, of Xiushui (Jiaxing); styled Wanru. At nineteen he was tonsured by Hanchu at Xingshan temple in his own prefecture. Four years later, moved at Yuanzheng temple in Tiaoshang, he pricked his blood and copied out the Lotus Sutra, then chanted it for three winters and summers without a break. Reading Yunqi Zhuhong's Chan Whip he took up Zhaozhou's 'No', and asked Wengu for guidance. An opening came while reading the Surangama; he crossed the Qiantang into Mt Yunmen and put the 'no-dream, no-thought' question to Zhanran. Then he went to Tiantong (Miyun Yuanwu) at Jinsu, and at thirty-nine he was thoroughly through. Miyun kept him on the mountain at his seventieth-birthday celebration in 1635. In the winter of 1640 he opened the dharma at Ruru cloister, then held Caoshan in Putian, and returned to Longchi when Miyun died. He died at the si hour on 29/10 of 1657, aged 64, with 45 dharma-years; he taught thousands and sealed several dozen heirs.

Lay surname Peng, of Weichuan village, Yunlin, Fuzhou fu; styled Guantao. Born in the spring of 1625. At nineteen, finding the taste of the world flat, he went to Mt Xiang to learn the dharma that leaves the world. He called on Tiesuo of Raoshan at Luyang and took the full precepts at the Longhu ordination platform in Shaowu. Sealing himself in a hermitage on Juexian peak in Xu, he turned over the line 'not thinking of good, not thinking of evil - which is the Reverend's original face?', and suddenly had an opening. After wide travels he came to Abbot Sheng of Tianjie (Juelang Daosheng) and received transmission. He held Chongxian Xianxiao on Mt Gaoting and Shouchang in Xincheng. He died on 10/7 of 1678, aged 54, with 35 dharma-years. His heir was Qiyuan Xingquan of Gaoting.

Lay surname Qiu, of Gui'an in Wuxing; styled Mingbiao, self-styled the Reverend At-Ease. At barely six he served Baoxian at Jiekong cloister on Mt Wu; he did not get the monk's robe until twenty-six. Watching a lion-dance he suddenly matched the mind-dharma, and went on to receive the essentials of the Surangama from the Tiantai master Renyue. Then he met Chan master Qiyue (Baojue); their meeting struck fire, and he leapt up unbidden and threw himself into the posture of a lion - which Qiyue approved, and from then on the monasteries elegantly nicknamed him 'Duan the Lion'. Chancellor Zhang Dun admired his way and invited him in person to open the dharma at Wushan; he later moved to Xiyu in Huzhou. He died on 5/12 of 1103, aged 74, with 49 dharma-years.

Lay surname Yan, of Wucheng; styled Yinzhong, sobriquet Songji. At seventeen he was tonsured at Mt Daochang, and then relied on Yuanxiu at Qingshan (Tianyin). He attended him long, and one day, hearing a thrush sing, had a great awakening; he received the dharma and succeeded to the seat at Qingshan. Illness took him to convalesce at Yangshan. One day he rose, bathed, changed his robes, sat cross-legged and wrote: 'In past years, at fifty, I knew my faults; this year, at fifty, I know where to stop. Do not say the sun comes out and affairs arise - trust in the plain, direct pointing.' He threw down the brush and died - then after a long while opened his eyes again and charged the assembly: on every new and full moon, gather and bow to the patriarchs of India and China, and then to the two ancestors of Longchi and Qingshan; do not neglect it. Then he closed his eyes and was gone. 22/8 of 1642, aged 50, with 34 dharma-years. His heir was Shending Yunwai Ze.

Linji master, dharma heir of Jie'an Wujin of Jinming (Jiaxing). His own dharma name is Zhenben. He is remembered mainly through his heir Tan'an Jijun, in whose recorded sayings his exchanges with his master are preserved - among them the question of how the insentient preach the dharma, where Jinming lifted a fallen stick of incense and Pingshan answered that the abbot's staff had gone leaping away.

Of Liutang in Songling (Gusu); a child of remarkable memory who is said to have recited a thousand words a day. Because his mother kept the pure precepts he came out of the womb, it was said, knowing nothing of blood and flesh. He went to Rizhu temple in Yuezhou at thirteen and was fully ordained at fifteen. He called on Shiwu Qinggong, then Lanmu at Sanqu, from whom he got the working of samadhi, and then Gumei at Gaoyang; returning home he set himself a limit and did wall-gazing for nine years, burning off a finger every three years - three fingers in all. One day it suddenly flashed clear. He went to Fulin, matched him in dharma combat, and was kept as head of the assembly, aged twenty-eight. Under the Hongwu emperor he was ordered to tonsure a thousand monks; at Fanchang the assembly asked him to open the hall on Mt Donglu. In 1407 the Yongle emperor again ordered him to Tianjie. He died having written 'Blank and abrupt, drifting and soaring - let it all be smashed to pieces, through every land and every mote', throwing down the brush and closing his eyes. His whole body was interred in a stupa on Mt Bafeng. His heirs include Wuji Mingwu.

Dharma heir of Mazu Daoyi, and abbot of Foguang temple in Luoyang; he had earlier lived at Jin'ge temple on Mt Wutai. He is best known for his exchange with Emperor Shunzong, put to him while Shunzong was still crown prince: 'Where does the Buddha come from, and where does he go in extinction? If he is said to abide constantly in the world, where is the Buddha now?' Ruman answered: 'The Buddha comes from the unconditioned and goes in extinction to the unconditioned; his dharma-body is the equal of empty space and abides constantly in the place of no-mind. Where there is thought, it returns to no-thought; where there is abiding, it returns to no-abiding. He comes for the sake of beings and goes for the sake of beings. The pure sea of suchness - still, and its substance constantly abiding.' In old age, living at Xiangshan temple by Longmen, he formed an incense-and-fire society with the poet Bai Juyi and joined the Nine Elders.

Ming Linji master of Xiushui; dharma heir of Xiao'an Xingmi. His one surviving encounter is with the monk who became his heir: Wunian Zhiyou of Shouzhou came to him, and he asked, 'Where have you walked?' - 'The south.' - 'And how is the Buddha-dharma there?' - 'The mountains and rivers are no different.' - 'How does my hand resemble the Buddha's hand?' Zhiyou stood a long time in silence, and Eryang said, 'Don't go saying there's no difference.'
Nun and direct disciple of the Second Patriarch Huike. One of few women in early Chan lineage histories.
Dharma heir of the Sixth Patriarch. Ancestor of the Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan lineages.
Most celebrated lay Chan practitioner. Dumped his wealth into a river and lived making bamboo utensils.
Famous for burning a wooden Buddha statue to warm himself. Studied with both Shitou and Mazu.
Fifth patriarch of Huayan and Heze Chan lineage holder. His Chan Prolegomenon is a landmark work classifying Chan schools.

A dharma heir of Baizhang Huaihai, resident in Yunzhou. The Jingde Chuandeng lu files him under Baizhang and preserves his exchanges; beyond that the record is bare. No birth or death year is recorded in any source I could reach — the roster's 800-860 has no evidence behind it and I have set both null.

Silla monk who received transmission domestically from Yeomgeo (a student of Doui), continuing the Gajisan school lineage. Did not travel to China. Attested in Korean stele records and traditional mountain school genealogies.
Woman Chan master who led her own monastery. Guanxi Zhixian bowed and served as her gardener for three years.
Originally a fisherman. Ancestral figure of the Fayan school. 'Three diseases' teaching.
Caodong lineage patriarch at Tongan Monastery near Nanchang. Successor of Yunju Daoying.
Dharma heir of Fayan Wenyi. Resided at Qingliang monastery in Jinling. Famous for the tiger bell koan. Dates corrected: previously d.938 predates teacher Fayan (d.958).
Founded the Yangqi branch, which became the dominant Chan lineage.
One of China's greatest poets. Deeply engaged with Chan Buddhism. Legend connected him to a rebirth of Wuzu Shijie.
His lineage became the dominant branch of the later Linji transmission.
Caodong master of the post-Furong northern lineage. Active in Hebei region during the Jin–Song partition.
Abbot of Tiantong monastery. Emphasized silent illumination (默照).
Known for extreme asceticism and fierce teaching style. His autobiography is a classic.

Korean Seon master best known as the compiler and printer of the Jikji simche yojeol (Anthology of Great Buddhist Priests' Zen Teachings), printed at Heungdeoksa temple in Cheongju in 1377 using movable metal type. This is the oldest known book in the world printed with movable metal type, predating Gutenberg's Bible by 78 years. Baegun traveled to Yuan China and received transmission from Shiwu Qinggong (Stone House), the hermit-poet of Tianmu mountain. His Jikji compiled essential Seon teachings from the patriarchs and was intended as a practical guide for practitioners. Attested in UNESCO Memory of the World Register (2001): the Jikji is recognized as the world's oldest extant movable metal type printed book, with the surviving second volume held by the Bibliotheque nationale de France.
Shaolin Monastery abbot. Teacher of Xiaoshan. Mid-Ming Caodong transmission through Shaolin.
Late Ming Linji master. Teacher of Miyun Yuanwu, the most influential 17th-century Chan figure.
Third dharma brother of Miyun and Tianyin. Controversially claimed transmission from the long-dead Yunmen Wenyan.
Yulin's student. Included in the Yongzheng Emperor's Yuxuan yulu.

Obscure transmission link in the Pyeonyang lineage between Hwanseong Jian (d.1729) and Cheongbong Geoan (1710-1793). No independent biographical sources survive. Known only from Joseon-era lineage charts. The 68th Korean patriarch in the Jogye reckoning.

Jialing Xingyin's dharma heir. 35th generation Linji (Yangqi branch). After him, the imperial Chan line faded — Qianlong shifted patronage to Tibetan Buddhism. Attested in DILA Authority Database (A026661).

Sixth and final patriarch of the Niutou school, residing at Helin Temple (Crane Forest Temple) in Runzhou (modern Zhenjiang, Jiangsu). His student Jingshan Faqin received the title 'National Teacher' (Guoyi) from Emperor Daizong, and his other famous student Niaoke Daolin ('Bird's Nest') became a celebrated figure through whom the Niutou lineage blended into the broader Tang Chan world.

Of the Li clan of Sangluo in De'hua county, Jiangzhou, born on the nineteenth of the eleventh month, 1621. Orphaned early, open-handed and hot-blooded, he was made a commander of a thousand men in the levies raised against the rebels — and after beheading three officers for breaking the law, something turned in him; he slipped away into the mountains under cover of a sortie. No one at Lushan would shave him; the old monk Zizhen of Donglin finally did. He worked as a cook, took full ordination in 1647, and was stuck for years on the 'dragging a corpse' line in Gaofeng's record until, crossing Ruo ridge in 1651, he stumbled in an ox-track and the thing in his chest broke like ice. He came at last into Jie'an Wujin's room, met him as if they had always known each other, and was given the seal. He died on the fifteenth of the ninth month, 1672, aged fifty-two; his disciples built his stupa at Donglin.

Named Daochong, self-styled Chijue ('utter fool'), of the Gou clan of Changjiang in Wuxin (Sichuan); his mother was surnamed Guo. He sat the jinshi examinations and failed, then took Buddhist learning at Miaoyin cloister in Zizhou, was tonsured by Xiuzheng, and studied the treatises at Dasheng Ci monastery in Chengdu. Out of the gorges in 1192, he found Caoyuan Daosheng and had a first opening under him. Songyuan at Lingyin then refused him a place for eight months and finally said: 'I threw the door wide open for him — he walked straight past it,' at which Daochong lost both mouth and ears and understood that Caoyuan's jeering and scolding at Miaoguo and Guifeng had been the whole teaching all along. He held Tianning, Jiangshan, Xuefeng, Lingyin, Fahua and Shuangjing, and was the thirty-sixth abbot of Ayuwang. He died on the fifteenth of the third month, 1250, aged eighty-two, sixty-one years a monk.

Surnamed Cao, of Danghu in Jiaxing. He asked his father to teach him the sūtras at ten, was working at the school of the ancestors at fifteen, and at twenty broke wide open; he took Xingshan Hongyuan as his tonsure master. Serving Puming (Yuanhu Miaoyong), he was asked 'My mind is uneasy — have you found peace yet?' and answered only 'Blue heaven! Blue heaven!' Another day Miaoyong raised a fist: 'Say a word.' Wuyuan slapped him; Miaoyong roared with laughter, and the thing was settled. He then sealed himself in retreat at Xingshan for more than ten years, came out to Yongzheng monastery in 1651, and died on the nineteenth of the fifth month, 1678, aged sixty-four.

Surnamed Han, of Boluo in Huizhou; styled Zuxin, called Shengren, 'the man left over.' He went to Kongyin Daodu (Zongbao Daodu) at Dongguan in Guangzhou, was set on Zhaozhou's 'no,' and after two years, hearing the case of the old woman seen through, broke open; Daodu said 'now you no longer doubt,' and shaved and ordained him at Lushan in the sixth month of 1639, in his twenty-ninth year. Arrested in Nanjing in 1648 with a manuscript recording the fall of the Ming, he became the first literary-inquisition case of the Qing and was banished to Shenyang, where he taught at seven great monasteries with five to seven hundred in the assembly. He died seated on the twenty-seventh of the eleventh month, 1659 (January 1660), aged forty-nine.

Named Puji, self-styled Dachuan, of the Zhang clan of Liuzhao in Fenghua; the youngest of three sons, given by his parents to the dharma. He was tonsured at nineteen at Xianglin cloister under Wenxian, studied vinaya and then Tiantai doctrine at Chicheng, and gave it up: 'Binding the body with precepts, splitting hairs over doctrine — how does that get past birth and death?' At Nengren in Yue he met Zhewong Ruyan, who asked where he was from, snatched away his sitting-cloth and struck him — and he came free on the spot. He held eight abbacies, ending at Jingci and Lingyin, and while at Lingyin compiled the Wudeng huiyuan (1252), the great synthesis of the five lamp records. He died on the eighteenth of the first month, 1253, aged seventy-five, having forbidden an expensive funeral and ordered his bones thrown in the river.

Styled Lianyue, of the Jiang clan of Yuechi. After his mother's death he heard a monk chanting the line about the 'burning house of the three realms' and turned from the world; he cut off his own hair, went to Fuling, and took the precepts under Poshan Haiming. Accompanying his master to a feast, he took a fall on the road — and in the exchange that followed, the dharma passed. He entered Dongyin monastery on Mount Jiuqing at Zunyi in 1658 and afterwards held Juelin, Baolun, Duda and Baoshou in Sichuan, and Longxing, Jingde, Yuquan and Tianhuang in Hubei. He compiled his master's records, for which the lamps call him 'a meritorious servant of Shuanggui.' He died on the tenth of the seventh month, 1691, aged seventy-eight.

Of the Wan clan of Panyu, born 1633. As a boy he got his father out of prison by shaming the magistrate in the road. At sixteen he went to Tianran Hanshi at Leifeng and was ordained; at seventeen, reading the Platform Sūtra at the passage on Elder Ming, he heard a cat cry, broke into a sweat, and felt the world split open — he went to his master at midnight and answered him with a cat's cry. At twenty-two he was sent on his master's orders out through Shanhaiguan to Qianshan Hanke, who thought him extraordinary and kept him three years. He took Haichuang monastery in Guangzhou in 1662 and held it twelve years, ordaining more than seventeen hundred. He died on the twenty-second of the ninth month, 1681, aged forty-nine.

Abbot at Yunju in Jiangzhou, dharma heir of Fozhao Deguang of Ayuwang and eighteenth generation below Huineng. He entered Yansheng Chan cloister on Mount Zhangxi in 1219, was invited in 1228 to the Zhenru Chan cloister on Mount Yunju, and later lived at the Donghu hermitage. His disciple Liaojian compiled his recorded sayings in one fascicle. No birth or death year survives in any source — DILA states this outright.

Of the Ye clan of Changshou in Yuzhou, born on the fifth of the third month, 1623 — a farming family, three generations at the plough. The wars destroyed his home: 'From Tianqi 1, when the rebels broke Yuzhou, to the jiashen year of Sizong, east and west of Shu, north and south of Ba, fields, houses, fathers and brothers were burned and slaughtered to nothing.' Orphaned and alone, he fled south to Qianzhou, met a monk from home, wept, and swore: 'If I do not leave home now, may I go the way of the old men of my village.' He was shaved by Dongming Xiao and named Fuhui, styled Sixiu. In 1652 a monk from Longmen told him of his master; he went, was shouted out of the room at the first meeting, and set to work on 'the ten thousand dharmas return to one.' He received the seal from Shanhui Wanbi (Zhuanjing) at Longmen and held Ciyun, Zhulin at Menghua, Wufu at Shunning, Fahua at Fumin, Mile at Chengjiang, and finally Songshan in Yizhou.

Of the Ke clan of Putian, born 1612. As a child the sight of hills and water made him want to leave the world; at eighteen he took the five precepts under Qiaoyun and devoted himself to nianfo, and at twenty-seven was tonsured at Guohuan monastery. Reading the Xuefeng record — Touzi pointing at a slab of rock and saying 'all the buddhas of the three times are in there' — he chewed on it half a year and got nowhere; then Baohua Ren at Cao shan raised his staff, touched him with it, and something opened. He went to Baichi Xingyuan of Jinsu at Mount Bai in Jianzhou, fitted him like needle to mustard-seed, and received the seal. He held Gushan at Xinghua, Jiuzuo Xingguo, Bao'en, Longhua Wanshou, Tongtian at Lushan, and Ximing on Mount Shi. He was still alive in 1691, aged eighty; his death year is not recorded.

Of the Zhu clan of Siming (Mingzhou). He was a full monk while still young and had mastered Tiantai doctrine when he changed his robes and went to Xuedou Mingjue, who sized him up and sneered: 'A lecture-hall abbot.' Stung, he went down the mountain, bowed back toward Xuedou and swore: 'If in this life my Chan does not surpass Xuedou, I will never go home.' He went to Letan and sat twelve years with the doubt unbroken; hearing that Yangqi Fanghui had moved to Yun'gai and could handle students, he went straight there, and before a word was finished the mind-seal was clear. After Yangqi died he studied on with his fellow-student Baiyun Shouduan. He held Baoning twice and died there. No dates survive in any source.

Born Chen Guobin at Gaoyang village in Ou'ning county, Jianning prefecture, on the fourth of the tenth month, 1614. He resolved on leaving the world at sixteen and was shaved by Ticong of Huangyan. Reading Zhongfeng's admonitions he felt something come clear; reading the Chuandeng lu he hit Zhaozhou's 'cotton shirt of Qingzhou' like an iron wall and could not get past it. He called first on Juelang Daosheng, then went to Miyun Yuanwu at Tiantong — and one word from him settled it. He served eight autumns at Miyun's side before taking a hut of his own. He held Cuiyan at Hongdu, then Huangyan, Baifa, and Foding in Jianzhou.

A Qing Linji master, dharma heir of Zhufeng Huanmin (1638-1707) and thirty-first generation below Nanyue. He opened the dharma at Changle Chan monastery. Only the first character of his dharma name (一) is recorded anywhere, and it is not expanded in any source I could reach. His recorded sayings survive in one fascicle, compiled by his heirs Mingman and Minghui. No dates.

Styled Sanyi, called Yu'an, of the Ding clan of Wulin in Qiantang, born 1599. He set his mind on leaving the world at fourteen and took the five precepts from Zhuhong at Yunqi; at sixteen a reading of Zhenjing's record opened something; he entered Zhenji as a postulant at twenty and was shaved at twenty-three. He went to Zhanran Yuancheng at Xiansheng, and Yuancheng entrusted him with the Caodong seal. Ill for years and worn to the bone, he called himself 'the White-Bones Wayfarer.' He held Longmen from 1635, then Huashan, took Xiansheng in 1643, Fanshou in 1650, Zhuming in 1656. He died on the eleventh of the tenth month, 1665, aged sixty-seven; thirty men inherited his dharma, of whom Zhe'an Jingfan is one.

Styled Weize, called Zhe'an, of the Ji clan of Wujiang in Gusu, born 1620. He left home at fifteen, was shaved at eighteen, heard Xuehang lecture on the Vijñaptimātratā at twenty, and while resting from communal labour at Bian shan heard a clap of thunder in the Zhengzhong pavilion and had his opening. He took full ordination at twenty-one at Ruiguang, called on Zhishi, Xueqiao, Yu'an and Tiantong, and in 1649, aged thirty, received the Caodong dharma-seal from Yu'an (Sanyi Mingyu). He held Zisheng at Zuili, Xiansheng at Yunmen, Husheng at Caoshan, Guangfu at Dongta and Tianhua at Dongguan. A fine calligrapher; his recorded sayings run to thirty fascicles. He died in 1692, aged seventy-three.

Surnamed Zhang, of Lingxiao in Shaanxi, born on the fifth of the twelfth month, 1662 (early 1663). His parents gave him to Jingyue at Lingshan monastery, who shaved him. At nine he was studying the Śūraṅgama and stopped short at 'if the original nature is pure, whence come the mountains and rivers?' At nineteen he took full ordination from Tenghuan of Xishan; at twenty-four he went to Gumei Dinglie on Mount Furong. In 1689 Dinglie sealed him in retreat in the Purple Bamboo Grove, where he broke through, and at Dinglie's death he received the entrustment. In 1691 he took the Miyin monastery on Mount Wei in Hunan and Guanghua at Furong. He died on the ninth of the fifth month, 1695, aged thirty-four, fourteen years a monk.

links.label: DILA Authority A018976 (his teacher 定冽)

masters.notes: Of the Zhou clan of Taizhou (Ninghai), born 1151. He was tonsured at Jingtu cloister, held Hanqing, Nengren and Guangxiao, then moved to Jiangshan and Tiantong, and in 1218 was commanded to Jingshan — the first monastery of the empire. He bore the title Chan Master Foxin. He is the hub from which four well-attested heirs hang: Yanxi Guangwen, Dachuan Puji, Huaihai Yuanzhao and Jieshi Zhipeng, each filed as 'eighteenth generation below Nanyue, heir of Zhewong Yan.' He died in 1225, aged seventy-five.
Qing monk of Fushan, disciple of Longchi Wanru Tongwei (龍池萬如通微禪師).

Of the Song clan of Ba county in western Shu, born on the twenty-fifth of the fifth month, 1611. Orphaned young and raised by his grandmother, he left home at twenty-three at the Baihe hermitage under the old monk Xingkong and practised the perfection of patience. A wandering monk sent him to Poxue (Xuebi Yinluan); he served six years, and when his master died he set out to travel. At Chongqing he had his understanding confirmed. He went into Guizhou and opened the dharma at Baoguo Chan monastery on Mount Muni, founded Chuanfa monastery at Xishan, and later held Qianming at Deshan in Dingzhou. He died on the fifth of the tenth month, 1666, in the guest hall of Tiantong monastery — where he had gone to sweep the stupa of the patriarch Miyun. His disciples carried his bones back to Guizhou and built his stupa by the Phoenix Pool at Xishan.

links.label: DILA Authority A010702 (his teacher 印巒)

masters.notes: Named Liaowu or Mingwu, called Wuji, also Canggu ('silkworm bone'); of the Mo clan of Anyue county, Tongchuan prefecture, Shu. He left home at twenty at Luowei monastery in Dingyuan under Benzhen, then went round the great monasteries of Shu. The Qing Bodhisattva raised Zhaozhou's 'no' for him and something opened; from then he carried the word 'no' walking, standing, sitting and lying. He went into the hills at Fanchang to Guzhuo Jun, who saw him, was astonished, and gave him the dharma on one word. He then settled at Daolin monastery at Jiguang for over forty years. In 1444 the new ordination platform at Wanshou monastery brought a summons to the capital, where he was made a master of the school. He died at dawn on the first day of the fourth month, 1446, aged sixty-six, forty-eight years a monk; his Daolin Record survives. Chushan Shaoqi and Guting Shanjian came from his gate.

The Seon master who ordained Jinul. Jinul's father, having prayed at the temple for his sickly son, gave the boy up at eight; Jinul 'went to the Seon master Chonghwi, a distant descendant of Caoxi, took tonsure and received the full precepts, and thereafter had no fixed master — he followed only the Way.' The record of Songgwangsa, written in 1207 while Jinul was still alive, says the same in its own words. Nothing else about him survives: his own teacher is named by no source I can reach.

A monk of the western capital (Luoyang), dharma heir of Yiyan Daoxian of the Xiangguo monastery. He died on the eleventh of the eighth month, 1458 — the Xudeng zhengtong records that he 'leaned on his staff and was transformed.' His heir was Yuanqin.
Third Patriarch. Attributed author of the Xinxinming (信心銘, Faith in Mind), one of the earliest and most influential Chan poems.
Listed in the Platform Sutra as one of Huineng's disciples.
Daughter of Layman Pang, depicted as matching or surpassing her father in insight. Died moments before him.

First Korean monk to transmit the Seon (Chan) lineage to the Korean peninsula, inaugurating the 'Nine Mountains' Seon movement. He traveled to Tang China and studied under Xitang Zhizang, a direct heir of Mazu Daoyi, receiving formal dharma transmission. Upon returning to Silla, he found the doctrinal Buddhist establishment hostile to Seon and was unable to teach openly during his lifetime. His disciple Yomgo later founded the Gaji Mountain school (Silsangsa), the first of the Nine Mountains Seon lineages. Doui is thus honored as the patriarch who planted Seon in Korean soil, even though its flowering came after his death. Attested in Zutangji (952): records his study under Xitang Zhizang with a transmission dialogue confirming his awakening.
Crucial link in the Caodong lineage as teacher of Dongshan. 'Whole body is hands and eyes' koan.
Known for dancing with the rice bucket — 'Bodhisattvas, come eat!'

Originally a sutra lecturer in Guangzhou; redirected to study with the boatman-monk Chuanzi Decheng, who pushed him into the river, triggering his awakening. He then established a major monastery on Mount Jia (Jiashan) in Hunan, where he taught for decades. His heir Luopu Yuanan carried his transmission forward.

Dharma heir of Dongshan. Known for 'three diseases and two lights of the dharmakaya' teaching. Yunmen served under him before succeeding Xuefeng. Appears in Gateless Gate Case 48 and Book of Serenity Case 61.

Heir of Dongshan Liangjie, nicknamed 'Uncle Dwarf.' Fellow students regarded him as the most penetrating among Dongshan's disciples and would say 'let's just go ask Uncle Dwarf' when difficult questions arose. Known for 'the price of the dharma body' exchange.

From Yanzhou in Zhejiang. Studied under Xuefeng Yicun for twenty-nine years and famously wore out seven meditation cushions before awakening upon rolling up a bamboo screen. Later headed Changqing Monastery in Fuzhou for twenty years. Appears in Blue Cliff Record cases 22 and 23.
Most important heir of Fayan Wenyi. National teacher of Wuyue kingdom.
His poetic verses on 100 cases became the foundation of the Blue Cliff Record. Greatest poet of the Chan tradition.
Also known as Baofeng Kewen. Second-generation Huanglong master. Known for expelling monks immediately after their awakening. Teacher of Doushuai Congyue.
Dharma heir of Lumen Zijue. Continued Furong Daokai's Caodong line in the Jin-controlled north while the southern branch (Danxia Zichun to Hongzhi) flourished under the Song.
Also known as Dahong Zuzheng. Song dynasty Yangqi-line master. Teacher of Yuelin Shiguan.

Jinul's foremost disciple and second master of Songgwangsa. He compiled a collection of 1,125 kongan (koans) titled the Seonmun yeomsong seolhwa (Seon Verses and Commentaries), the first indigenous Korean koan anthology. This monumental work, completed in thirty fascicles, selected cases from Chinese Chan collections and added Korean commentary, establishing an independent Korean Seon literary tradition distinct from mere importation of Chinese texts. He also expanded Songgwangsa's monastic community and received the posthumous title 'National Teacher' (guksa). His koan collection remained central to Korean Seon training for centuries. Attested in Korean Buddhist historical records: the Seonmun yeomsong seolhwa is the earliest known indigenous koan anthology in East Asian Buddhism outside China.
6th National Teacher of Suseonsa (originally numbered 7th; numbering corrected per CBETA sources).

One of the most celebrated Korean Seon masters of the late Goryeo dynasty, remarkable for having received dharma transmission from two masters of entirely different lineages. He first studied under the Indian monk Zhigong (Dhyanabhadra, d. 1363), who had come to Yuan China and gave Naong transmission in an Indian-derived lineage. He then received a second transmission from the Chinese Linji master Pingshan Chulin, a heir in the mainstream Yangqi-Linji line. This double transmission from both Indian and Chinese sources gave Naong unique authority. He became Royal Teacher (wangsa) and initiated major reforms of Korean Seon before his sudden death. Attested in Korean Buddhist records and Chinese Chan genealogies: both transmissions are documented, with his Indian lineage through Zhigong preserved in Goryeo-era inscriptions.
Maintained Seon transmission during severe Joseon suppression. Name ('Green Pine') suggests mountain hermit life.
One of the 'four great monks'. Leading advocate of Chan-Pure Land synthesis.

One of the most prominent female Chan masters in Chinese history. A Linji heir of Shiche Tongcheng, she became abbess of Crouching Lion (Fuwo) Chan Monastery, which flourished under her leadership. She left seven female dharma heirs, and her recorded sayings and poems survive in full.
Bridged 17th into 18th century. Maintained the Pyeonyang lineage through deepening Joseon suppression.

Mid-18th century Seon master in the Pyeonyang lineage. One of the few masters in the Hwanseong-to-Gyeongheo chain with attested dates (1710-1793). The 69th Korean patriarch. Carried the lineage through the deepest period of Joseon Neo-Confucian suppression of Buddhism.

Dharma heir of Wuzhun Shifan who served as abbot at Jingci Temple in Hangzhou, one of the Five Mountains monasteries. He gave Gaofeng Yuanmiao two of his most important huatou, including 'The myriad dharmas return to one - where does the one return to?' which triggered Gaofeng's awakening in a dream. While Gaofeng formally received transmission from Xueyan Zuqin (Duanqiao's dharma brother), Duanqiao's direct role in shaping Gaofeng's practice was indispensable.

Born in Jingzhou (Hubei Province). Already in his forties, he traveled to Huangmei where he studied under both Daoxin and Hongren, maturing as a practitioner of the East Mountain School. After time at Jade Spring Monastery alongside Shenxiu, he settled permanently on Mount Song (Songshan). Listed in the Lengqie Shizi Ji alongside Shenxiu and Huineng as one of Hongren's principal dharma heirs. He represents a third stream from the Fifth Patriarch, distinct from both the Northern and Southern schools. Said to have lived to age 128.

Of the Juyun branch. He followed Chuiwan Guangzhen and then Tiebi Huiji before receiving the robe and whisk from Tiemei Huili ('Three Slaps') on the latter's deathbed in 1650. At his own enthronement he offered incense to 'my late master, the venerable Tiemei of the Three Slaps, to repay the debt of the dharma-milk'.

Dharma name Jiwu, hao Hefeng; thirty-third generation in the Linji seat. Of the Fei clan of Wumen (Suzhou); his father was Simei, his mother of the Gu clan. Tonsured at twelve at Luohan monastery in Songling under the vinaya master Ruizhi, and fully ordained at twenty under Poushi of Wanfeng. Judu Hongli of Lingyin singled him out and set him on 'the original face'; he had a first opening on seeing a lamp-wick spark, and broke through fully during a seven-day sitting in the Great Compassion hall, overhearing Judu goading the attendant at the next seat. He served as head of practice at Huayan, Guangxiao, Xianning, Jingshan and Tianning, spent a period at Jingdezhen building a road and giving out tea, then returned to Lingyin, where Judu confirmed him and gave him the robe and bowl. He held Longtan Fushan, Baoshu, Zhuyin, Jizhao, Fushan and Fushou. Died 1687 aged 62.

Of Jianzhou in Sichuan, zi Jianguan. A dharma heir of Wuzhun Shifan. He headed Xinghua monastery in Longxing prefecture from 1239, then moved to Yunyan Shouning, and in 1265 took Xichan Yishan Changqing monastery in Fuzhou. He died in 1267.

Of Mochi in Zizhou, Sichuan, surname Jia; hao Huanxi. Tonsured in his twentieth year and ordained at Ganlu monastery in Chengdu. At twenty-two he attended the Daci lectures, then called on Hui'an Guang, Netang Bian and Tu'an Gui in turn, working day and night at his own matter. He then found Wuzhun Shifan at Ayuwang and became his heir. From 1246 he held Ruiyan in Jianning, then Huili in Linjiang, Baofeng in Hong, Xuefeng in Fu, and finally, by imperial order, Tiantong in Siming. Died 1281 aged 80.

Of Huanggang, surname Kang; zi Tianze, also styled Jingshan. Tonsured at Anguo monastery, where he studied the Mahayana and Hinayana divisions and concluded that 'the matter' does not lie in words and letters; he took the precepts at Xingyan. He called first at Tianjie in Jinling, where he was set on 'the three are not it' and had an opening, then went on to Tiantong and to Yunmen, and found his depth with Shanweng Min at Daochang, who made him head of assembly. War drove him back to Yishui in Chu, where he built a hut on Mt. Yuqi. He afterwards came to Shanduo Zhenzai and received transmission from him in the autumn of 1665. He held Yilin at Yishui. Still living in 1677, aged sixty.

A heir of Shanduo Zhenzai in the Linji line. He entered Jinming Chan monastery in Jiaxing on the third day of the tenth month of 1683. His incense honours Shanduo as his late master, and Jie'an (Wujin) as his 師翁 — his grand-teacher — placing him one generation below Shanduo and two below Jie'an.

Of Wuyi in Jinhua, surname Xu; zi Miaoyun. His mother died when he was nine and he was tonsured at Huayan by the vinaya master Zihua, who gave him the name Shoufeng. He took the precepts under Jude at Lingyin. Sent out one day to haul firewood, he lost his way, wandered up to Beigao peak, sat down, and at nightfall looked up to find the moon bright and the whole landscape transparent and without obstruction. He then called on Zuyin, Feiyin, Ruo'an, Fushi, Yulin and Muyun in turn. In the spring of 1670 he went to Jie'an Wujin at Jinming, and in 1672 received transmission from him. He held Dabei in Linqing (Shandong) and Jingde at the Three Pagodas in Jiaxing.

Of Jinghai in Tongzhou, surname Pan; zi Shengtu, hao Huaihai. Tonsured and ordained at nineteen, he went to Zhewong Ruyan at Jingshan and became his heir. From 1233 he held Guangxiao in Tongzhou, then Shuangta at Wucheng, Qingliang at Jinling, Wannian at Tiantai, Wanshou at Suzhou and Jiangxin at Dongjia. Appointed to Ayuwang as its forty-fifth abbot, he went on to Jingci, Lingyin, and finally Jingshan in Hangzhou — the summit of the Five Mountains system. He fell ill and died on the tenth day of the sixth month, 1265, having written his parting verse.

Of Tongchuan prefecture, surname Wang; zi Jingsou. Ordained by Tucheng at Guangfu cloister in his home county, he studied under Biefeng and Tudu at Jingshan, working in silence; reading Wan'an's record one day, he had an opening. He then went to Fozhao Deguang at Ayuwang, connected with him, and came and went at his door for fifteen years. He held Boruo and Bao'en in Taizhou, then swept out a single room on the northern side of Feilai Peak and lived there ten years — men would not presume to use his personal name, and called him simply 'North Torrent', Beijian. He was later called to Tiefo, Xiyu, Bijun, Huiri and Daochang, and in the Jiaxi era was ordered to Jingci Guangxiao. Died 1246 aged 83. His Beijian collections shaped Japanese Gozan literature.

Of Bazhou in Shuntian, north China, surname Zhao. Born the eighteenth day of the eighth month of 1579. He went vegetarian at twelve and wanted the robe; refused by his parents, he simply left at fourteen, met the Wutai master Huiren on the road, and when Huiren would not tonsure him he took a knife and cut off his own hair. At eighteen he ran away by night to the Lion's Den on Mt. Wutai to study under Kongyin Zhencheng, mastering the Surangama and Lotus. At twenty-five, walking under the moon holding his huatou, he broke through. He spent nineteen years at Wutai hermitage near Shaoling, where he would sit in the open at night under a great umbrella — whence his name 'the Umbrella Dweller'. He held Yunju, Qingyuan and Qingliang, and in 1644 founded Zizhulin at Shicheng. Died the sixth day of the fifth month, 1646, aged 68.

Of Tongcheng, surname Yan; zi Hansong, also styled Yinweng. He put off white robes in 1643 at eighteen and took full ordination at twenty-two. Studying under Baiyu at Qinglong, he knocked a lamp to the floor and broke clean open. He received Baiyu's charge in 1652. He held Longfu at Qinglong in Songjiang, Shanquan at Guoshan, Xianglu on Mt. Baiyun, Yunji at Baoyan, Anle at Jingxi, Li'an at Shanjuan and Longhua at Bianshan. Died 1688 aged 63. He edited his master Baiyu's complete records into the canon.

Of Zhangpu in Fujian, surname Cai. Orphaned young and raised by his brother, he failed of a career by twenty, met the master Zhenjie, and had himself tonsured at Shishi crag in Changtai. Reading the Changuan Cejin he found 'the ten thousand dharmas return to one' and took it up. In the spring of 1634, aged twenty-four, he came to Feiyin Tongrong at Huangbo, who beat him out of the room at every question — and before long he entered the depths and was made recorder.
