In 1638, when Feiyin took Jinsu, he served as West Hall and received the robe and whisk. He held Jinsu for six years from 1648, spending the whole of his private means on the assembly. In 1662 he copied out a hundred more leaves of dharma-talk into his complete record and said: 'From today this mountain monk will preach no more.' Told by a physician to take medicine, he answered: 'My karmic term is done; medicine is useless.' He washed, changed his robe, and died. His stupa is at Mt. Dengwei near Wu.

Of Chengdu, surname Hu. Abbot of Danxia, and of Xiangyan monastery in Dengzhou. At his enthronements he offered incense six separate times to his late master Dangshan Yuan of Xiangyan, calling himself the thirty-second generation in the orthodox Linji transmission.

A heir of Bie'an Xingtong. He took Yongshou Chan monastery in Hangzhou in 1691, swept the stupa of the patriarch Hui at Jingshan and made his bows at Caoxi. At his enthronement he offered incense to Bie'an, then living at the Zhenhai hall on Mt. Putuo.

Of Shaoling, surname Wang. He studied at the county school and, gripped by the greatness of birth-and-death, was tonsured and ordained. He relied on Huishan Zhihai and worked under him for fifteen years. He went out to head Guanghua on Mt. Furong, and on the twenty-first day of the ninth month of 1669 succeeded to the seat of Miyin monastery on Mt. Dawei — the great Guiyang site. His heir was Tianyi Juxiang.

Of Cixi in Mingzhou, surname Mao; hao Xiaoweng. Ordained in 1197. He studied with Yeying Daoqin, then Xue'an Guan at Jinshan, then Songyuan Chongyue at Lingyin — and connected with none of them. He went at last to Wuyong Jingquan at Tiantong; as he opened his mouth Wuyong struck him across it with the bamboo staff, and he answered on the instant with a verse — 'the great poison-smeared drum, it shakes heaven and earth; turn your head, and corpses lie ten thousand li' — which Wuyong approved. He held Miaosheng, Jinwen and Guangxiao in Mingzhou, Bao'en in Tai, Huqiu at Pingjiang and Xuefeng in Fuzhou, and was ordered by decree to Lingyin. Prince Shi of Wei built Daci monastery in Mingzhou and made him its founding abbot. He later held Ruiyan, Jiangxin, Jingci, Tiantong and Ayuwang. Died 1248 aged 72.

Of Huai'an circuit. Abbot of Jingshan in Hangzhou, twenty-second generation below Huineng. In 1284 Khubilai asked after masters of Southern Chan; the Right Chancellor Harghasun put his name forward, and he presented a verse arguing against the taking of life, which the emperor accepted with approval, receiving the precepts from him. His heirs include Nanchu Shiyue and Yuejiang Zhengyin.

Of Duchang, surname Liao. Tonsured at fifteen at Xianglin on Mt. Lu. He called on the master of Shishuang at Yangshan, then on Chijue at Jingshan in Zhe, without connecting; he then came to Wuzhun Shifan at Jingshan, and afterwards to Xiyan Hui at Tiantong. His presentation of the teaching followed Wuzhun's throughout, and he secretly matched his intent; he was made keeper of the canon, and later first seat under Wuwen Can at Kaixian. In the Jingding era he headed Yuantong, then Donglin, in 1292 moved to Ayuwang, and withdrew to Xuedou. In 1300 he took Tiantong. Died 1308 aged 88.

Abbot of Guangshan monastery on Mt. Bafeng in Taiping prefecture — the same mountain held by his dharma-grandfather Guzhuo Jun. He was a teacher of consequence in his day: the Buxu Gaoseng Zhuan records that Cuifeng Deshan 'burned his incense as an heir to the venerable Tan'.
A late master of the Linji line, thirty-eighth generation below Nanyue (his heirs stand at the thirty-ninth). Two sobriquets are confirmed for the one man — his heir's record uses both 古雲沛 and 廬夢沛.

A master in the line that runs from Dahui Zonggao down to the Juyun branch of Sichuan. His teacher was Fadu Puci of Fenzhou; his heir was Xiao'an Mi. He is otherwise invisible — he survives only as a link in a chain, named in the stupa inscription of a descendant five generations below him.

links.label: DILA Authority A015518 (his teacher 筏渡普慈)

masters.notes: Traditionally credited as the first to bring Chan teachings to Korea from the Fourth Patriarch Daoxin. Semi-legendary but foundational for Korean Seon.
Dharma heir of Huineng. Ancestor of the Linji and Guiyang houses. Famous for 'polishing a tile' exchange with Mazu.
Second generation Heze lineage. Dharma heir of Shenhui.
Pivotal figure linking Shitou's lineage to the later Caodong school through his student Yunyan.
Known for the 'rhinoceros fan' koan (Blue Cliff Record, Case 91).
Reclusive monk in Gao’an, Jiangxi. Triggered Linji Yixuan’s great awakening when Huangbo sent Linji to him. Teacher of Moshan Liaoran.

Silla monk associated with the Huiyang-san school, one of the Nine Mountain Schools. Unlike most Nine Mountain founders, he did not travel to Tang China for transmission, making his lineage claim domestically attested only.

One of the most celebrated Chan masters, appearing in more koans than any other figure. Met Nanquan at age 18, studied under him over 20 years. At 80, settled at the dilapidated Guanyin Temple in Zhaozhou where he taught for 40 more years. Famous for 'No' (無), 'wash your bowl', 'the cypress tree in the garden', and 'have a cup of tea' (喫茶去). Lived to 120. His lineage died out by c. 1000 CE, but his recorded sayings (趙州錄) preserved his enormous influence.

Heir of Cuiwei Wuxue, from Shuzhou in Anhui. Settled on Mount Touzi and lived there as a hermit for over thirty years, drawing many students. Visited by Zhaozhou Congshen in a famous encounter. Appears in Blue Cliff Record cases 41, 79, 80, and 91.

Late Silla / early Goryeo monk who studied under Yunju Daoying (Dongshan Liangjie lineage) in Tang China. Founded the Sumi-san school, the last of the Nine Mountain Schools. Attested primarily in Korean stele inscriptions.
Preserved the Linji lineage during Five Dynasties persecutions.
Dharma brother of Shishuang Chuyuan.
His three principal disciples became the most influential Chan teachers of the next generation.
Song dynasty Chan master at Langye Mountain. Teacher of Yu Daopo, his only dharma heir.
His most prominent heir Songyuan Chongyue continued the dominant Linji line through Po'an Zuxian and Yunan Puyan.

Khitan statesman, chief advisor to Genghis Khan and Ögedei Khan; architect of early Mongol civil administration in North China. Lay disciple of Wansong Xingxiu from 1215, dharma name Zhanran Jushi ('Layman Clear-and-Still'). Commissioned Wansong to reconstruct the Book of Serenity in 1224 — without him, Hongzhi Zhengjue's 100 verses would have been lost.
Lived on Tianmu mountain in a hermitage. Writings on the huatou (critical phrase) method and 'great doubt' highly influential.
Late Yuan / early Ming Linji master. Key link between Yuan-era Chan and the Ming revival.
Ming dynasty Linji master. Teacher of both Xiaoyan Debao and Yungu Fahui.
Dharma brother of Hyujeong/Seosan. Founded the Buhyu branch, one of two major streams of Korean Seon.
Last of the 'four great monks'. Primarily Tiantai and Pure Land, fierce advocate of Vinaya reform.

Linji heir of Maoxi Xingsen in the Yulin Tongxiu line. Taught at Li'an monastery in Hangzhou and later became abbot of Bailin monastery in Beijing. His student Jialing Xingyin became the Chan teacher of the Yongzheng Emperor.

Transmission link in the Pyeonyang lineage. The 70th Korean patriarch. No independent biographical sources survive. Known from lineage charts where dharma was transmitted 'from Cheongbong and Geo-ae to Yulbong and Cheonggo.'

One of Dahui Zonggao's most prominent dharma heirs. Served as abbot at major Southern Song monasteries including Ayuwang (Ashoka) Temple and Lingyin Temple in Hangzhou. He also transmitted Dahui's kanhua Chan (keyword meditation) method to the next generation.

Fifth patriarch of the Niutou (Oxhead) school. He maintained the community at Mount Niutou and transmitted the lineage to Helin Xuansu, the sixth and final patriarch. He appears in the Jingde Chuandeng Lu (juan 4).

Chan master of Puguang cloister and later Jingxin cloister; of the Xiao clan of Jinling. He was a dharma heir of the layman-turned-monk Ci'an Zhenben — better known as the Herdsman of Old Bottle Mountain (古瓶山牧道者), whose lay name was Xiang Qian, styled Mugong, of Xiushui in Jiaxing, a descendant of the Ming minister Xiang Zhongyi. Zhenben himself received the seal from Jinming Jie'an Wujin in 1659. Jijun compiled his teacher's record, the Guping shan mudaozhe jiuxin lu, and signed it 'dharma-heir'. He also edited the Records of the Old Bottle Mountain Herdsman's mind-searching.

Of Meishan in southern Sichuan, Gong clan; father Gong Fu, mother of the Liu clan. As a boy he heard a lecture on the Diamond Sutra and, hearing how the Buddha left the palace for the snow mountains, resolved to leave home; his mother refused and he went two days without drinking until his father relented. Tonsured by Cihang, ordained under the Vinaya master Daru. He travelled, and got the great dharma from Zhangxue Tongzui at Zhaojue in Chengdu. He then founded Yuquan monastery at Pitong on Panlong mountain, where the assembly grew large. Died 1690 in the summer heat, the body reportedly unaltered; buried under a stupa on the south slope of Pan mountain.

Chan master of Wulei/Lingfeng monastery on Mount Wulei in Cixi, Mingzhou. A dharma heir of Muchen Daomin: he is named among the 嗣法門人 who edited Muchen's own recorded sayings (the Tiantong Hongjue Min chanshi yulu), which is about as direct as an heirship claim gets. His own 語錄 was taken down by his attendant Haicheng, and a preface was written by his 'dharma-brother of the same gate', Bing'an Zhang Lilian.

Of Langzhou in northern Sichuan, Hou clan; his mother was Lady Su. Sickly as a child, bookish, orphaned before he came of age, he took tonsure at Wanyuan monastery, studied at Guixi, took precepts from the monk Baochi, and finally received the dharma from the old master Yi'an — 'and Yi'an was a dharma-son of Poshan, who transmits the true Linji lineage'. He taught at Guiqing in Nan'an, at Zuo'e in the Zhongnan range, at the Chongwen stupa-cloister at Jinggan, and at Haibao monastery in Ningxia — an unusually far northwestern career, from Shaanxi into the Ordos. When Yi'an died he settled at Daxingshan in Chang'an, built his teacher's stupa and presided there for eight years. Died 1679, aged 68; five-coloured flames and countless relics at the cremation, says his stele.

Of Xianju in Tiantai, Ye clan, from a prominent local family. A quick child who read anything once and had it; a passing monk told his parents not to hold him back. He was tonsured by Gutian Hou at Tianning, took precepts, then went the rounds — Zhencang at Tianfeng, and Fangshan Wenbao at Xi'an hermitage on Ruiyan, going back and forth between the two. Dissatisfied, he built a hut on Huading peak of Mount Tiantai and drove himself hard; one day while working he broke through, and Fangshan sealed him with a verse. He then sat on Huading for forty years and never once crossed the threshold — 'his foot never passed the door-sill' — while his reputation drew the whole southeast. Born 1265, died 1334, aged 70, fifty years ordained. Imperially styled Miaoming Zhenjue; his stupa is the Jiguang.

names: 江寧弘濟方融如璽禪師
masters.notes: Of Jingyang in Xi'an prefecture, Ren clan. A Caodong master: he received the dharma from Juelang Daosheng at Tianjie in Nanjing and succeeded him in that seat, lighting his transmission incense 'for my original master Juelang, thirty-third generation of the true Caodong lineage'. He had earlier spent ten years at Yunju and had lived at Kuanglu. He later moved to Hongji monastery. His recorded sayings carry an appended collection of Pure Land poems, and his invitation-letters are signed by a long roll of Nanjing literati.

Of Xiushui in Jiaxing, the Gu clan of Xincheng; mother of the Zou clan, the middle of three sons. The family was too poor for the schooling he wanted, and he lit up whenever a monk passed the door; his parents sent him to Songyuan hermitage at Jingshan. At nineteen he took tonsure and full precepts from the great master Wengu at Zhenji, shut himself up for three years with the Huayan commentary, then made a name in the lecture halls — 'the assemblies called me a horned tiger', he says, but he did not trust it. In 1637 he met the master Xue at Jingshan and was undone by one question; they exchanged poems on the pond for ten years. Later he saw Xueguan and Yongjue without spark; then Juelang; and finally, under Feiyin Tongrong at Jingshan, he broke through one night at the sound of a door. He became abbot of Puming at Jiaxing. Sixty in the winter of 1673.

A man of western Shu (Sichuan) who made his career in the east: he came out at Folong, moved to Fahua in Suzhou in 1260, was ordered to Xuedou in 1264 and to Ruiyan in 1269. A dharma heir of Wuzhun Shifan. He was a considerable writer — the Wujia zhengzong zan (Encomia on the True Lineage of the Five Houses) is his, and it is one of the sources used elsewhere in this batch to fix Mi'an Xianjie's teacher. He was dead by the autumn of 1279. Heirs: Kewong Shao and Fangwai Yuan.

Of Nanchong, Yang clan; abbot of Qingguo Chan cloister on Mount Jin'ao in Shehong county, Tongchuan, from the autumn of 1664. A dharma heir of Poshan Haiming — Poshan's own recorded sayings contain the transmission verse he gave him: 'You have got my eye: it sees through the shallow and the deep; do not join the great herd of blind donkeys — to whom will you chant the broken-sandbowl line?'

Of Dingyuan county in eastern Sichuan, Wang clan; born 1634. He would not touch meat or wine from birth and was nicknamed 'the little monk'. In 1644 Zhang Xianzhong's armies destroyed his family — father, mother, brother and sister all killed — and he spent years on the road sleeping in grass and dew. Adopted by a garrison commander in Zunyi who wanted an heir, he refused and kept refusing until at twenty-two he was tonsured at Luohan monastery in Rongchang. In 1658, sweeping incense in the courtyard, he saw the moon come out of a fold in the mountain and 'set down a heavy load'. He served Zhangxue Tongzui, and in 1681 — his teacher then seventy-two — was recalled by letter to succeed him at Zhaojue in Chengdu. He was abbot of Fenglin on Mount Qingcheng. In 1693 he had the Jinjiang chandeng cut and printed.

Southern Song Chan master, abbot of Jingci among other houses; also called Shuanglin Jieshi. He is a fair verse-writer and is quoted repeatedly in the Chan poetry anthologies alongside Xiangtan Yong, Mingji Jun and Yuji Hui — the Jingshan circle. His teacher is disputed in the sources: the Xu chuandeng lu makes him an heir of Zhewong Ruyan of Jingshan (himself an heir of Fozhao Deguang, also in this batch), while the Xudeng zhengtong index files him under Nangshan Dexiu.

Named Yuancheng, styled Falan; of Zhijiang in Jingzhou, Chen clan. At twenty he was tonsured by the Chan master Sucheng at the Bodhi-site; at twenty-five he took full precepts from the dharma master Daze. At thirty-three he went to Shaweng Hai (Shuijian Huihai) at the Tianwang monastery in Jingzhou, served as prior, then head of the hall, then first seat; one day Hai raised his whisk and said 'if you understand it here, the hundred flavours are complete', and he awoke at the word — Hai gave him the whisk as a token. He came out at Tianwang, then Dumen, then Putichang, and finally was invited by the provincial commander Xu Zhidu to open Bao'en monastery as its first abbot. He fell ill as Bao'en was being finished and died in 1689, aged 64, forty-four years a monk.

Of the Erhai region in Yunnan, Wang clan, mother of the Duo clan; born 1613. At twelve his parents told him he did not look fit to stay in the world and should become a monk 'to lengthen your years'; at fourteen his father took him up Jizu shan to Jiguang monastery to be tonsured. He fretted openly about death while the other novices laughed at him. He studied under Dali, Yeyu, Cheyong and Liaofan, then heard the Lotus and Surangama lectures for a few years, and worked the 'not mind, not Buddha, not a thing' phrase for twelve or thirteen years with no way in. At thirty-six, in a sealed room, reciting the Sutra of Ten Thousand Buddha Names, he had barely opened his mouth on the words 'namo' when body and mind fell away 'like one wheel of a bright moon'. He then took it to Wumu Wuzhu. His dharma came by letter and whisk from Mixing Jiren at Nanyun cloister in Hengzhou, in 1671. He taught across Yunnan — Jiutai shan, Fucheng at Chuxiong, Dafangguang, Xianyang. Died 1689, aged 77; his stupa is on Jizu shan.

Named Yinsu; of Yichun county, Yu clan. A dream at six sent him to the monk Xian at Shoulong cloister; he shaved his head at twenty-seven and took precepts the year after. Told to recite sutras, he answered that the Buddhas' meaning must be realised in the mind, not counted off in ink, and left to travel Hunan, where he called on Mu'an Fazhong at Dawei. Back at his home cloister, in 1153 the neighbouring Cihua monastery asked him to preside. It had no endowment; he lived on gruel and paper robes and, apart from meditation, read only the Huayan sutra and its commentary — until one day he broke into a sweat all over and said, 'I have touched the Huayan realm myself.' From then his sayings, verses and healing became famous across a thousand li: he gave herbs and verses to the sick and to plague villages, prayed for rain, tore down shrines, and above all built — bridges and roads everywhere, so that anyone discussing meritorious works had to mention Pu'an. Died 1169, aged 55, twenty-eight years ordained; entombed whole on the first of the eleventh month. He was later absorbed into popular religion as the deity Pu'an Zushi.

Of Gaizhou in Liaodong, Wang clan — a rare northeasterner in this literature. He preached in Manchuria: at Puci monastery in Guangning and at the Great Guanyin cloister on Mount Lü, where he gave his account of conduct in 1658. His transmission incense names Jiewei Xingzhou of the Ruru hall at Nanhu in Xiushui, Jiaxing, as his original master, in the 36th generation of the Caoxi line. He also records earlier study at Jinsu under Feiyin Tongrong, but names only Jiewei as 本師. His record preserves a scene in which a rival sect sent a man called 'Solitary Step' to crowd his seat with a mob.

Of Fushun county in Sichuan, Gao clan, mother of the Yang clan, the fourth son. By the account of his dharma-brother Jienan Huixian he 'never studied the classics as a boy and could not read' — an illiterate who became an abbot. He was tonsured at twenty-five under Shengke Deyu, took his precepts at Yunfeng and did his Chan at Zhaojue, then came to Huayan monastery in Chongqing, where he and Shengke 'met like needle and mustard-seed' and he served as head monk for fifteen years without a divided thought. In 1684 Shengke left on pilgrimage and Huanchu took the Huayan seat; his opening sermon there in the tenth month of 1684 lights the incense to Shengke. He was fifty-five in 1685.

Of Jiashan, Chen clan; born 1593. A Caodong master and a dharma heir of Zhanran Yuancheng. His record, the Shiyu chanshi fatan, runs to twenty fascicles and contains his 行狀. He had a large following of heirs whose dharma names all begin with 淨 — Jingzhu, Jingfu, Jingxin and others — several of whom became compilers and lamp-historians in their own right. Died 1648, aged 56.

Of Xuzhou (Yibin) in Sichuan, Fan clan, descended from a Fan who had been a prefectural commander; a monk of Chaoyang monastery in Xuzhou. A dharma heir of Tieniu Deyuan. He matters chiefly as the transmission link he is: Poshan Haiming's grand-teacher line runs through him, and Zhangxue Tongzui's stele quotes the sentence 'he got the dharma from the old man Yueming Lianchi'. Died 1639, sitting upright, aged 66.

Of Dazhou in western Shu (Sichuan), Zhao clan. A dharma heir of Linye Tongqi. He restored and presided over Xiangyan Xiantong monastery at Nanyang in Henan — his own heir Gusu Zun credits him in his transmission incense with 'reviving Xiangyan at Dengzhou'. His teacher Linye Tongqi was an heir of Miyun Yuanwu and is NOT yet a node on the chart.

Of Suizhou, Qiu clan; born 1620. Abbot of Baiyun monastery at Qizhou, where he is styled Xianglin. A dharma heir of Tieguan Xingneng. His recorded sayings, the Baiyun Xianglin Benzhen chanshi yulu, contain his 行實, which records that he died sitting cross-legged in the summer of 1691, aged 72.

Chan master of Tianning monastery in Jiaxing prefecture. A dharma heir of Baoyue Tan. The Jingshi diru ji records that he first went to Chushan Shaoqi — Baoyue's dharma-brother — and 'at once tallied with the subtle purport', before receiving Baoyue's seal: another case where the first teacher is not the transmitting one. Only his dharma character 宣 is attested; I have not expanded it.

Of Fenzhou in Shanxi; born 1264, died 1351/52 at the age of 88. His dharma name is 普慈 — the batch had only the bare sobriquet plus a single character. The Xudeng zhengtong files him as 'Fadu Puci of Fenzhou, heir of Yi of Taiyuan' — that is Kukou Liangyi, the batch's 苦口益. A separate index, however, lists a 'Wufeng Yuanshu Puci' as an heir of Yuansou Xingduan. He is remembered in Qing Sichuan: Qingzhong Tiebi's record says a monk 'travelled to Fenzhou and called on Fadu, who recognised him at once as a vessel'.
Dharma heir of Baizhang.
Disciple of Linji Yixuan at Baoshou Monastery in Zhenzhou. Known for exchanges with Zhaozhou and Sansheng.

Korean Seon master, fifth patriarch (第五世) of the Susonsa 修禪社 community on Mt. Jogye 曹溪山 (Songgwangsa). Dharma name 天英 (Cheonyeong); lay surname 梁; father 宅椿, mother of the 金 clan. Born 高宗二年乙亥 (1215), sixth month, thirteenth day. Tonsured in 1225 (高宗十二年己丑) at Jogye under 真覺國師 (Jingak, i.e. 慧諶) — a TONSURE (得度), not a transmission. He then consulted 清真國師 (Cheongjin, i.e. 夢如, the 3rd patriarch) and 'received the essentials of the dharma' from 真明國師 (Jinmyeong, i.e. 混元, the 4th patriarch), whom he succeeded in the seat. In 1233 he was made 座元 at a 談禪法會; in 1236 he took first place in the 禪選. Appointed 三重大師 and then 禪師 by the 晉陽公, he was installed at 斷俗寺 (1248) and presided at 昌福寺 (1249). He held the seat at Jogye for thirty years. He died aged 72 (法臘 57) and was posthumously titled 慈真圓悟國師 — hence 'Wono' 圓悟 — with the stupa-name 靜照. It is under this posthumous 圓悟 that his disciple Manhang's stele calls him 「其師曹溪圓悟和尚」. His own stele stands at 佛臺寺 in 高興郡, composed by 李益培.

Silla Seon master, the SECOND patriarch of the Gajisan 迦智山 school — the middle man of the founding Korean Seon chain 道義 → 廉居 → 體澄. When Doui, who had received the mind-seal from 西堂智藏 (Mazu's disciple) in Tang China, found Silla unready for the Chan teaching and withdrew into the mountains, he 'transmitted the dharma to Chan master Yeomgeo' (付法於廉居禪師). Yeomgeo dwelt at 億聖寺 (written 偣聖寺 in the stele, whose own compiler flags the character as doubtful — 「偣或疑信字亦疑倍字之誤」) on 雪山 = Seoraksan 설악산. There 體澄 came and served him, and Yeomgeo 'bestowed the dark pearl and conferred the dharma-seal' upon him. His stupa (the Yeomgeo Hwasang stupa, 844) survives and is a Korean national treasure; 朝鮮佛教通史's index carries the entry 「廉居禪師塔」. He is the reason the Gajisan line is counted from Doui rather than from Chejing.

Tang Chan master of the NORTHERN school (北宗), an 入室 (inner-chamber) disciple of 普寂 of Songshan — 大照禪師, the chief heir of 神秀. He is known almost entirely through the stele of his Korean disciple 神行: the Silla monk crossed to Tang, came to 志空, attended him morning and evening for three years, and was given the 元珠 (the primal pearl) and, as 志空 lay dying, the 灌頂授記 — the anointing and the prediction that sent him home to Silla. Through him the Northern school entered Korea: 朝鮮佛教通史 records 「北宗神行先導。南宗道義繼至」 — Sinhaeng led the way with the Northern school, and Doui followed with the Southern. NAME CORRECTION: he is 志空 (wikisource prints the variant 誌空), NOT 智空.

masters.teacher: Miaofeng Zhishan 妙峰之善 (靈隱妙峰之善)
masters.notes: Southern Song Linji master, abbot of Jingshan 徑山. Dharma name 善珍, style 藏叟; son of the 呂 family of Nan'an in Quanzhou. Tonsured at thirteen under 崇福南和尚 (a TONSURE master, not his dharma-father); at sixteen he travelled to Hangzhou and took the full precepts. He then 'called on Miaofeng Shan at Lingyin, entered his chamber and awakened to the purport' (謁妙峯善公于靈隱，入室悟旨) — 妙峰之善 being the heir of 佛照德光 (1121-1203). He came out at 光孝 in his home district, rose to 承天, moved to 思溪圓覺 in Anji and 雪峰 in Fujian, and by imperial command to 育王 in Siming and finally 徑山 at Lin'an — six great monasteries. 補續高僧傳 closes his life with the decisive sentence: of all his many students, 「入室得髓者，唯元叟端公一人而已」 — the only one who entered the chamber and got the marrow was Yuansou Duan. His stupa is at 南塔院. NOTE: the roster's ascription of 元叟行端 to 高峰原妙 is contradicted by every source consulted.

Qing-dynasty Linji master, thirty-third generation of the orthodox Linji transmission (傳臨濟正宗三十三世) — so styled by his own heir in open assembly. Heir of 養拙正明 (養拙明), who was himself the heir of 五峰如學 (1583-1631) and who dwelt at 密印寺 on Mt. Dagui 大溈山, dying in the spring of 1649. Zhihai's seat gives him his name, 慧山. His disciple 古梅定冽 attended him for fifteen unbroken years and received the 記莂 (the prediction/certification) from him in the midst of the assembly, and afterwards led the same 大溈山密印寺 / 芙蓉山廣化寺 community. Other recorded heirs: 與峰智, 明應, 揆庵空, 上湛, 月憨權, 千如一. No dates and no stele have been found for him; he is known through his heir's 語錄 and through the Qing lamp-records.

Yuan-dynasty Linji master (1257-1345), of Ninghai, lay surname 陳. Heir of 橫川如珙 (himself heir of 滅翁文禮). He dwelt at 紫籜 in 仙居 for close to forty years — 「住仙居之紫籜垂四十年矣」 — a recluse so austere that travelling monks were afraid of him; he is also linked with 薦嚴寺 at Kunshan (hence 薦嚴道) and appears in the 淨慈寺志. 柳貫 wrote the preface to his recorded sayings. When 無慍 and two companions climbed to him they found him sitting on a slab across the stream 'like a Luohan painted by the recluse Wu'; 無慍's first question drew a shout that dissolved his long-standing doubt about the 狗子無佛性 koan, and the verse he then offered — 「狗子佛性無，春色滿皇都」 — was deeply approved. ⚠ HE IS NOT the 妙道 already on the chart (Dahui's female disciple): this is a Yuan-dynasty male monk, and DILA holds them as separate persons.

Northern Song master of the YUNMEN house, seated at 德山 in 鼎州. His teacher was 雙泉郁, a direct heir of 雲門文偃 — the lamp lineage table files him under the explicit heading 「雙泉郁禪師法嗣：德山慧遠禪師、含珠山彬禪師」 — so he stands exactly two generations below 文偃. This is independently corroborated by 契嵩's 鐔津文集 (11th century, contemporary), which calls 德山遠公 a 法孫, a dharma-GRANDSON, of 雲門匡真大師. His heirs include 開先善暹, 欽山悟勤, 鹿苑圭, 含珠山彬 and 盛懃. ⚠ HE IS NOT 廬山慧遠, the Pure Land patriarch who died in 416 — six centuries separate them; this man is a Song Yunmen monk at Dingzhou. ⚠ NAME: the corpus gives his teacher as the single character 郁 (雙泉郁). The expansion to 仁郁 rests ONLY on DILA, whose citation is （望月）— a 20th-century Japanese encyclopedia, i.e. EXTERNAL rung. I therefore record the teacher as 雙泉郁 and do not adopt the expansion.

Qing-dynasty Linji master, heir of 破山海明 (1597-1666) — the great Sichuan revivalist — and thus part of the 破山 line that carried Linji Chan into Sichuan and Guizhou. His seats were 盛京聖恩寺 (Shengjing/Shenyang), 潭淵普照寺 in 大名府, and the 二祖墖院 on the 滹沱 in 磁州. He certified 語嵩傳裔, who carried the line south into Guizhou (the 黔南 lamp-record descends from him), and 書雲旵. NAME NOTE: he is 雪臂 ('Snow Arm'), not 雪竇 or 雪壁; the corpus writes 雪臂巒 and 印巒.

THE MISSING MAN. Absent from our roster entirely — and his absence is the whole reason the forgery worked. A SECOND master styled Haizhou: born Hongwu 27 (1394) at Chengdu in Shu, surname YU 余 (not Qian); tonsured at Jingde si on Dasui shan in Peng county under Duzhao Yue 獨照月; after Yue died in 1413 he lived eight years alone in a hermitage on Xishan. Heir of Dongming Huichan: he received Huichan's robe and verse in Jingtai 2 (1451), delivered by the head seat Faguang to Dongshan on the day the bequest matured. Founding abbot (開山) of Yishan chan si 翼善禪寺 on Dongshan, Jinling, from Zhengtong 2 (1437), installed at the request of the eunuch defence-commissioner Yuan Cheng. Died Chenghua 2 (1466), aged 73; stupa behind Tuiju si; ONE HUNDRED AND FOUR dharma-heirs, of whom Yunxi Zhiying 雲溪智瑛 is one. His 行實碑 stood in front of Yishan si; it was rediscovered in 1657 and circulated from 1662, and it is what finally proved there were two Haizhous.

A SECOND man styled Baofeng, heir of Haizhou YONGCI — routinely merged with Baofeng MINGXUAN, heir of Haizhou Puci. He received Yongci's own hand-written charge on the 11th day of the 2nd month of Jingtai 5 (1454), with the verse 「迷悟猶如空裏雲」 and a robe and whisk. His stupa stands behind Tuiju si, not beside Dongming si. In Tianshun 5 (1461) he and Zhixi 智璽 reverently recorded Yongci's 行錄. Note 智楷 also reports that Yongci's chief heir styled Baofeng was 智忍 — so the 寶峯 sobriquet may cover a third man; keep 智瑄 distinct from 明瑄 and do not claim more. He is NOT Tianqi Benrui's teacher: the forgers made him so by fabricating a transmission verse 'found in a broken basket of waste paper' in 1662.

A SEPARATE MAN from Wuwen Mingcong — this is the answer to the question. A genuine dharma-heir of Tianqi Benrui, whom Zhikai locates at GUANTAO 館陶 (the 闢妄救 instead seats him at Longquan si, Guanziling, Suizhou, which Zhikai disputes because that seat belongs to Guangze Wuwen). He is NOT the teacher of Xiaoyan Debao. The 禪燈世譜 filed Xiaoyan under him, and later compilers welded the two Congs into one person; DILA still does (A004731). Zhikai states the distinction three separate times and puts the resulting absurdity in one line: 「天奇有二子．可也。笑巖有二父．可乎」 — Tianqi may have two SONS; may Xiaoyan have two FATHERS?

One of the 104 dharma-heirs named on Haizhou Yongci's 行實碑 at Yishan si. He belongs to the DONGMING branch (Wanfeng - Baozang Puchi - Dongming Huichan - Haizhou Yongci - Yunxi Zhiying), not to the Wanfeng-direct branch. He is a dharma-brother of Zhixuan (「瑛與寶峯瑄為昆季」). His heir Jing'an Zhisu wrote the 聯芳圖 that preserves this line. The 禪燈世譜 wrongly filed him and Jing'an Su under PUCI — Zhikai's 'error three': 「以永慈法嗣．混收為普慈一人之嗣」.

Heir of Yunxi Zhiying, second-generation descendant of Haizhou Yongci. Author of the 聯芳圖 — the lineage chart that runs Gaofeng - Zhongfeng - Qianyan - Wanfeng - Baozang Puchi - Dongming Huichan - Haizhou [Yongci] - Yunxi Ying. That chart is genuine and belongs to HIS branch. Its misuse is the hinge of the whole forgery: because it says 'Haizhou' without a personal name, and because only one Haizhou was known, Longchi and then Tiantong read it as proof that Haizhou PUCI descended from Dongming, and spliced Baozang and Dongming into the other branch. The chart was never wrong; the reading of it was.

Ming-Qing Caodong monk of Qiantang/Hangzhou, reckoned the 37th generation of the Qingyuan line. He is best known as a compiler — of the 宗門拈古彚集, the very anthology in which the other Ming-Qing commentators of this batch are quoted.

Five Dynasties master of Jianzhou, titled Zhenji (真寂); a native of Yongzhen (朱 clan). Tonsured under Gushan Shenyan, he was the only one in the assembly to grasp his teacher's wordless gesture of opening his robe; he later moved to Fengxian.
Fayan-school master of Baizhang in Hongzhou. He awakened under Fayan Wenyi while asking about the case of the non-Buddhist who questioned the Buddha, when Wenyi cut him off mid-sentence with 「住。住。」.

Tang master of Mount Baizhang, one of Mazu Daoyi's heirs (widely, though disputedly, identified with the epithet 百丈涅槃和尚). The lamps preserve his exchange with Nanquan on whether there is a dharma the masters do not preach, and the story of his pointing at a braying donkey.

Song Linji master of the Huanglong line at Baizhang in Longxing, an heir of Huanglong Huinan. Asked to reveal the meaning of the coming from the West, he answered 「泥牛吞巨浪」 (the clay ox swallows the great waves).

Song Yunmen-school master of Mount Baizhao in Anzhou, heir of Fayun Fashiu of the Eastern Capital. His sermons press the point that the self-nature is already complete in ordinary walking, sitting and lying.

Fayan-school master of Baoen in Hangzhou (蔣 clan), who left home young and mastered the three trainings. After roaming the Chan assemblies of Min and Yue without finding his mind, he met Fayan Wenyi at Linchuan and teacher and student matched; he then dwelt in a hermitage on Damei mountain and worked to restore the Xuansha orthodox line in Wuyue.

Five Dynasties master of the Baoci cloister in Fuzhou, personal name Guangyun, titled Huijue; an heir of Changqing Huileng in the Xuefeng line. He told his assembly that the medicine which cures the illness needs no donkey to carry it.

Fayan-school master of Baoci in Jinling, a native of Hangzhou (陸 clan). He had made an elaborate sectioned commentary on the Surangama Sutra; when he presented it, Fayan Wenyi asked what the 'eight returns' return to, and at the second question he was struck dumb — the encounter that turned him from scholarship to Chan.

Fayan-school master of Baoci in Jinling, titled Xuanjue; a native of Quanzhou. He warned pilgrims that merely setting down bowl and bottle at a monastery is not the end of the bodhisattva path, likening practice to sifting sand until the gold shows.

Song Linji master of the Yangqi line at Baoen in Ezhou (later Wuchang), an heir of Yunju Faru. His best-known sermon opens 「秋雨乍寒，汝等諸人青州布衫成就也未」 — the autumn rain turns cold; is your Qingzhou cloth shirt finished yet?

Song Yunmen-school master of the Baoen cloister on Zhongshan at Zhuji in Yuezhou, an heir of Yungai Jipeng. Asked about 'the great way is without difficulty, it only dislikes picking and choosing', he replied 「昨日初三今日初四」 — yesterday was the third, today is the fourth.

Song master of Baohua in Pingjiang, titled Foci (佛慈); a local man of the 周 clan who refused meat as a child and was tonsured at Jingde monastery. After failing to connect with Jueyin Ying he entered Zhenjing Kewen's room, awakened on the Shishuang attendant story, and presented a verse beginning 「枯木無華幾度秋」, which Kewen approved.

Song Linji master of the Yangqi line at Baohua in Pingjiang, a local man and an heir of Yuanwu Keqin. He mocked added effort: having eaten the gruel is putting a head on your head, washing the bowl is drawing legs on a snake.

Ming Linji master of Tangcheng, a native of Guyu Tangcheng (Chongqing, 張 clan). He served Xichan Xuefeng Rui for years but his teacher died before granting him formal approval (「因峰遷化，未獲印可」), so he travelled far to call on Chushan Shaoqi — his late teacher's dharma-brother.

Song Yunmen-school master of Mount Baizhang in Hongzhou, titled Baoyue (寶月); an heir of Zhimen Guangzuo. The lamps record a monk asking him whose song he sings and whose lineage he succeeds to. The 續傳燈錄 index credits him with two heirs of his own.
Tang master in the Hongzhou line, an heir of Mazu Daoyi. He is preserved chiefly through his sparring with the layman Pang Yun (龐居士), who asked what Danxia meant by striking the attendant.

Fayan-school master of Yongxi cloister on Mount Zhiti in Fuzhou, a native of Mingzhou. His sermons turn on the towering 'real mark' (實相) that fills space yet is neither colour nor shape nor an object of perception.

Ming-Qing Linji master of the Qingshan line, abbot at Dàxióng in Wulin and at Gaotai on Nanyue, and a disciple of the national teacher Yulin Tongxiu. He left his own recorded sayings, and his dharma-brothers included Baisong Xingfeng.

Tang/Five Dynasties Caodong master of Cao'an in Huazhou, an heir of Caoshan Benji. Asked how a student advances when 'intending misses and stirring a thought goes wrong', he answered that the miss is already made.
Song Yunmen-school master of the Baoji cloister on Mount Cao in Fuzhou, an heir of Heshan Chucai. Asked 'what is Buddha?' he answered 「寒猫不捉鼠」 — a cold cat does not catch mice.

Song Linji master of the Huanglong line at Letan in Longxing, a native of Nanxiong (何 clan). He first called on Dawei Zhe without result; under Huitang Zuxin he long failed to penetrate the wind-and-banner koan until Zuxin asked whether he had watched a cat stalk a mouse — eyes unblinking, whole body single-directed.

Song master of Chaling in Hengzhou, a local man tonsured young who famously never went on pilgrimage (「茶陵郁山主不曾行脚」). An almsman from Lushan gave him the koan 「百尺竿頭，如何進步」 (Fadeng's answer: 「噁」); after three years he awakened when his donkey stumbled crossing a bridge and pitched him off, producing the celebrated verse 「我有神珠一顆，久被塵勞關鎖，今朝塵盡光生，照破山河萬朵」. He was the ordination master of Baiyun Shouduan, who wrote a verse in his praise.

Song Yunmen-school master of Changlu in Zhenzhou, titled Yuanjian (圓鑑); an heir of Tianyi Yihuai. Looking left and right from the seat he invoked the bearing of the lion and the elephant king, and closed 「丈夫自有衝天志，莫向如來行處來」.
Fayan-school master, abbot of the Changshou cloister at Anguo monastery in Suzhou; a native of Yongjia (秦 clan). One of Tiantai Deshao's forty-nine heirs.

Tang master of Tanzhou in the Qingyuan/Shitou line. Returning from paying respects at the Sixth Patriarch's stupa at Caoxi, he met Shitou Xiqian, who asked whether the merit of Dayu Ridge was complete; Kuang said it was long complete but still lacked the dotting of the eyes. His heir was Shishi Shandao.

Song Linji master of the Huanglong line at Heshan in Jizhou, an heir of Sixin Wuxin. His surviving 語錄 includes a sermon surveying all five houses — Linji, Yunmen, Caodong, Guiyang and Fayan — only to dismiss even a clear grasp of them as 'matters at the edge of light and shadow' beside the question of birth and death.
Song Linji master of the Chenghui cloister in Luzhou, an heir of Yunfeng Wenyue. Asked to step past both Deshan's stick and Linji's shout, he answered 「總不恁麼」 — neither of them at all.

Song Yunmen-school master of Chengtian in Quanzhou (also recorded at Hangzhou), an heir of Xuedou Chongxian. When a monk shouted at him he said 「臨濟兒孫」 — a child and grandchild of Linji; when the monk shouted again, he struck him.
Song master of the Chengtian cloister in Pengzhou, an heir of Bajiao Huiqing in the Guiyang house. He taught turning the light around to search minutely beneath one's own heels to see what this is.

Song Yunmen-school master of Chengtian in Wuzhou, an heir of Letan Huaicheng. Asked whether Buddha and sentient beings are one or two, he answered that when the flowers open the whole tree is red, and when they fall ten thousand branches are empty.

Song Yunmen-school master of Chengxin in Yuezhou, an heir of Xuedou Chongxian. Holding up his staff he asked which is the seed of buddhahood and which the condition, warning that having met Old Sakyamuni here one should not then buy straw sandals and go wandering.

A Tang/Five-Dynasties Chan monk of Chongzhen temple in Yizhou (modern Chengdu, Sichuan), recorded in the Jingde Chuandeng lu as one of the six dharma-heirs of Lumen Chuzhen of Xiangzhou, and thus a third-generation descendant of Caoshan Benji in the Caodong line. Only two of his exchanges survive, including the celebrated answer to 'What is Chan?' — 'Angling for the jade rabbit in a clear pool.'

names: 福州西禪此庵守淨禪師
masters.notes: A Southern Song Chan master of the Linji/Yangqi line, abbot of Xichan monastery in Fuzhou, known by the hermitage-name Ci'an. A dharma-heir of the great Dahui Zonggao, he left a one-fascicle recorded sayings collection and is remembered for blunt, iconoclastic sermons deriding abstract 'talk of the mystery' as so much wasted breath.

A Northern Song Chan master of Ciji cloister in Xingyuan prefecture (modern Hanzhong, Shaanxi), dharma-heir of Fayun Faxiu of the Yunmen school. His surviving exchanges are terse and concrete — asked the meaning of the Way he replied 'thirty-seven stages from here to Chang'an', and to the question of the colour-taking mani-jewel, 'Green green the bamboo, lush yellow the blossoms.'

A Northern Song Chan master of Ciyun cloister at Lin'an (modern Hangzhou), a dharma-heir of Huanglong Zuxin in the Linji/Huanglong branch, thirteenth generation below Nanyue. He is remembered chiefly for a set of four 'hanging phrases' (垂語四則) posed as public tests to his assembly, on precise response, answering north when asked south, unrestricted function, and cold-ash stillness.

A Northern Song Chan master of Ciyun cloister in Tanzhou (modern Changsha, Hunan), dharma-heir of Yunju Yuanyou in the Linji/Huanglong branch. His recorded sermon takes up Xuansha Shibei's famous saying that 'the whole great earth is one bright pearl', which he dismissed as 'chewing food to feed an infant' — spoon-feeding that robs the student of his own seeing.

A late-Ming/early-Qing Chan master of Cuiting at Mt. Baiyun in Shuzhou, known only from the supplement to the Wudeng quanshu. A dharma-heir of Shanzi Yu of Lotan Baofeng, in the Linji line descending through Shanweng Daomin. His surviving sermons are pointedly anti-scenic and earthy — 'the mountains aren't clear, the water isn't pretty, yellow dirt and rocks, coarse as a dog' — and to a monk boasting of being 'not one thread attached' he shot back, 'You'd die of shame.'

Cuiyan Kezhen (d. 1064) was a Northern Song Linji master, a native of Changxi in Fuzhou and a dharma-heir of Shishuang Chuyuan (Ciming). So proud of his wide pilgrimage that the monasteries nicknamed him 'Zhen Who Jabs His Chest' (真點胸) for his habit of pointing at his own breast, he was humbled and then awakened under Ciming. He taught at Cuiyan in Nanchang and later at Mt. Daowu in Tanzhou; Huang Tingjian wrote the preface to his recorded sayings.

Shouzhi (fl. mid-11th c.) was a Northern Song Linji master, a native of Taiyuan surnamed Wang. Ordained at Chengtian temple in Luzhou, he first made his name lecturing on the Diamond Sutra — 'famous throughout the Three Rivers' — before abandoning exegesis for Chan under Fenyang Shanzhao, who confirmed him. He taught at Dayu in Gao'an and later at Cuiyan on Mt. Xi near Nanchang, whence his two names; he died in the Jiayou era and was entombed on Mt. Xi.

names: 潮州靈山大顛寶通禪師
masters.notes: Dadian Baotong (732-824) was a Tang Chan master of Mt. Ling in Chaozhou (Guangdong), a dharma-heir of Shitou Xiqian. He and Yaoshan Weiyan both first studied under Huizhao at Xishan before Dadian went to Shitou and awakened to the essential purport. After five years on Mt. Luofu he returned to Chaozhou and founded the Lingshan Chan cloister. When Han Yu was banished to Chaozhou in 819 after his notorious memorial against the Buddha-relic, he struck up a friendship with Dadian — the encounter in which, asked his age, Dadian simply held up his rosary.

names: 建寧府斗峰大圭正璋禪師
masters.notes: Dagui Zhengzhang (b. 1304), styled Hengbai and known as Da'gui ('Great Jade Tablet'), was a Yuan-dynasty Linji/Yangqi master from Jinjiang in Fujian. He awakened under Dongyu Dehai on hearing his verse on Juzhi's raised finger, and later taught at Ziyun temple in Quanzhou and at Doufeng in Jianning, where he died. A noted literary monk, he left the Mengguan ji (夢觀集) and the Kaishi zhuan; the Siku catalogue praises his poetry as 'bold-boned'.

names: 慶元府大梅祖鏡法英禪師
masters.notes: Damei Faying (hall-name Zujing) was a Song Chan master of Mt. Damei in Qingyuan prefecture (modern Ningbo), a native of Yin county surnamed Zhang who abandoned Confucian study and doctrinal lecturing at Yanqing for Chan under Jiufeng Jianshao. He is remembered above all for his defiance during Huizong's forced Daoicization of the sangha: when the edict restoring monks and nuns came in the early Shaoxing era (c. 1131) he alone had never changed his resolve, and mounted the seat in birch cap, crane cloak, ivory tablet and vermilion shoes, discarding each with a verse — 'Bodhidharma carried one sandal home; ever since, his children and grandchildren go barefoot.'

Daning Daokuan was a Northern Song Linji master of Daning in Longxing prefecture (modern Nanchang), a dharma-heir of Shishuang Chuyuan (Ciming). Taking up his staff in the hall he declared that 'the life of the Buddhas before and the discipline of the Buddhas after are all right here'; asked why the temple director's eyebrows fell out when Danxia burned the wooden Buddha, he answered, 'Thieves don't rob a poor man's house.'

Danyuan Yingzhen was a Tang Chan master of Mt. Danyuan in Jizhou, a dharma-heir of the National Teacher Nanyang Huizhong, whom he served as attendant. He is chiefly remembered through his encounters with the young Yangshan Huiji, to whom tradition says he transmitted the set of circular figures inherited from Huizhong — the seed of the Guiyang school's distinctive symbolism.

names: 金陵鍾山章義院道欽禪師
masters.notes: Zhangyi Daoqin was a Five-Dynasties Chan master from Taiyuan, a dharma-heir of Fayan Wenyi and thus a ninth-generation descendant of Qingyuan Xingsi in the Fayan school. He first taught at Qixian on Mt. Lu, and was then invited by Li Jing, the Southern Tang ruler, to head the Zhangyi cloister on Mt. Zhong at Jinling. His teaching insisted the Way is not far off: 'Encounter any matter and it is real — is the sacred far away? Embody it and it is numinous.'

Datong Ji was a Tang Chan master of Datong in Lizhou (modern Hunan), recorded among the dharma-heirs of Shitou Xiqian. His surviving anecdotes are almost entirely wordless contests of gesture — when Mihu arrived with his assembly, Ji dragged his meditation seat around, sat facing the wall, and the two men circled and overturned seats at each other without a syllable — and he also traded barbs with the famous Layman Pang.

Dawei Fabao was a Southern Song Linji/Yangqi master from Fuzhou, a dharma-heir of Dahui Zonggao and seventeenth generation below Huineng, who taught at Mt. Dawei. He is remembered for a vivid restatement of Dahui's bamboo-stick dilemma and for the image that became his signature: 'Be a lion that bites the man — don't be like the Han hound chasing the clod', i.e. go for the one who threw it, not the thing thrown.

Deng Yinfeng was a Tang Chan master of Mt. Wutai, a native of Shaowu surnamed Deng, said to have seemed dull as a child. He first studied with Mazu Daoyi, twice went off to test himself against Shitou Xiqian and twice came away beaten — prompting Mazu's famous warning that 'Shitou's road is slippery' — before finally receiving Mazu's seal of mind. He is one of the great eccentrics of the Hongzhou school, remembered in legend for pushing a wheelbarrow over Mazu's outstretched leg and for dying standing on his head.

Dengjue Puming was a Song Chan master of Dengjue cloister in Fuzhou, a dharma-heir of Jianfu Daoying of Raozhou. At his inauguration sermon he struck the block and simply looked at the assembly: 'How marvellous! How wondrous! Can any of you see it?' He warned that even reaching that point one still falls into the courtyard of expedient teaching — not yet the monk's one direct road.

Zhongdu was a Five-Dynasties Chan master of Dengzhou, a dharma-heir of Luopu Yuan'an in the Shitou (Qingyuan) line. Little of his teaching survives beyond a couplet of the wooden-man type beloved of the Caodong-influenced lineages: 'The wooden man is forever answering back; possessed of nature, yet unable to speak.'

Dongshan Daoquan (d. 894) was a Tang Caodong master from Changzhou surnamed Xuan, a dharma-heir of Dongshan Liangjie. Asking his teacher for the essential of escape, he was told 'Smoke is rising under your feet, Reverend' — and awakened on the spot, never wandering again. When Liangjie died the assembly asked him to succeed to the abbacy. In 893 Minister Dai invited him to head the Long'an cloister, and he died the following year; he was posthumously titled Chan Master Zhengzhen.

Dongsi Ruhui (744-823) was a Tang Chan master from Qujiang in Shixing, a dharma-heir of Mazu Daoyi. After first visiting Jingshan Daoqin he studied under Mazu; his assembly grew so large that the benches in the monks' hall gave way, earning him the nickname 'Huì Who Broke the Benches'. Installed at Dongsi in Changsha, his gate flourished so that it was called 'the Chan grotto of Dongsi'. After Mazu's death he grew impatient with disciples endlessly reciting 'this very mind is Buddha', and countered with the challenge: 'Mind is not Buddha; knowing is not the Way.'

Dongyan Kexiu was a Tang/Five-Dynasties Chan master who led an assembly at Dongyan in Yuezhou (modern Shaoxing), a dharma-heir of the great Xuefeng Yicun. Asked 'What is the road upward?' he answered without a word — simply lifting the collar of his robe and showing it.

Dongyang Dehui (fl. 1329-1336), also called Baizhang Dehui, was a Yuan-dynasty Linji/Yangqi monk of uncertain birthplace and dates. He took charge of Baizhang monastery in 1329 and rebuilt its dharma hall in 1330. In 1335 he was commanded by imperial edict to re-edit the Baizhang monastic code; the resulting 勅修百丈清規 was promulgated to every monastery in the empire the following year and became the definitive rule of Chan monastic life, transmitted to Japan and Korea. He is the compiler behind the code's famous restatement of Baizhang's maxim: 'A day without work is a day without food.'

Doushuai Huizhao was a Song Chan master of Doushuai cloister in Longxing prefecture (modern Nanchang), a dharma-heir of Doushuai Congyue in the Linji/Huanglong branch. His recorded teaching turns on effortless arrival: 'One who truly walks does not shift both feet; one who truly enters does not move both door-leaves.'

names: 杭州西天目山斷崖了義禪師
masters.notes: Duanya Liaoyi (1263-1334) was a Yuan-dynasty Linji/Yangqi master of West Mt. Tianmu near Hangzhou, born in Deqing surnamed Yang. As a boy he recited the Lotus Sutra with his mother; at seventeen he took the tonsure under Gaofeng Yuanmiao, whose dharma he inherited, becoming a dharma-brother of the famous Zhongfeng Mingben. In 1326 he took charge of Zhengzong temple on Mt. Tianmu. His signature phrase for awakening is 'revived after being utterly cut off — like cold ashes bursting into flame, like a withered tree blooming again.'

Fada was a Tang Chan monk of Hongzhou (Fengcheng), a dharma-heir of the Sixth Patriarch Huineng. He left home at seven and had recited the Lotus Sutra three thousand times by the time he met Huineng — to whom he bowed without touching his head to the ground, betraying his pride. Huineng's diagnosis produced the couplet that made him famous: 'Three thousand recitations of the sutra — and with one phrase of Caoxi, all of it gone.' His story in the Platform Sutra is the classic Chan parable about mastering the scripture instead of being turned by it.

Fahua Quanju was a Northern Song Linji master, a dharma-heir of Fenyang Shanzhao and thus a dharma-brother of Shishuang Chuyuan and Dayu Shouzhi. Known as 'Ju the Wayfarer', he was famously abrasive: asked to say a phrase that does not tread the road, he slapped his sitting-cloth down once and snapped, 'Fabricating abbots — thick as hemp, thick as millet!' — then shook out his sleeves and walked out.

names: 衡州南嶽後洞方廣有達禪師
masters.notes: Fangguang Youda was a Song Chan master of the Fangguang cloister in the rear grotto of Mt. Nanyue in Hengzhou, a dharma-heir of Dawei Huaixiu in the Linji/Huanglong branch. His surviving sermon plays on Zhaozhou's old sayings and ends in the earthy register the Linji house loved: 'The turnips of Zhenzhou have flavour!' — followed by a shout.

names: 舒州太平佛鑑慧懃禪師
masters.notes: Fojian Huiqin (1059-1117) was a Northern Song Linji/Yangqi master of Taiping in Shuzhou, surnamed Wang, a dharma-heir of Wuzu Fayan. With Yuanwu Keqin and Foyan Qingyuan he made up the 'Three Buddhas' of Fayan's assembly, the trio through whom the Yangqi branch came to dominate later Chan. He was awarded the purple robe and an honorific title at the petition of Deng Xunwu. He used the 'Qiannü's departed soul' story as a teaching device to break students' doubt, and left the pointed couplet: 'Not finding the mind is what settles the mind — but how is awakening any deeper than not having awakened?'

Fuyan Baozong was a Northern Song Linji master of the Fuyan cloister on Mt. Nanyue, a dharma-heir of Shishuang Fayong. His surviving sermon is a piece of cheerful iconoclasm at the expense of the tradition's own heroes: the Sixth Patriarch's transmission of the robe through six generations was 'angling for a petty profit'; Mazu's shout in Jiangxi 'did not know how to guard the beginning'; Deshan's whole display 'did not know how to guard the end.'

Fuyan Liangya was a Northern Song master of the Yunmen school, a dharma-heir of Dongshan Shouchu under whom he served as head monk at Dongshan. He is the witness to the birth of the 'three pounds of flax' koan: when a monk asked Shouchu 'What is Buddha?' and got that answer, Shouchu afterwards came to Liangya's room asking whether the reply had been any good — and Liangya deadpanned, 'You just happened to catch me shaving my head.' He later taught at Fuyan on Mt. Nanyue, where the statesman Wang Sui consulted him on the 'Qiannü's departed soul' story.

Guaishi Qi ('Qi of the Strange Rock') was a Song/Yuan Chan master of Tiantong monastery in Mingzhou (modern Ningbo), a dharma-heir of Yunfeng Miaogao of Jingshan in the Linji/Yangqi line. His recorded teaching insists on first-hand practice over description: 'What cure is there in talking about drinking and talking about eating? You must drink the water yourself and eat the rice yourself — only then is there any real effect.'

Yuanlian of Guanghui cloister in Ruzhou (951–1036), a native of Quanzhou surnamed Chen and a dharma-heir of Shoushan Xingnian in the Linji line. Seven heirs are recorded under him, including Huayan Daolong and the eminent statesman-poet Yang Yi, who called on him while governing Ruzhou and inherited his dharma as a layman.

Qingshun of Guanghui monastery in Mingzhou, a dharma-heir of Zhimen Guangzuo in the Yunmen school, resident at Yunyan temple on Huqiu in Suzhou in the years 995–998. He was a noted recluse-poet, paired with Kejiu as a monk who shunned the city, and Su Shi counted him among his poetry friends.

names: 杭州橫山光明圓智本緣
masters.notes: Benyuan, titled Yuanzhi, of Guangming cloister at Hengshan in Hangzhou, a Qing-dynasty dharma-heir of Muchen (Shanweng) Daomin — the Tiantong abbot summoned to the Shunzhi emperor's court in 1659 — in the Linji-Yangqi line descending from Miyun Yuanwu.

Huijue of Guangxiao monastery in Yangzhou, attendant and one of the few recorded dharma-heirs of the great Zhaozhou Congshen. Nicknamed 'Jue Iron-Mouth', he was well versed in the classics and an able poet; a single heir, Daoyan, is recorded under him.

Daowu of Guannan in Xiangzhou, a dharma-heir of Guannan Daochang in the Hongzhou line of Mazu. He awakened on hearing a village shaman's spirit-music and had it sealed by his teacher; he famously ascended the hall in a lotus hat and robe, beating a drum and blowing a flute, calling himself 'Lu the Third' and singing 'Strike up the Guannan drum, raise the Deshan song'.

Muzhe of Dawei (Guishan) in Tanzhou, surnamed Wen of Linchuan, a dharma-heir of Cuiyan Kezhen in the Linji line. He headed Yuelu, Huiguang and Dawei, and in 1094 was summoned to court, granted the purple robe and the title Zhenru, and appointed to Zhihai cloister at the Great Xiangguo monastery; he died in 1095. His comments on old cases are widely quoted in later anthologies.

Yuncong of Guyin (965–1032), styled Cizhao and also known as Shimen Cong, surnamed Zhang of Nanhai. He first trained under Baizhang Daochang before awakening under Shoushan Xingnian, whose heir he became; he headed Shimen shan in Xiangzhou from 1006 and Taiping Xingguo cloister on Guyin shan from 1020, leaving the Fengyan ji and some ten heirs.

Shanjian, styled Guting, born 1414 in Kunming, a dharma-heir of Wuji Mingwu of Daolin monastery in Puzhou in the Linji-Yangqi line. He headed monasteries from Nanjing's Tianjie to Mount Fu in Anhui and left the 古庭禪師語錄輯略 along with the 山雲水石集 and 華嚴大意; he died in 1493.
Daobian of Hengyue monastery on Mount Nanyue, a Northern Song dharma-heir of Donglin Zhaojue Changzong in the Huanglong branch of the Linji school.

Shouxun of Heshan in Huzhou (1079–1134), titled Fodeng and surnamed Shi. He first approached Guangjian Ying without accord, then took Taiping Fojian Huiqin as master and became his heir in the Yangqi branch of Linji; he led Heshan, Tiansheng and Tianning, and is remembered for his handling of the 'old woman burns the hermitage' case.

Yi'an Yue of Huangbo in Ruizhou, a native of Yangzhou surnamed Tu and a dharma-heir of Ruo'an Tongwen in the Linji-Yangqi line. He headed the ancestral Huangbo mountain and died in 1655, a few months before his teacher, leaving three heirs.

Zujue of Huayan at Zhongyan (1087–1150), styled Chi'an and surnamed Yang of Jiazhou. A scholar who once wrote polemics against Buddhism before converting, he ordained in 1115, awakened reading Fushan Yuanjian's essay, and became a dharma-heir of Yuanwu Keqin; he wrote a six-hundred-fascicle history of the buddhas and patriarchs along with commentaries on the Huayan and Diamond sutras.

Jingyuan of Huguo monastery in Taizhou (1094–1146), styled Ci'an and nicknamed 'Yuan the Cloth-Bag', surnamed Zhang of Yongjia. Ordained at eighteen and first trained in Tiantai doctrine, he abandoned it for Yuanwu Keqin at Zhongfu and became his heir in the Yangqi branch of Linji; he opened the dharma at Renshou and ended his days back at Huguo.

Qingdan of Huitong in Tanzhou, a native of Pengzhou surnamed Yan and a dharma-heir of Dawei Foxing Fatai in the Yangqi branch of Linji, making him a grand-heir of Yuanwu Keqin. He was released on hearing Fatai raise Zhaozhou's 'the old woman of Mount Tai has been seen through' at Deshan, served him long, and succeeded to his seat; his community was known for its strict and pure discipline.

Xingsheng, styled Benchong, a Quanzhou man surnamed Wu who left a degree-track literary career to take the robe at 28, awakened under Feiyin Tongrong at Jinsu, and became abbot of Huiyun Chan monastery in Hangzhou. He wrote the 禪林寶訓拈頌 and 古鑑錄, and died in 1671; his body was reportedly found incorrupt when his reliquary split open seven years later.
Fang of Jiangshan in Yuezhou, a Northern Song dharma-heir of Langye Huijue of Chuzhou in the Linji line.

Faquan of Jiangshan in Jinling, titled Fohui and surnamed Shi of Suizhou, a dharma-heir of Yunju Xiaoshun in the Yunmen school. A prodigious reader nicknamed 'Quan of the Ten Thousand Scrolls', he headed five monasteries before being summoned to Zhihai cloister at the Great Xiangguo monastery, and left three heirs and a verse commentary on the Song of Enlightenment.

Miguang of Jiaozhong monastery in Quanzhou (d. 1155), styled Hui'an and nicknamed 'Guang the Top Graduate', surnamed Li of Fujian. Tonsured at fifteen, he trained under several masters before his great awakening under Dahui Zonggao, whose heir he became in the Yangqi branch of Linji; he opened the dharma at Jiaozhong for ten years at a vice-councillor's invitation before moving to Mount Gui.

Ziling of Lingquan at Jiashan in Lizhou, surnamed Zhou of Yixing, a dharma-heir of Fori Zhicai in the Yunmen school. Ordained in his home prefecture and fully ordained at eighteen, he wandered the monasteries before clarifying the mind-essence under his teacher; three heirs are recorded under him.

names: 杭州靈隱介菴用真輔良
masters.notes: Fuliang, styled Jie'an, a Suzhou man of the Fan family, dharma-heir of Xiaoyin Daxin and abbot of Lingyin monastery in Hangzhou. Born in 1317 under the Yuan, he died in 1371 in the early Ming aged 55 with forty years in the robe.

Jiesan Hong of Hongguang monastery in the capital, a native of Jiading in Suzhou surnamed Ge, and a dharma-heir of Dabo Xingqian of Panshan in the Linji-Yangqi line descending through Wanru Tongwei from Miyun Yuanwu. Tonsured at seventeen, he was first set on the Zhaozhou 'wu' huatou by Feiyin Tongrong, trained intensively under Xingqian from 1666, and spent six years in sealed retreat at Qianmu Garden; five heirs are recorded under him.

names: 潤州金山龍游寺佛鑑惟仲
masters.notes: Weizhong of Jinshan at Zhenjiang, titled Fojian, a native of Tingzhou and a dharma-heir of Fayun Weibai — the Yunmen master who compiled the Jianzhong Jingguo Continued Lamp Record. He awakened on the 'cypress in the courtyard' case at Guishan, attended Weibai at Fayun in the Eastern Capital, and on the recommendation of chief councillor Zeng Bu opened the hall at Jinshan in 1101.

masters.school: 北宗 (Northern School — 神秀 → 普寂 line)
masters.notes: Mingzan, known as Lanzan ('Lazy Can'), an eighth-century recluse who studied under Puji on Mount Song in the Northern School and silently accorded with his mind, then lived idle at Hengyue — while the other monks laboured he stayed at ease, earning his nickname. From the early Tianbao era he did menial work at the Nanyue temple and slept beneath the oxen for twenty years. The chancellor Li Mi sought him out at midnight and was cursed and spat at, then handed half a taro raked from a dung fire, which Li ate kneeling in thanks. He is celebrated for the 'Song of Enjoying the Way'.

Fansi of Tianning monastery in Quzhou, styled Natang, a man of Suzhou surnamed Zhu and a dharma-heir of Yuanwu Keqin in the Yangqi branch of Linji. Three heirs are recorded under him, among them Chengzhao Xingqi.

Daolin of Hangzhou (741–824), called the 'Bird's Nest monk' for dwelling in a canopy-like pine on Qinwang shan, and 'Magpie's Nest' for the bird that nested beside him. A native of Fuyang surnamed Pan, he studied Huayan and the Awakening of Faith at Chang'an before meeting Jingshan Daoqin and receiving the dharma in the Oxhead line. He awakened his attendant Huitong by plucking and blowing a tuft of down from his robe, and famously told the poet Bai Juyi that although a three-year-old could recite 'do no evil, practise the good', an eighty-year-old still could not do it.

Huizhong of Mount Niutou (683–769), sixth patriarch of the Oxhead school, surnamed Wang of Jiangning. He trained at Zhuangyan monastery from the age of twenty-three and served Zhiwei, inheriting his dharma; he lived with minimal possessions, later presided at Yanzuo monastery, and left some thirty-odd successors, the most notable being Weize of Foku cliff on Mount Tiantai.

Xingcong, styled Hanpu (1611–1667), a native of Shaowu in Fujian surnamed Lian, ordained at fifteen and a dharma-heir of Baichi Xingyuan of Taiping monastery in Hangzhou. He held seats from Hangzhou to Beijing, and in 1657 the Shunzhi emperor summoned him to the Wanshan Hall retreat and granted him the title Chan Master Mingjue — he is the monk who first drew that emperor to Chan.

Daoming of Mount Meng in Yuanzhou, formerly the layman Huiming — a grandson of Emperor Xuan of Chen who had held a fourth-rank general's commission, hence his nickname 'the General'. He trained under the Fifth Patriarch Hongren without breakthrough, then led dozens in pursuit of Huineng to Dayu Ridge; unable to lift the robe from the rock, he awakened instead at 'think neither good nor evil'. Huineng refused to be called his master, declaring them fellow disciples of Huangmei, so the lamp records file him as Hongren's collateral heir; he taught at Mengshan with three heirs of his own.

names: 建寧府高仰山古梅正友
masters.notes: Zhengyou, styled Gumei (1285–1352), a dharma-heir of Juexue Shicheng of the Prajñā monastery in the Linji-Yangqi line. After some thirty years wandering the Jiang-Huai region he entered Fujian and in 1324 opened Dajue Miaozhi on Mount Gaoyang under an imperial plaque; his instruction on sustaining doubt in huatou practice was anthologized in the Changuan cejin, and his recorded sayings survive.

Tang-dynasty Chan master from Hongzhou who awakened under 百丈懷海. Drawn by the fame of Mount Tiantai, he withdrew there, built a hut, and eventually founded the 平田禪院 (Pingtian Chan Cloister), from which he takes his name. The Wudeng Huiyuan records a celebrated exchange in which 臨濟義玄 visited him. His verse to the assembly begins 「大道虗曠，常一真心」. He died at his own cloister in 862.

Tang-dynasty Chan master of Mount Song, dharma heir of National Teacher 嵩嶽慧安. His real name and family are unrecorded — 「不稱名氏，言行叵測」 — and he is known only by the nickname "Stove-Breaker" (破竈墮), earned when he struck a shrine's stove three times with his staff, declaring 「此竈只是泥瓦合成，聖從何來，靈從何起」 ("This stove is just clay and tile joined together; whence the sacred, whence the numinous?"), whereupon the stove toppled and its resident spirit was released. He has his own heir-section in the lamp records, headed by 嵩山峻極.

Song-dynasty Linji master who taught at 慶善院 in Hangzhou. Dharma heir of 淨土善思 of Lin'an (himself an heir of 菩提光用); the 建中靖國續燈錄 records Shansi as having exactly two heirs, 萬壽法詮 and Shoulong. His recorded exchanges are brief — at his opening sermon, asked to show the jewel long hidden in his bag, he replied 「多少分明」 ('How utterly plain it is').

Tang-dynasty Chan master of Mount Yao in Raozhou, dharma heir of 福州大安 (Changqing Da'an, 793–883, second abbot of Guishan and himself an heir of 百丈懷海). Only a short set of exchanges survives in the Jingde Chuandeng Lu: asked the meaning of the coming from the West he answered 「仲冬嚴寒」 ('Midwinter, bitter cold'); asked about his deepest place, 「待汝舌頭落地，即向汝道」 ('When your tongue falls to the ground, I'll tell you'). He is also recorded in dialogue with 長慶慧稜.

Song-dynasty Yunmen-school master at 瑞相 in Ruizhou, one of the fifty-nine dharma heirs of 法雲法秀 (Fayun Faxiu, 1027–1090, the 'Yuantong' master of Dongjing, himself an heir of 天衣義懷). In his recorded sermon he surveys the assembly and says that a true master 「隨處提綱，應機問答，殺活臨時」 — raises the essential everywhere, meets each question as it comes, kills or gives life as the moment demands.

Song-dynasty Yunmen-school master of 聖壽香積 in Lizhou, one of the fifty-nine dharma heirs of 法雲法秀 (1027–1090). His surviving sermon opens with the image 「木馬衝開千騎路」 — a wooden horse charging open a road for a thousand riders.

names: 舒州山谷三祖冲會圓智
masters.notes: Song-dynasty Yunmen-school master, a native of Lin'an and dharma heir of 天衣義懷 (Tianyi Yihuai, heir of 雪竇重顯). He was abbot of the 山谷寺 on 三祖山 in Shuzhou — the Third Patriarch's temple associated with 僧璨 — from which his name derives. Asked at his opening sermon what the first principle was, he answered 「百雜碎」 ('Smashed to a hundred pieces'); asked what the immovable Honoured One was, 「寸步千里」 ('An inch of step, a thousand miles').

Ming–Qing Linji master, personal name 通雲, sobriquet 石奇, of the Xu family of Loudong. A grave childhood illness brought on a visionary experience; he left his mother and was tonsured at Nanguang, was set the huatou 'your face before your parents were born', and his doubt-mass broke open while wandering at Pingyao Xiansheng. He became a dharma heir of 密雲圓悟 at Tiantong and served as abbot of 雪竇山資聖禪寺 in Ningbo (Mingzhou), where his recorded sayings (雪竇石奇禪師語錄, Jiaxing Canon B183) were compiled by his heir 行正.

Song-dynasty Linji master of the Huanglong branch, abbot of the 太平寺 at Yongzhou (also recorded as 永州元豐太平寺安禪師). Dharma heir of 寶峰克文 (Zhenjing Kewen, 1025–1102, himself an heir of 黃龍慧南). His surviving sermon plays on Zhaozhou's stock sayings: 「有利無利，莫離行市。鎮州蘿蔔極貴，廬陵米價甚賤。爭似太平這裏，時豐道泰」 — 'Profit or no profit, don't leave the marketplace… but how does that compare with here at Taiping, where the harvest is rich and the Way is at ease?'

Tang-dynasty master of the Oxhead (Niutou) school, a native of Pengzhou of the Chen family and a dharma heir of 牛頭智威. In the early Qianyuan era (c. 758) he went to Mount Tianzhu in Shuzhou and founded a monastery there, which received its imperial name-plaque in 765. Asked what the Way is, he answered 「白雲覆青嶂，蜂蝶戀庭華」 — 'White clouds cover the green peaks; bees and butterflies love the courtyard blossoms.'

Song-dynasty Linji (Yangqi) master, sobriquet 卍庵, from Tongchuan of the Xianyu family, abbot of the 東林寺 at Jiangzhou. He trained long under 圓悟克勤 and gained a partial awakening; when Yuanwu returned to Shu he directed Daoyan to go to 大慧宗杲 (Miaoxi), sending a letter of introduction ahead of him — and it is under Dahui that the lamps record his transmission. His style is austere: 「須是入得無門之門，方可坐登堂奧」 ('You must enter the gateless gate before you can sit in the inner hall'), and he offers students only 「木札羹、鉄釘飯」 — woodchip soup and iron-nail rice.

Song–Yuan Linji master, sobriquet 皖山, from Dahu in Shuzhou of the Li family. Orphaned at seventeen, he was tonsured under 雙泉道瑛 and ordained at Kaiyuan. He tried 環菴璉, 癡絕道沖 and 長蘆南山哲 without a match, got a first opening from a punch delivered by 雙塔無明性, then went into Fujian to 孤峰德秀, who set him Zhaozhou's 「狗子無佛性」; after half a year he broke through and was eventually sealed with 「善自護持」 and made incense attendant. He followed Gufeng to Xichan and Nangshan, and after his teacher's death went to Xuefeng; he later headed Gushan in Fuzhou.

Tang-dynasty Chan master, personal name 仁儉 of the 福先寺 in Luoyang, universally known by his nickname 騰騰和尚 ('Abbot Helter-Skelter') for the free, unbuttoned life he led in the towns after finishing his study on Mount Song. Dharma heir of National Teacher 嵩嶽慧安. Summoned before Empress Wu in the Tiance Wansui era, he stared at her a long while and said only 'Understand?' — and when she said no, 'This old monk keeps the vow of not speaking,' and walked out. He presented nineteen short songs the next day; the Empress praised them and heaped gifts on him, all of which he refused. His 樂道歌 ('Song of Delighting in the Way') is his enduring legacy: 「問道道無可修，問法法無可問…煩惱即是菩提，淨花生於泥糞。」

Song-dynasty Linji (Yangqi) master of 無為 in Hanzhou, a native of Fucheng and one of the roughly twenty dharma heirs of 五祖法演 (d. 1104) — making him a dharma brother of 圜悟克勤, 佛鑑慧懃 and 佛眼清遠. The lamps record his awakening around Zhaozhou's 'go wash your bowl' huatou, which Fayan set him on the day he offered incense, and the sharp follow-up in which Fayan told him 「爾秖知路上事，不知路上滋味」 ('You only know what's on the road; you don't know the road's flavour').

Xiatang Huiyuan (1103–1176), also 佛海慧遠 and 靈隱慧遠, a leading Southern Song master of the Linji Yangqi line and dharma heir of 圜悟克勤. Of the Peng family of Meishan in Sichuan, he was ordained at thirteen and studied the canon at Daci monastery in Chengdu before going to Yuanwu. In 1170 Emperor Xiaozong summoned him by decree to the abbacy of 靈隱寺 and granted him the title 佛海禪師. The lamps describe his teaching as deliberately unmoored — 「說法格外作用，不守規轍，脫略窠臼」 — and his room-encounters as sheer and impossible to get a footing on. His recorded sayings survive as the 瞎堂慧遠禪師廣錄. His most famous disciple was 道濟, remembered in legend as the mad monk Jigong.

Tang-dynasty master of the 西園蘭若 on Mount Nanyue, who received the mind-seal from 馬祖道一 and afterwards called on 石頭希遷, becoming (in the lamp's phrase) 「瑩然明徹」 — lucidly clear. Under him the Xiyuan community grew steadily. He is remembered for a wry exchange preserved in the koan literature: asked why, having no novices or postulants, he heated his own bathwater, he simply clapped three times — a gesture 曹山本寂 later compared, not altogether kindly, to Judi's one-finger Chan.

masters.teacher: 雪竇大歇仲謙 (Xuedou Daxie Zhongqian)
masters.notes: Song–Yuan Linji master of the 國清寺 in Taizhou, dharma heir of 雪竇大歇仲謙 and thus in the Songyuan branch of the Yangqi line. His surviving general sermon (普說) presses the matter of birth-and-death on travelling monks with a four-cornered dilemma: if birth-and-death exists, no one from antiquity has escaped it; if it does not exist, what do you make of the birth-and-death right in front of you? — and, holding all four horns at once, 「還有漏網底麼？」 ('Is there anyone who slips the net?').

Song-dynasty Linji master, personal name 仲謙, sobriquet 大歇, of the Ying family of Yiwu; abbot of 雪竇 in Mingzhou (Qingyuan). A boyhood reading of Fu Dashi's 心王銘 set him on the monastic path. His first teacher 息菴 valued him but held him down: 'You are a Confucian — with those habits unshed, how can you study the Way? You must reach the ground of great rest and great cessation (大休大歇), and go like a wooden puppet.' The rebuke stuck, and when he finally had an opening he took 大歇 as his own name. His full awakening came under 松源崇嶽 (1132–1202), in the room, on the case of Mimo's forked staff. He has his own heir-section in the lamps.

Song-dynasty Linji (Huanglong) master (1084–1158), personal name 法一, sobriquet 雪巢, also styled 貫道 — a great-great-grandson of Li Zunmian, Prince of Xiangyang, whose family lived at Xiangfu in Kaifeng. He received the dharma from 草堂善清 (1057–1142) at Shushan, headed four great monasteries, then retired from Changlu and returned to the 萬年觀音院 on Mount Tiantai. Falling lightly ill, he wrote his death verse — 「今年七十五，歸作庵中主。珎重觀世音，泥蛇吞石虎」 ('Seventy-five this year, I go back to be master of the hut; farewell, Guanyin — the clay snake swallows the stone tiger') — then sat cross-legged in his coffin and died.

Northern Song Yunmen-school master, abbot of 雪竇 in Mingzhou, a native of Quzhou of the Du family and dharma heir of 保寧覺印子英. His recorded sermon turns on discernment: 「向這裏辨得，羅紋十字，一任橫行；苟或未然，切忌亂走」 — 'Discern it here and you may cross the grain in any direction you please; if not, whatever you do, don't go wandering about.'

Southern Song Linji (Huanglong) master (1096–1158), 福州雪峯東山慧空禪師, dharma heir of 草堂善清 (1057–1142) and reckoned the fifteenth generation below the Sixth Patriarch. Tonsured at fourteen, he studied 圜悟克勤 at Yunju alongside 大慧宗杲 (妙喜) before going on to serve 草堂 at Shushan, who transmitted to him. He opened the dharma at Xuefeng and later retired to the East Hermitage (東菴), from which his alternate name 東山慧空 comes. His disciple 慧弼 compiled his 語錄 in one fascicle (X69n1346).

Northern Song Yunmen-school master, 山主 (hermitage-head) of Xuefeng in western Sichuan, dharma heir of 潞州妙勝臻. A single short sermon survives, and it is all urgency: 「昨日一，今日二，不用思量，快須瞥地。不瞥地，蹉過平生勿巴鼻。咄！」 — 'Yesterday one, today two. No pondering — catch a glimpse of it, quick. Miss the glimpse and you botch your whole life with nothing to grab hold of. Bah!'

Song-dynasty Yunmen-school master (1071–1145), personal name 思慧, sobriquet 妙湛, of the Yu family of Qiantang; dharma heir of 法雲大通善本 (1035–1109) and reckoned the fourteenth generation below the Sixth Patriarch. He was ordained under Datong as a boy and awakened on reading in the Yuanjue Sutra 'knowing illusion, you are already free of it, without contrivance; free of illusion, you are already awake, without stages'. He headed Zhachuan, then Jingshan and Jingci, was summoned by decree to Zhihai in the capital, and later moved through Xianqin, Huangbo and Xuefeng, retiring at last to the East Hermitage. The lamps credit him with fourteen dharma heirs, chief among them 照堂了一 and 月堂道昌. His sermon on Yaoshan — who let a month go by without teaching, then walked back to his room the moment the assembly gathered — turns on the wry judgement 「彼時佛法早自淡薄，論來猶較些子」: even that thin gruel of a Dharma was still somewhat better than today's drum-beating and chatter.

Song-dynasty Yunmen-line master, full title 福州雪峰宗演圓覺禪師. A native of Enzhou 恩州, surname Cui 崔. Dharma-heir of Yuanfeng Qingman 元豐清滿; DILA records that he 「唱雲門之道」 (propagated the Yunmen way). Summoned in Zhenghe 8 (1118) to head Tianning monastery in the capital, and during the Xuanhe era (1119-1125) Emperor Huizong called him to preach in the inner court and bestowed the purple robe. He presided over thirteen monasteries in all, ending at Yunfeng, and left two dharma-heirs.

Linji (Yangqi branch) master (1089-1151), styled Xuetang 雪堂, full title 衢州烏巨雪堂道行禪師. A native of Kuocang in Chuzhou 處州括蒼, surname Ye 葉. Ordained at nineteen under Jueyin Ziying at Puzhao; after a fruitless stay with Zhiyuan Run he went to Longmen and became attendant to Foyan Qingyuan, awakening on the story of Xuansha stubbing his toe, and inherited Foyan's dharma. From Jianyan 2 (1128) he opened the hall at Shouning, then successively led Fahai, Tianning, Nanming and Wuju, declining eight later invitations to major monasteries; he died at Jianfu in Raozhou. Author of 雪堂行和尚語要 and 雪堂行和尚拾遺錄; Dahui Zonggao wrote the preface to his recorded sayings.

Yunmen-line master (1024-1084), full title 南昌武寧延恩法安禪師. A native of Linchuan 臨川, surname Xu 許; ordained at twenty. He first studied under Xuedou Chongxian and, after Xuedou's death, attached himself to Tianyi Yihuai, whose dharma he inherited. After a decade at Ruyi cloister on Mt. Huang he settled at Yan'en monastery in Wuning, refusing the magistrate's offer to rebuild its ramshackle halls on the grounds that coerced donation 「是名作業，不名佛事」 — yet a full monastic community grew there over ten years. Known for the saying 「萬事隨緣，是安樂法」 (take all things as they come — that is the law of ease). Died in the 8th month of Yuanfeng jiazi (1084), aged 61, with 41 summers.

Song-dynasty Yunmen-line master, 雁蕩文吉禪師, based at Mt. Yandang 雁蕩 (also written 雁宕). A dharma-heir of Wuzu Shijie 五祖師戒, he is recorded in the 建中靖國續燈錄 among Shijie's forty heirs and left one heir of his own, Jingguang Weijue. He is remembered for the exchange on dharma-succession in which, asked whom he had inherited, he answered 「無角鐵牛眠少室，生兒石女老黃梅」 — prompting the questioner to identify him as 「韶陽兒孫」, a descendant of Yunmen Wenyan.

Tang/Five-Dynasties master 福州永隆院彥端禪師, of Yonglong cloister in Fuzhou. A dharma-heir of Anguo Hongtao 安國弘瑫 (Mingzhen 明真) of Fuzhou, placing him in the fourth generation from Xuefeng Yicun (Hongtao himself studied under Xuefeng). He appears in the lamp records chiefly through a cake-eating exchange with Luohan Zhiyi 羅漢智依 on the 「不二體」 (the non-dual substance).

Linji (Huanglong branch) master (1019-1081), full title 袁州仰山行偉禪師. A native of Heshuo 河朔. He began from study of the Yuanjue (Perfect Enlightenment) Sutra, and when doubts arose took up the travelling bag to seek the ancestral meaning. He spent six years in Huanglong Huinan's assembly; one day, pressing Huinan with a question, he was shouted out of the room, and as his foot crossed the threshold he abruptly awakened to the profound import. He then taught at Mt. Yang (Yangshan) in Yuanzhou, where his teaching flourished, leaving eight dharma-heirs.

Southern Song master 隱山璨, active around the Chunxi era (c. 1174), abbot of Fashi 法石 in Quanzhou. A native of Jinjiang in Quanzhou 泉之晉江. The 枯崖漫錄 describes him as blunt and hot-tempered, given to sharp criticism, saying of himself that he was 「業林一害」 (a blight on the monastic groves). His recorded sayings survive as 隱山璨和尚語 in the 續古尊宿語要 (X68).

Fayan-house master, 杭州永明寺道潛禪師, died 961. A native of Hezhong prefecture 河中府, surname Wu 武. He came to Fayan Wenyi already a Huayan specialist; Wenyi asked which gate the six characteristics (總別同異成壞) belonged to, and Daoqian answered from the Ten Stages chapter that all worldly and world-transcending dharmas possess them. Wenyi then asked whether emptiness also possesses the six characteristics; Daoqian was struck dumb, so Wenyi told him to put the question back — and to Daoqian's 「空還具六相也無？」 answered simply 「空」. At that Daoqian awakened and bowed in delight. He is the Daoqian of Yongming monastery in Hangzhou, the house later made famous by Yongming Yanshou.

Tang/Five-Dynasties master 台州涌泉景欣禪師, of Yongquan hermitage in Danqiu, Taizhou. He took his training at Baiyun 白雲山, then received the teaching of Shishuang Qingzhu of Tanzhou and settled at Yongquan. He appears in the anecdote literature as the master of the 「涌泉騎牛」 (riding the ox) exchange with the two Chan travellers Jiang and De.

Southern Song Linji (Yangqi) master, 太平隱靜圓極彥岑禪師, styled Yuanji 圓極. A native of Taizhou (Huangyan per the 五燈全書, Xianju per DILA).
