Described as aloof and uncompromising to a degree rare in his age, he served Yunju Faru for seventeen years in the scriptorium; when Faru died he returned to Zhejiang and attached himself to Zhengtang Bian at Daochang, who soon made him head seat. He first taught at Bianshan in Zha, then led a series of major monasteries, retiring at last to Huazang Daochang in Changzhou, where he died. His 20-fascicle recorded sayings circulated with a preface by Vice-Minister Zeng Zhonggong.

Song master 撫州靈巖圓日禪師, of Lingyan in Fuzhou (Jiangxi), the sole recorded dharma-heir of Yuanjue Tan. He survives in the lamp records through a single hall-address: 「悟無不悟，得無不得，九年面壁空勞力。三脚驢兒跳上天，泥牛入海無蹤跡」 — nine years facing the wall was wasted effort; the three-legged donkey leaps into the sky, the clay ox enters the sea and leaves no trace.

Northern Song Linji (Huanglong) master (1047-1114), full title 江州圓通圓機道旻禪師. A native of Xinghua, surname Cai 蔡; he left home under Dexiang of Jingde monastery. He first followed Weishan Muzhe, then received the seal from Letan Yingqian. Early in Huizong's reign he opened the hall at Guanxi and later moved to Yuantong in Jiangzhou. In the Zhenghe era he was granted the title Yuanji Chanshi 圓機禪師, and popular devotion came to call him 「圓機古佛」 — the Ancient Buddha Yuanji. He left both monastic heirs and a notable circle of官員 lay heirs.

Northern Song Linji master (997-1062), 雲峰文悅, of Nanyue. A native of Nanchang, surname Xu 徐; tonsured at seven at Longxing monastery and travelling the Jiang-Huai region with a staff from nineteen. He awakened to the mind-seal under Dayu Shouzhi and served him diligently for eight years. Nanchang issued a formal request that he take up Cuifeng, and he later moved to Yunfeng, the mountain that gives him his name. He died on the 8th day of the 7th month of Jiayou 7 (1062), having lived 66 years and kept 59 summers as a monk, and left seven dharma-heirs.

Northern Song Yunmen-house master, 衡州南嶽雲峰元益禪師, also styled 雲峯元益首座 (head seat). A dharma-heir of Xuedou Chongxian, he taught at Yunfeng on Mt. Nanyue in Hengzhou. The lamp preserves his encounter with the official Li Linzong, who asked how to leave the dust of the world; when Li presented an awakening verse (「心鏡從來瑩…沙石化為金」) Yuanyi cut him down with 「正趣地獄」 — 'straight to hell with you' — and Li replied 「覿面不識」, face to face and still not recognising. Li Linzong went on to become Yuanyi's sole recorded dharma-heir.

Northern Song Yunmen-house master, 潭州雲蓋繼鵬禪師. He first called on Shuangquan Ya, who made him attendant and set him the Bajiao staff story; nothing came of it for a long while, until one day, standing by as Shuangquan warmed himself at the fire, he was told to bring the staff story up for discussion — and as he began, Shuangquan jabbed at him with the fire-tongs, at which he greatly awakened. Once installed, he answered the question 'What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?' with 「舌頭無骨」 — the tongue has no bone in it. He left four dharma-heirs.

Northern Song Linji (Yangqi) master (1035-1107), 潭州雲蓋山智本禪師. A native of Gao'an in Yunzhou, surname Guo 郭; he passed the sutra examination at nineteen, was fully ordained the next year, and set out travelling at once. In the years when Yunju Xiaoshun and Kaixian Xian led the foremost assemblies on Mt. Lu he moved between the two, then heard that Fahua Duan (Baiyun Shouduan) was a true den of the dharma, went to him, and stayed ten years — after which his name carried far. Li Duanchen, prefect of Shuzhou, invited him to preach at Longmen; he later returned to Mt. Lu, and when Chancellor Zeng went out to govern Changsha he installed him with full ceremony at Falun on Nanyue, where students vied to follow him. He went on to Nantai, Daolin, Yungai, Shishuang and Jiashan, and on the Lantern Festival night of Daguan 1 (1107) bathed, changed his robes, sat upright and died at Jiashan, aged 73 with 52 years in robes.

Northern Song Yunmen-house master, 潭州雲蓋山智顒禪師 (his name also written 志顒). One of the forty dharma-heirs of Wuzu Shijie recorded in the 建中靖國續燈錄. The lamp preserves his hall-address in which he surveyed the assembly, gave a shout, and pressed them with the Linji categories — 「莫是賓主歷然麼？莫是先照後用麼？莫是照用同時麼？」 (Is this host and guest plainly distinct? Illumination first then function? Illumination and function at once?). He left two dharma-heirs.

Fayan-house master (929-997), 洪州雲居道齊禪師, reckoned the 11th generation from Huineng. A native of Hongzhou, surname Jin 金; he was ordained under Mingzhao of Mt. Baizhang and travelled the Chan assemblies without his questing mind settling, until he met Fadeng (Qingliang Taiqin) and the connection took at once. When Fadeng took up Shanglan cloister, Daoqi headed the sutra library. He taught in three places over thirty years — Dayu at Gao'an, Shuanglin at Yougushan, and finally Mt. Yunju — and compiled the 搜玄, 拈古 and 代別 collections, which circulated widely in the monasteries. In the 9th month of Zhidao 3 (997) he fell ill; on the 8th he had the bell rung to assemble the community and delivered the address the batch cites — 「老僧今日火風相逼，特與諸人相見，諸人還見麼！」 (fire and wind press me today; I meet you all one last time — do you see?) — entrusted the mountain gate to Qigui, and died as soon as the assembly dispersed, aged 69 with 48 years in robes.

Northern Song Yunmen-house master, known as Yunju Shun 雲居舜 and also as Dayu Xiaoshun of Yunzhou. A native of Ruizhou, surname Hu 胡; a dharma-heir of Dongshan Xiaocong. The records praise his plain directness — he trimmed the lamps and swept the floors himself rather than delegate. He led Qixian monastery on Mt. Lu, where he had a reputation for purity, then Jingyin monastery in the capital, where Emperor Renzong praised him: 「道韻奇偉，山林達士」 (his way-resonance is remarkable — an accomplished man of the mountains and forests). Late in life he went to Yunju in Nankang. He left several heirs.

Five-Dynasties/early-Song Fayan-house master, 雲居山義能禪師, a dharma-heir of Baoci Xingyan of Jinling and thus in the third generation of the Fayan house. The lamp preserves his answer to the question 'What is Buddha?' — 「即心是佛」 — and, when the monk pleaded that he did not understand and begged for expedient means, his follow-up: 「方便呼為佛，迴光返照看身心是何物」 (as an expedient it is called Buddha; turn the light around and look back — what are this body and mind?).

Song Linji (Huanglong) master, 隆興府雲巖典牛天遊禪師 — Dianniu ('Herding the Ox') Tianyou. A native of Chengdu, surname Zheng 鄭. He passed the examinations at two prefectures but declined the registration and slipped out through the pass under an assumed name. He first called on Sixin without connecting, then attached himself to Zhantang Wenzhun at Letan and inherited his dharma; his preaching was said to carry Zhantang's manner. He taught at Yungai, then Yunyan, and finally built a hermitage at Wuning and never left it again. His sobriquet comes from ox-herding verses like the one the batch cites, capping Attendant Zhong: 「兩角指天，四足踏地。拽斷鼻繩，牧甚屎屁」 — two horns point at the sky, four hooves tread the earth; snap the nose-rope — what the hell is there to herd?

Major Song Linji (Yangqi) master (1085-1150), 明州育王佛智端裕禪師, honorific Fozhi 佛智 (Buddha-Wisdom). A native of Shaoxing, surname Qian 錢; ordained at Dashan monastery. He first called on Jingci Yi and worked through Longmen Yuan, Ganlu Zhuo and Letan Xiang before coming to Yuanwu Keqin, whom he first attended at Tianning Wanshou monastery as recorder and then as sub-abbot sharing the seat. He opened the hall at Danxia, then Huqiu, Wanshou and Baoning, then Xuanmiao and Xichan at Shoushan in Fujian; by imperial order he was installed at Lingyin, and late in life moved to Ayuwang, the seat that names him. He is remembered for the saying the batch cites: 「一法若有，重重鐵壁銀山；萬法若無，處處沈空滯寂」 — if a single dharma exists, iron walls and silver mountains layer on layer; if the myriad dharmas do not, then everywhere is sunk in emptiness and stalled in quiescence.

Yuan-dynasty Linji (Yangqi) master (1292-1357), 寧波府育王雪窗悟光禪師, styled Gongshi 公寔 and known as Xuechuang 雪窗 ('Snow Window'). Surname Yang 楊. He studied the doctrinal teachings at Tianwang monastery and was ordained by Liaochong, then went to Jingci to call on Dongyu Dehai, whose dharma he inherited. He opened the hall at Baima monastery in Pingjiang in Zhishun 1 (1330), took Kaiyuan in Yuantong 1 (1333), and went on to Ayuwang and Tiantong. In the Zhizheng era he received the title 佛日圓明普濟禪師. He wrote the 四會錄, for which Song Lian supplied the preface, and left fourteen dharma-heirs.

明州育王曇振真戒禪師, a Song Yunmen-line master, 13th generation below Huineng, and the eighth abbot of Ayuwang shan in Mingzhou. Dharma heir of Ruiyan Zihong (d. 1096), who was in turn an heir of Tianyi Yihuai (993–1064) — placing him securely in the Yunmen line, as the 雲門山志 succession table also shows. A recorded 上堂 opens 「今日布袋頭開，還有買賣者麼？」— when a monk answered 「有」he replied 「不作貴，不作賤，作麼生酬價？」and, at the monk's silence, 「老僧失利！」

隆興府泐潭湛堂文準禪師 (1061–1115), a native of 興元府, lay surname 梁. Dharma heir of Zhenjing Kewen, 14th generation below Huineng in the Linji Huanglong branch. He first met Zhenjing at Toulao'an, served him ten years, and awakened when water splashed his robe as he cleared an irrigation ditch. He taught at Yunyan and then Letan. Dahui Zonggao trained under him but took transmission from Yuanwu Keqin, so is not counted among his heirs.

成都府正法希明禪師, a native of 漢州, dharma heir of Qingyuan Weixin in the Linji Huanglong branch. His recorded 解制上堂 begins 「林葉紛紛落，乾坤報早秋。分明西祖意，何用更馳求」and argues that once the source is fathomed, 「動靜施為，經行坐臥，頭頭合道，念念朝宗」— walking, sitting and every act accord with the Way; without it, 「百劫熏功，千生鍊行」are wasted effort.

東京智海本逸正覺禪師, lay surname 彭 of Fuzhou; ordained at nine. Yunmen-line master, 11th generation below Qingyuan, dharma heir of Kaixian Shanxian, under whom he awakened when Shanxian raised Bodhidharma's transmission verse. First abbot of 薦福 in Raozhou; Emperor Shenzong then summoned him to 智海 and granted him the title 正覺 — whence the name 正覺逸.

常州正勤院蘊禪師, lay surname 韓 of Weifu; ordained young and said to have kept a youthful face into old age. Caodong master, dharma heir of Shushan Kuangren (himself an heir of Dongshan Liangjie). Asked 「如何是禪？」he answered 「石上蓮華火裏泉」; asked 「如何是道？」— 「楞伽峰頂一莖草」; asked how far apart Chan and the Way stand — 「泥人落水木人撈」. He died peacefully in the Jin Tianfu era; two years after burial his disciples opened the stupa and found the body intact with hair and nails grown, whereupon they cremated him and re-enshrined the relics.

鎮州大悲和尚, a Tang-dynasty Linji master and dharma heir of Sansheng Huiran (himself a direct heir of Linji Yixuan) — i.e. a dharma-grandson of Linji. Recorded exchange: a monk said 「除上去下請師便道」; he answered 「我開口即錯」. The monk replied 「真是學人師」, and he said 「今日向弟子手裏死」.

涿州紙衣和尚, better known as 克符道者 ('Kefu the Wayfarer') — a direct dharma heir of Linji Yixuan, so a first-generation Linji master. He awakened on the spot when Linji answered his four questions on the 四料簡 (the four discernments of person and object), and afterwards composed the celebrated set of verses on them. The batch citation 「人境俱不奪。思量意不偏。主賓言少異。問答理俱全。」is the fourth of those verses. He also left a well-known four-fold answer on 賓主 (guest and host).

泉州法石中庵慧空禪師 (1106–1174), a native of Ganxian in Ganzhou, lay surname 蔡. A scholar in his youth, he took the tonsure only at thirty-six at the prefectural Guanyin cloister, then found insight with Yangshan Zu; next he studied with Cuiyan Guangzhao Deng, who found his talk congenial and put him in charge of correspondence. He received transmission from Hui'an Miguang, a leading heir of Dahui Zonggao, and taught at Fashi in Quanzhou.

真州長蘆宗賾慈覺禪師, lay surname 孫 of Xiangyang; 12th generation below Huineng and the 7th of the Yunmen line. Raised on Confucian studies, he left home at twenty-nine under Faxiu at Changlu si in Zhenzhou and took dharma transmission from Guangzhao Yingfu, succeeding him at Changlu. He held Chan practice and Pure Land aspiration together: in 1089 he founded the 蓮華勝會 lotus assembly on the model of Lushan's White Lotus society, urging universal buddha-name recitation. In 1103, as abbot of Hongji chan cloister in Zhending, he compiled the 禪苑清規 in ten juan — the earliest extant Chan monastic code and the foundation of all later ones. He also wrote the 坐禪箴, the 葦江集 and a 勸孝文 in 120 sections.

隨州大洪山報恩禪師 (1058–1111), lay name 劉欽憲, of Liyang in Wei; born into a family of established Confucian scholars. He passed the 方略 examination at the top of the list before he was capped, then wearied of official life and petitioned the throne to be released from office to become a monk. He went to Touzi Yiqing and grasped the essence of mind within a short time — Yiqing told him 「汝再來人也，宜自護持」(you are one who has come again; guard this well). Chancellor Han Zhen invited him to open the dharma. A Caodong master and dharma-brother of Furong Daokai. He debated the essentials of the three teachings with the chancellor Zhang Shangying (無盡居士), arguing that neither the Indian heterodox schools nor Confucianism and Daoism escape the four views.

潭州道吾悟真禪師 (also 道吾法真), a Song Linji master of unrecorded origin, 12th generation below Huineng. Dharma heir of Shishuang Chuyuan (Ciming), listed among his fifty heirs alongside Huanglong Huinan and Yangqi Fanghui — the founders of the two great Linji branches. He taught at Xinghua si on Mount Daowu in Tanzhou and left a one-juan 潭州道吾真禪師語要. Recorded exchanges: asked 「如何是常照？」he said 「針鋒上須彌」; 「如何是寂照？」— 「眉毛裏海水」; 「如何是本來照？」— 「草鞋裏𨁝跳」.

東京法雲佛國禪師惟白, lay surname 冉; 12th generation below Qingyuan and 6th of the Yunmen line, dharma heir of Yuantong Faxiu (1027–1090). He first headed Tiantong, was then commanded by the throne to Fayun si in the Eastern Capital, and in old age returned to Tiantong in Mingzhou. He compiled the 建中靖國續燈錄 in thirty juan — one of the 'five lamps' — for which Emperor Huizong wrote the preface, gathering the sayings of more than 1,700 teachers of the eighty years after the 廣燈錄 under five rubrics. He also produced the 大藏經綱目指要錄 (a guide to the whole canon) and the 華嚴善知識頌.

臨安府鹽官廣福院惟尚禪師 (1074–1140/41), lay surname 曹; 14th generation below Huineng in the Yunmen line, dharma heir of Puzhao Ziying (d. 1117). He awakened after failing to answer his master's probing on Nanquan's cat: sent back to the monks' hall, he suddenly understood and said 「古人道，從今日去更不疑天下老和尚舌頭，信有之矣」, presenting a verse beginning 「須是南泉第一機」; when his master raised a fist and asked what he would do just then, he overturned the meditation seat. He held Shousheng and Jianfu in turn. After his death Zhang Zishao composed his stupa inscription.

台州洪福子文禪師, a Southern Song Linji master of the Yangqi branch, 15th generation below Nanyue and a dharma heir of Yuanwu Keqin — listed among his heirs alongside Dahui Zonggao and Huqiu Shaolong. His recorded 上堂 turns on the wild-fox kōan: 「不昧不落作麼會？會得依前墮野狐。一夜涼風生畫角，滿船明月泛江湖。」

溫州淨光為覺禪師, a Song Yunmen-line master and the sole recorded dharma heir of Lingfeng Wenji of Yandang shan. Asked 「雲門一曲師親唱，未審西來意若何？」he replied 「道什麼」, and when the monk pressed 「恁麼則便是和尚為人處也」he said simply 「錯」. His 上堂 praises his cloister — 「淨光紺宇，古佛祇園…面臨郛郭，背靠林泉」— and closes with 「鴛鴦繡了從君看，莫把金針度與人」(the mandarin ducks are embroidered for you to see, but the golden needle is not passed on).

東京淨因枯木法成禪師 (1071–1128), lay surname 潘, a native of Heshuo. Caodong master of the 12th generation below Qingyuan, dharma heir of Furong Daokai. He first headed the Jingyin cloister in the Eastern Capital, then Jinshan and Xiangshan in Ruzhou, and ended his days at Jiaoshan. He was devoted all his life to seated 'dead-tree' meditation, whence the sobriquet 枯木 ('withered tree'). His 上堂 declares that only one who knows the matter above buddhas and patriarchs has any right to speak, describing such a one as 「六根不具，七識不全，是大闡提，無佛種性，逢佛殺佛、逢祖殺祖，天堂收不得、地獄攝無門」. Gao'an later criticised the luxury of his establishment at Jinshan.

東京淨因蹣菴繼成禪師, of Yichun in Yuanzhou, lay surname 劉; 14th generation below Nanyue and dharma heir of Zhihai Daoping. Raising his staff he would ask the Śūraṅgama's question — 「清淨本然，云何忽生山河大地？」— then answer by throwing the staff down and calling to the assembly: 「虛空翻筋斗，向新羅國裏去也」, warning them not to take leaves for gold to stop a child's crying, nor notch the boat to find the sword. Another 上堂: 「茫茫盡是覓佛漢，舉世難尋閑道人。棒喝交馳成藥忌，了忘藥忌未天真。」

開封淨因佛日惟嶽禪師, of Changxi in Fuzhou, lay surname 陳. Ordained at seven at Xilin, he studied under Yuanzhao Zongben and had an insight while standing in attendance as the story of the kalpa-ending fire was raised. A Yunmen-line master, he emerged as abbot of Chengtian in Changzhou, moved to Huayan in the Eastern Capital, and then to Jingyin. On the day he opened the hall, Emperor Zhezong sent a palace envoy to offer incense; he took the seat and said that this dharma gate lies neither in trap nor snare and has nothing to do with question and answer — 「直饒盡十方剎土抹為微塵，一一微塵盡為衲僧…到者裏一點用不著」. His heir Tichun of Gushan carried the line on.

台州（天台）般若寺敬遵通慧禪師, a Five Dynasties master and a direct dharma heir of Fayan Wenyi (885–958) — a first-generation master of the Fayan school. He lived at Huguo si and founded the Boruo (Prajñā) monastery on Xi'ao shan in Taizhou. Summoned to court he declined to attend, and refused the gold chain the palace bestowed; his end is not recorded. His 上堂: 「皎皎烜赫地，亘古亘今，也未曾有纖毫間斷相…所以道，山河大地是上座善知識」. Asked 「優曇花拆人皆覩，般若家風賜一言」he answered 「不因上座問，何曾舉似人？」

雲林諦暉慧輅禪師 (1627–1725), lay surname 沈; also written 諦輝輅. Orphaned at six and with his household ruined by conscription, he left lay life after his mother died and travelled widely before taking transmission from Jude Hongli at Lingyin. He presided at Lingyin and at Jinsu in Yanguan. While at Lingyin he called to a monk doing walking meditation and said 「一動不如一靜」; then, seeing a monk sitting in meditation, called him over and said 「一靜不如一動」— when his attendant asked about forgetting both motion and stillness, he simply lowered his head and returned to the abbot's room. He died in 1725 aged ninety-nine, with seventy-four years in robes.

names: 潤州金山曇頴達觀禪師
masters.notes: 潤州金山曇穎達觀禪師 (989–1060), lay surname 丘 of Qiantang. He first called on Dayang Jingxuan (元), asking what matter Dongshan's 偏正君臣 was meant to clarify — 「父母未生時事」came the answer; asked how to realise it, 「夜半正明，天曉不露」. Baffled, he went to Guyin Yuncong, who said Dayang was not wrong, only tight-lipped, and answered the same questions with 「糞墼子」and 「牡丹花下睡猫兒」, leaving him more astonished still — and it was from Yuncong that he finally took transmission. A Linji master, abbot of Jinshan in Runzhou, with a wide circle of monastic and lay heirs. Asked about the vajra eye he paused and said simply 「瞎」(blind).

嘉定府九頂寂惺惠泉禪師 (1079–1145), lay surname 張 of Chengdu. Linji master of the Huanglong branch, dharma heir of Sixin Wuxin. Asked how to understand 「心迷法華轉，心悟轉法華」he answered 「風暖鳥聲碎，日高花影重」. He is best known for setting his own three phrases against Yunmen's: where Yunmen had 「函蓋乾坤、截斷眾流、隨波逐浪」, Jiuding offered 「飢來喫飯句、寒即向火句、困來打睡句」— adding that measured by the buddhadharma Jiuding stands downwind of Yunmen, but measured by worldly truth Yunmen stands downwind of Jiuding.

Northern Song Linji master of the Huanglong branch, a native of Zizhou in western Shu and dharma heir of Letan (Baofeng) Zhenjing Kewen. Abbot at Jiufeng in Junzhou; the monastic community nicknamed him 'Guang the No-Mind' (廣無心) for his kindness and his refusal to fuss over petty rules.

masters.teacher: 雪竇大歇仲謙 (Xuedou Daxie Zhongqian)
masters.notes: Southern Song Linji (Yangqi branch) master, dharma heir of Xuedou Daxie Zhongqian (1174-1244). He first admired Wuzhun Shifan's teaching, then went to Zhongqian; late one night he raised his head, saw a glass lamp, and awakened. He taught successively at Yongqing, Lianyun and Heshan in Jizhou before becoming abbot of Chengtian at Suzhou (Pingjiang). 21st generation from Huineng.
Northern Song Fayan-school master at Gongchen monastery in Hangzhou, dharma heir of Guizong Yirou on Mt. Lu. Four dharma heirs of his own are recorded.
Northern Song Yunmen-school master, abbot of Kaisheng cloister in Hezhou; dharma heir of Tianyi Yihuai.

Song Linji (Huanglong branch) master titled Guangjian, dharma heir of Donglin Zhaojue Changzong. Ordained at Puti monastery in his home prefecture; he first glimpsed the essential meaning under Qingxian, then settled all his doubts with Changzong, and went on to head Kaixian monastery on Mt. Lu. He was a close friend of the poet Huang Tingjian (Huang Luzhi). Two dharma heirs are recorded — and the corpus independently confirms both.
Northern Song Yunmen-school master styled Xinyin ('Mind-Seal'), dharma heir of Fayun Faxiu. Abbot of Kaixian monastery on Mt. Lu in Nankang; his heir Kaixian Zong carried the line on.
Northern Song Yunmen-school master at Kaiyuan monastery in Jianning (Jianzhou), Fujian; dharma heir of Yunju Xiaoshun.

Yuan-dynasty Caodong master at Kongxiang monastery on Mt. Xiong'er in Henan — the site traditionally held to be Bodhidharma's stupa. Dharma heir of Huanyuan Fuyu, with nine recorded heirs of his own spread across northern China, from the capital Dadu to Shaanxi and Liaozhou.

Northern Song Linji master of the Huanglong branch (1012-1070), dharma heir of Huanglong Huinan and abbot at Letan in Longxing, Jiangxi. Known also as 'Ying of Shaowu' after his home prefecture; seven dharma heirs are recorded.

Late Ming / early Qing Linji master, styled Huifu, dharma heir of Tianyin Yuanxiu of Mt. Qing. He taught at Zhulin in Zhenjiang and at Jiashan in Jingkou (d. 1646/47), in the same generation cohort as Miyun Yuanwu's heirs.

Five Dynasties Fayan-school master, titled Liaowu, a native of Fuqing county in Fuzhou and a direct dharma heir of the school's founder Fayan Wenyi. Abbot of Lingyin monastery at Hangzhou, with eleven recorded dharma heirs.

Southern Song Linji (Yangqi branch) master, dharma name Dening and style Tuigeng ('Retired to Ploughing'); dharma heir of Wuzhun Shifan of Mt. Jing and abbot of Lingyin monastery at Hangzhou. He has a 法嗣 heading of his own in the Xu chuandeng lu, so his line continued.

Tang-dynasty Guiyang-school master at Lingyun in Fuzhou, famous throughout Chan for awakening at the sight of peach blossoms in bloom after thirty years of searching — the episode known as 'Lingyun sees the peach blossoms and clarifies the mind'. Guishan Lingyou (771-853) read his verse, probed his understanding, and sealed it.

Northern Song Yunmen-school master (12th generation from Qingyuan), dharma heir of Yuquan Chenghao of Jingmen. He taught at Xingjiao monastery at Linxi in Yingzhou, then moved to Qixian, where he presided for twenty years until his death.

Northern Song Linji master at Longtan in Tangzhou, dharma heir of Fenyang Shanzhao (11th generation under Nanyue). The lamp record preserves his staff exchange with Fenyang, who said of him: 'hereafter he will not yield to Linji' — to which he answered, 'the true command has already been carried out'.

Northern Song Linji master styled Wuxiang ('No-Marks') at Lushan in Mingzhou; dharma heir of Guangxiao Huilan, the eccentric known as the 'Daoist of Biluo' who wrote the names of the seven buddhas on his loincloth and was nicknamed 'Lan of the Cloth Trousers'.
Tang-dynasty Guiyang-school master at Luyuan in Tanzhou, dharma heir of Zifu Rubao of Jizhou; recorded alongside his dharma brothers Zifu Zhensui and Fushou (南嶽下七世).

Northern Song Yunmen-school NUN and Chan teacher, abbess of Miaozhan monastery at Pingjiang (Suzhou), and the sole recorded dharma heir of Ganlu Zhongxuan (himself an heir of Huilin Zongben). A biography of her survives in the collected lives of nuns, and DILA records her explicitly as Zhongxuan's female disciple.
Northern Song Fayan-school master at Xingjiao cloister on Nanshan in Hangzhou; dharma heir of Qixian Chengshi of Mt. Lu.

Tang-dynasty eccentric master, dharma heir of Panshan Baoji and third generation under Nanyue. A monk of Zhending prefecture, he hid himself in Zhenzhou and played the madman — feigning wildness, speaking without restraint, forever carrying a small bell and ringing it in people's ears. In 860, knowing his time had come, he shouldered his own coffin out the north gate and, still ringing the bell, climbed in and died. He runs through the Record of Linji as Linji Yixuan's foil and companion, and the Japanese Fuke (komusō) tradition later claimed him as its founder.

Southern Song Linji master of the Huanglong branch, abbot of Puxian monastery in Fuzhou; dharma heir of Shangfeng Bencai (titled Foxin), who descended from the Huanglong line through Lingyuan Weiqing. 16th generation from Huineng.

Five Dynasties Yunmen-school master at Fengguo in Xiangzhou, a direct dharma heir of the school's founder Yunmen Wenyan. The lamp record preserves his reply to the question 'the green bamboo is entirely suchness — what is suchness?'

Tang-dynasty Caodong master (d. 904), a native of Yuhang surnamed Chen, and a direct dharma heir of the school's co-founder Dongshan Liangjie. Caught at Nanzheng in the Huang Chao rebellion, he was picked out by a court official who looked at him a long while and said 'this is a Dharma King, not merely a dragon or elephant.' He taught from Handong to Qinglin; after his death in 904 his followers collected three hundred of his sayings as the Xuanji shihui ji. Five dharma heirs are recorded.

Song Linji master of the Huanglong branch at Qingyuan in Jizhou, dharma heir of Huitang Zuxin. Author of the single most quoted passage in all of Chan — that before he practised, mountains were mountains; when he entered, mountains were not mountains; and now, at rest, mountains are simply mountains again. Four dharma heirs are recorded.

Song master at Shanzheng Chan cloister on Mt. Quyuan in Quzhou; dharma heir of Shimen Ya of the same prefecture, who descended from Jiangshan Zanyuan. His sermon survives: 'You must look for it yourself and not seek it from another. As it is said — climbing the mountain, each must make his own effort; drinking the water, one knows for oneself cold from warm.' 14th generation under Nanyue.

Master of Renwang cloister in Hangzhou, dharma heir of Longhua Yanqiu (d. c.960-963), who had received Changqing Huileng's mind-seal in Fujian. The lamp record preserves his answer to 'the road upward that the thousand sages do not transmit': 'Ask about the upward — bring it here.'

Five Dynasties / early Song Fayan-school master (942-1008/09), surnamed Zheng. He studied Confucian texts first, left home at twenty-five at Jiqing cloister in Wenzhou, and took full ordination at Guoqing monastery on Mt. Tiantai. After attending National Teacher Tiantai Deshao (891-972) for ten years he became abbot of Ruilu monastery in Wenzhou. His Zhulin ji in ten fascicles survives. A dharma brother of Yongming Yanshou.

Northern Song Linji master at Chengtian cloister in Bingzhou (Taiyuan), also known as Tangming; dharma heir of Shoushan Xingnian and thus a dharma brother of Fenyang Shanzhao. His heir Fushan Fayuan became one of the notable teachers of the next generation.

Northern Song Linji master of the Huanglong branch; a native of Jiulong in Pengzhou, surnamed Li. He left the pass while still young, found his entry as soon as he reached Huanglong under Huitang Zuxin, and in time exhausted all his doubts. He returned to head Sansheng monastery in Hanzhou, later moving to Yunju. Known for the sermon 'the wooden buddha does not cross fire'.

A Chan master at Jingmen, recorded in the 續傳燈錄 as a direct dharma heir of Fayan Wenyi, founder of the Fayan school. His surviving record consists of short question-and-answer exchanges; asked who wins when two dragons fight over a pearl, he answered 'I win.'

Chan master of Shanquan in Changzhou, a dharma heir of Yunju Yuan in the Yunmen line. His recorded sermon distinguishes superior students who leap through at a word from middling and lesser ones who must clarify the mind-ground by degrees.

names: 隆興府泐潭山堂德淳禪師
masters.notes: Chan master of the Letan monastery in Longxing (Jiangxi), a dharma heir of Dawei Guo in the Linji line, 南嶽下十六世. Known from a sermon capping Juzhi's one-finger Chan: 'One finger of Juzhi — one hair hauls nine oxen.'

Chan master of Shengguang in Taizhou, a dharma heir of Zihu Lizong (himself an heir of Nanquan Puyuan), 南嶽下四世. Asked his house style he replied 'Fuzhou lychees, Quanzhou coral-trees.' He also appears as the interlocutor who tested 西川定慧禪師 with a whisk at the monks' hall.

Chan master of Shengyin in Huai'an, a dharma heir of Fayun Bai in the Yunmen line, 南嶽下十三世. Asked how his own seeing-of-nature compared with a bodhisattva's daylight and a sravaka's moonlight, he answered 'struck out with one stroke of the brush.'

Chan master of the Shengyin cloister at Linping, Hangzhou, a dharma heir of Yuwang Huailian in the Yunmen line, 南嶽下十一世. His sermon likens the matter to sun and moon hanging in the sky: it shines everywhere, but the blind do not see it and those under a basin do not know it.

A hunter from Fuzhou (Jiangxi) who became one of Mazu Daoyi's dharma heirs, 南嶽下二世. Chasing a deer past Mazu's hut he was asked how many he could shoot with one arrow; when Mazu said he shot a whole herd with one arrow and then asked why he did not shoot himself, Huizang threw down his bow and ordained. He later settled on Shigong mountain and habitually met students by drawing his bow at them.

Chan master of Shimen in Xiangzhou, also known as 谷隱蘊聰 (Guyin Yuncong), with the honorific 慈照. A dharma heir of Shoushan Shengnian in the Linji line, 南嶽下第十世. His teaching turns on refusing both horns: 'Contrive a thought and you miss; stir a thought and you go askew — but neither contriving nor stirring is making a living in stagnant water.'

names: 嘉興府石門真覺元翁信禪師
masters.notes: Chan master of Shimen in Jiaxing, honorific 真覺, dharma heir of Kongyan You of Zhongzhu (Hangzhou) in the Linji line, 大鑑下第二十一世. His small-convocation teaching presses past every stock gesture: the ten directions are a seamless iron wall Bodhidharma never knew, a holeless iron mallet Kasyapa never grasped.

Chan master of Shishuang in Changsha, a dharma heir of Huanglong Huinan, 臨濟宗 黃龍派, 南嶽下十二世. On pilgrimage with 夾山齡 he studied under 佛日; when the two heard Huangbo's small convocation and missed its point, his companion beat him and stormed off while he alone stayed on — and soon awakened to the Huanglong teaching, becoming famous enough to be ranked with 文關, 西英 and 邵武.

Chan master of the Stone Pagoda (Shita) monastery in Yangzhou, a dharma heir of Mingzhao Wenhui of Wuyi, Jinhua, in the Linji line, 南嶽下十五世. Asked whether mountains, rivers and the earth are the same as oneself or different, he answered: 'The cool moon over the long pavilion spreads itself out mostly for travellers.'

Senior monk (上座) in the Linji line, listed in 古尊宿語錄 among the dharma heirs of Xinghua Cunjiang. He is best remembered for a shouting duel at Huayan's assembly in Xiangzhou — shout answered by shout until he bowed, then cried 'Look at this blind fellow's rout!' and clapped his way back into the ranks. Fengxue Yanzhao, then serving as rector, defended him to the furious Huayan as 'a descendant in Linji's house — this is simply his portion.'

Chan master of Shuangling in Longxing (Jiangxi), a dharma heir of Huanglong Zuxin, 臨濟宗 黃龍派, 南嶽下十三世. His sermon: 'Green bamboo and yellow blossoms are no outer realm; white cloud and bright moon reveal the whole real. Every single thing is a possession of my house — yet pick one up offhand and it still is not dust.'

names: 臨安府淨慈水庵師一禪師
masters.notes: Shui'an Shiyi (1107–1176), a native of Wuzhou surnamed Ma, ordained at sixteen. He first studied under Duanyu at Xuefeng, who probed him with the 'hiding the body leaving no trace' story; after several days he presented a verse ('The old mirror needs no polishing to shine of itself') and, pressed further, answered 'The stone tiger has swallowed the wooden lamb' — which Duanyu firmly approved. He later became abbot of Jingci in Lin'an and had four dharma heirs.

Chan master of Shuilao in Hongzhou, a dharma heir of Mazu Daoyi, 南嶽下二世. He asked Mazu the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West and Mazu kicked him square in the chest, knocking him flat; he got up clapping and laughing — 'How extraordinary! A hundred thousand dharma gates and measureless subtle meanings, all recognised at their source on the tip of a single hair!' — and bowed.

Benjing of Sikong shan, a native of Jiangzhou surnamed Zhang, who took the robe as a boy in Caoxi's room and received the seal from the Sixth Patriarch Huineng, then settled at Wuxiang monastery on Sikong shan. In 744 (Tianbao 3) Emperor Xuanzong's envoy Yang Guangting, sent into the mountains to gather ivy, came to his cell and begged instruction; Benjing deflected him ('the great scholars of the Chan school are all gathered in the capital — ask them; I lean on the mountain and lie by the water with nothing to occupy my mind'), and Guangting wept and bowed.

Fayan of Sizu shan in Qizhou, a native of Guizhou and a dharma heir of Huanglong Huinan, 臨濟宗 黃龍派, 南嶽下十二世. Asked what the attributes of mind are he said 'mountains, rivers, the great earth'; asked then what the substance of mind is, he turned it back: 'What do you call mountains and rivers?'

names: 杭州府中天竺懶堂中仁禪師
masters.notes: Lantang Zhongren, a native of Luoyang who left home young at the Fengxian cloister in the Eastern Capital and was tonsured by imperial certificate in the early Xuanhe era. He mastered the sutras and sastras at the translation bureau but had no faith in the Chan school until he called on Yuanwu Keqin at Tianning: Yuanwu demanded 'Explain by the sutras and you slander the buddhas of the three times; depart one word from them and it is demon talk — speak, quick!' — and struck him across the mouth as he hesitated, knocking out a tooth, at which he greatly awakened. He later opened the hall at Dajue and moved to Zhongtianzhu and Lingfeng.

names: 北京天鉢寺重元文慧禪師
masters.notes: Chan master of the Tianbo monastery at the Northern Capital, a dharma heir of Tianyi Yihuai in the Yunmen line, 南嶽下十一世. His sermons are blunt about the cost of monastic upkeep: 'In winter you take no cold, in summer no heat; the clothes on your back and food in your mouth come right on time — and none of it is spontaneous or natural, it is every bit the blood and fat of other people.'

names: 江寧府保寧仲方天倫禪師
masters.notes: Zhongfang Tianlun, Chan master of Baoning in Jiangning, a dharma heir of Huiji Yuanxi of Jingshan in the Linji line, 大鑑下第二十一世 (Yuan dynasty). He moved to Foyan in Mingzhou; when Xiaoyin Daxin was residing at Longxiang he invited Tianlun to share the seat and preach, and the censor Tulu then recommended him as abbot of Baoning.

Chan master of Tianzhang in Yuezhou, a dharma heir of Tianyi Yihuai in the Yunmen line. His sermon on holding fast and letting go: 'Hold fast, and a dripping drop freezes, rivers stop running; let go, and the sun warms, the wind softens, mountains and streams vie in beauty.'

names: 衡州靈雲銕牛持定禪師
masters.notes: Tieniu Chiding, Chan master of Lingyun in Hengzhou, a dharma heir of Xueyan Zuqin, 臨濟宗 南嶽下二十一世. He went seven days without closing his eyes until at midnight the whole world seemed snow and his single body could not be contained by heaven and earth; hearing the sounding-board struck he broke open, drenched in sweat, and his illness lifted at the same moment. When Zuqin later raised 'the dead monk is burnt — where does he go?' and answered himself, Chiding's doubt scattered and he came forward laughing that the stone lions before the hall were dancing.

Chan master of Wangxian shan in Yizhou, a dharma heir of Tianyi Yihuai in the Yunmen line, 南嶽下十一世. Asked for the ordinary one-phrase matter he answered 'Heshan beats the drum'; pressed whether that was where a student should apply effort, 'Guizong drags the stone.' His sermon is a list of drugs — 'Nantai lindera, Beihai gastrodia, Silla aconite, Chenjin cinnabar.'

names: 杭州雄聖尼惟極致禪師
masters.notes: A NUN (尼) — Weiji Zhi of Xiongsheng in Hangzhou, daughter of a notable Yaojiang family who entered the way as a virgin child. She regularly accompanied her father to see the old man Yuanwu at Tiantong, and later studied with Tongyun at Xuedou, who tested her on Shun's 'ancient mirror' story. Asked about the mirror before polishing she said 'Look at your feet'; after polishing, 'Two eyes facing two eyes.' Struck by Tongyun, she answered 'The sweet melon is sweet through to the stem, the bitter gourd bitter down to the root,' then shouted and offered a verse: 'Without bones of frost and ice, who could study the Xuedou Chan?'

Weizheng of Zhongnan shan, a native of Pingyuan surnamed Zhou. He trained under the dharma master Quancheng at Yanhe monastery in his home prefecture and received the dharma from Puji of Songshan, then entered Taiyi shan, where his hall filled with students. He is remembered for the clam episode: Emperor Wenzong of Tang was fond of clams, and when one in the imperial kitchen would not open, the emperor burned incense and prayed over it — it opened to reveal the form of a bodhisattva, which he enshrined in a sandalwood box and gave to Xingshan monastery, then questioned his ministers about it.

Chan master of the Yuanfeng cloister in Weizhou, a dharma heir of Tianbo Chongyuan Wenhui in the Yunmen line, 南嶽下十二世. Asked what the Way is he said 'I won't say' — 'Why not?' — 'Saying is an idle name.' His sermons are playful: the wooden uncle in the hall gets slapped once by the holy monk and twice by the rector while the bare pillar laughs out loud.

Zhengdao of Wenshu in Changde, a native of Danleng in Meizhou surnamed Xu, ordained at thirty. He studied Yogacara at Chengdu and thought he had mastered it, until a fellow resident floored him: 'The three realms are mind only, the ten thousand dharmas consciousness only — but with the myriad forms clattering right in front of you, where are mind and consciousness?' He could not answer, left the pass, wandered the Jiang-Huai region, and on reaching Taiping in Shuzhou heard Fojian's night convocation and became his heir.

Chan master of Wenzhou, a dharma heir of Mazu Daoyi, 南嶽下二世. Whenever anyone approached he would plant his staff on the ground and say 'The buddhas before were just so; the buddhas after are just so.' Asked what the 'different species' is, he tapped his bowl and called 'Huanu! Huanu! Come and eat!'

Wufeng Ruxue, Chan master of Dawei, a dharma heir of Miyun Yuanwu of Tiantong and, by his own stupa inscription, the 35th generation in the direct Linji succession traced back through Nanyue. His recorded sayings survive as J25nB175 大溈五峰學禪師語錄. Recalling his career he dismissed it: 'braving cold and heat for twenty-six years, covering tens of thousands of li — all upside-down dreams and illusion, mind and strength wasted in vain; what is any of it worth mentioning?' He had earlier gone into sealed retreat at Hongji monastery in Nanjing.

Chan master of Wufeng in Yuezhou, a dharma heir of Fayun Shanben in the Yunmen line, 南嶽下十三世. Asked for instruction he said 'A thousand blossoms open in beauty'; told the student still did not understand, 'After rain, ten thousand mountains are green.'

names: 安吉州烏回唯菴良範禪師
masters.notes: Wei'an Liangfan, Chan master of Wuhui in Anjizhou, a dharma heir of Changling Shouzhuo in the Linji line, recorded in the 續傳燈錄. His sermon on the matter before the dust-kalpas: 'Upright, with no front or back; motion and stillness cannot cover it; it rolls out and up quick as lightning.' On Zhaozhou's 'the Way is not difficult, it only dislikes picking and choosing' he said Zhaozhou had an eye on the crown of his head, sorting black from white in a spark from struck stone, seizing and releasing in a lightning flash.

names: 杭州靈隱無文本褧禪師
masters.notes: Wuwen Benjiong, a native of Dinghai in Siming surnamed Xie. He left home at fourteen at Wutai monastery in his prefecture, took full ordination and studied the Vinaya strictly, then heard that Gufeng Dewang was teaching at Baoning and went to knock. Dewang asked him to recite his matching verses on Liangshan's Ten Oxherding Songs and, as he opened his mouth, clapped a hand over it: 'Where is the ox?' — 'I have already trampled your crops,' he said; told 'not yet, say more,' he covered his ears and walked out, and Dewang marked him. He later became abbot of Lingyin in Hangzhou.

Song-dynasty Chan master who taught at Boshan in Xinzhou (信州博山). The Wudeng quanshu lists him among the dharma heirs of Huanglong (Lingyuan) Weiqing, placing him in the Huanglong branch of the Linji school alongside Changling Shouzhuo. Known from a New Year's Day sermon on the verse 'the wooden man divines an auspicious omen; at midnight the tortoise-trigram is revealed'.

Song Chan master (1137-1207), styled Wuyong, a native of Zhuji in Yuezhou, surname Weng. He left home under Shenbian of Mt. Dabei, then received full ordination and the dharma from Dahui Zonggao. He opened the dharma at Langshan in 1189 and later headed Chengtian in Suzhou, Guangjiao in Xuancheng, Baoning in Jianye, and finally Tiantong in Siming. While at Lingyin, Emperor Xiaozong summoned him to discuss the Way and lodged him in the Inner Contemplation Hall.

Southern Song Chan master of Tiantong in Qingyuanfu, a native of Yiwu, surname Zhao. He first studied with Ying'an at Tiantong and Wu'an at Daochang, then awakened in the room of Shui'an Shiyi at Jingci and became his heir. He was head seat at Longxiang's Baitang, opened the dharma at Lingyan in Yanzhou, headed four monasteries, and was appointed by imperial order to Lingyin.

Northern Song Chan master of Xiangshan in Mingzhou. The Xu chuandeng lu places him among the dharma heirs of Shishuang Chuyuan (Ciming) in the eleventh generation below Nanyue, a peer of Cuiyan Kezhen. Known for terse answers on the 'phrase that penetrates the dharma-body' and a sermon opening with a long silence followed by sudden laughter.

Tenth-century Chan monk, abbot (上座 / 和尚) of Xingjiao in Yunzhou. He is known almost entirely from a single celebrated encounter: he challenged Tiantai Deshao with a question about Kasyapa's robe and Maitreya's thousand-foot body, stormed out at Deshao's answer, then vomited blood for seven days; urged by Fuguang, he repented before Deshao and vowed lifelong service. He also appears delivering a letter in a 勘辯 exchange preserved in the Xu gu zunsu yuyao.

Southern Song Chan master, abbot of Qingzhen cloister in Jiankang (from 1211) and later of Lingyin cloister in Qingyuanfu. His recorded sayings were compiled by his attendants Juexin and Zhiqing; the preface is dated 1243 and Wuzhun Shifan supplied a colophon. He calls Dahui Zonggao his 師祖 (teacher's teacher), which fixes him two generations below Dahui, and he composed a lament for Dun'an (遯庵宗演), a direct Dahui heir.

Tang-dynasty Chan master of Xiuxi in Tanzhou (Hunan), counted among the dharma heirs of Mazu Daoyi. He is known chiefly from his exchange with Gushan on 'sound and form are purely real — what is the Way?', in which Gushan paced east and west, seized him as he stepped down from the meditation seat, and received a slap; Gushan then laughed aloud.

Qing Chan master of Xiufeng in Suzhou (1610-1676), a native of Changzhou, surname Gu, ordination name Faheng. He was tonsured at fourteen at the Xiyin quarters of Huqiu; at twenty-five he accompanied Gunan Tongmen to see Miyun Yuanwu at Tiantong, where he washed dishes and endured repeated blows. Gunan's taunt 'you've washed bowls a long while — have you touched the bottom of one?' threw him into great doubt, and he broke through one night while rolling up a blind; Miyun smiled his assent. When Gunan opened the dharma at Gunan he made him head seat. He died in 1676 aged 67.

Northern Song Chan master of Xuedou in Mingzhou, titled Jueyin, a native of the same commandery, surname Chen. A dharma heir of Changlu Yingfu in the Yunmen school and a fellow heir of Changlu Zongze. His own heir Xuefeng Dazhi headed Xuefeng in Fuzhou. Known for 'when Hanshan met Shide, what then?' — 'raised brows flash lightning'.

Northern Song Chan master of Yaoshan in Lizhou, listed in the Jianzhong Jingguo xudeng lu (1101) as a dharma heir of Juxin of Qianming in Dongchuan. Known from brief exchanges: the Buddha before appearing in the world is 'a big tree wrapped in big bark', after appearing 'a small tree bound in small bark'; the Immovable One is 'what the Four Kings cannot lift'.

Tang-dynasty recluse Chan master of Longshan in Tanzhou, counted among Mazu Daoyi's dharma heirs. He is famous for the encounter in which Dongshan Liangjie and Shenshan, following stray cabbage leaves down a mountain stream, found him living hidden; asked how long he had been there he said 'spring and autumn do not reach me', and what he had realised: 'I saw two clay oxen fight their way into the sea, and to this day there has been no news of them.' He answered Dongshan on guest and host ('green mountains covered by white clouds'), then burned his hut and vanished deeper into the mountains — whence later generations called him the Hidden Mountain monk.

Song Chan master of Yuelin in Mingzhou, a dharma heir of Zhen of Ayuwang. Known from a sermon that turns the old saying 'at the turn of autumn, when the summer retreat ends, thirty blows are due' onto the World-Honoured One holding up the flower and Kasyapa's smile: 'just then, thirty blows would have been in order — why? In a time of peace, to raise weapons.'

Song Chan master of Yungai in Tanzhou, a native of Jianzhou, surname Chen. Humbled by Fachang Yu ('in Wu there is a stone buddha many have never managed to see'), he then studied long with Cuiyan Kezhen without insight, and finally resolved all his doubts under Huanglong Huinan at Jicui, becoming his heir. He was head seat at Shishuang, opened the dharma at Daowu, and later moved to Yungai. Doushuai Congyue and Jiufeng Xiguang both sought him out — he sent Congyue off to 'go study in that piss-stink' of Dongshan Wen.

Song Chan master of Ayuwang in Mingzhou, a dharma heir of Shan of Fuchang. Known from exchanges on 'the within-within' ('atop Golden River peak') and 'the without-without' ('before the Prajna hall'), and a sermon distinguishing the upward phrase, the downward phrase, and the phrase that touches neither road: 'know it, and the crown of your head vents breath; miss it, and a clay ox ploughs a stone field.'

Five Dynasties Chan master of Zifu in Shaozhou, a dharma heir of Yunmen Wenyan and thus a first-generation Yunmen master. He is remembered for refusing a monk's request for the mind-seal — 'I don't answer that question; it would not match what was said before' — and for his verse reply on Yunmen's 'guan-jian-yi': 'the phrase before the point transcends the Tamer; ask how, and you miss it for kalpas.'

Five Dynasties Chan master, titled Minghui, of Bao'en cloister in Quanzhou; he first headed Xingguo. The Jingde chuandeng lu names him first among the seven dharma heirs of Fayin of Zhaoqing in Quanzhou, in the Xuefeng line. Known for meeting the demand 'without entering deliberation, state the vehicle of the ancestors directly' with a long silence, and then answering the monk's complaint with 'already sticky'.

Chan master of Dasheng monastery, styled Bifeng, placed by the Xudeng zhengtong catalogue in the twenty-ninth generation below Dajian (Huineng) as a dharma heir of Ci of Jinling, alongside eight dharma-brothers including Baofeng Mingxuan and Xiaoshan Zhisheng.

Ming Chan master styled Dufeng, of Tianzhen. His Essential Sayings (Jiaxing canon B159) were compiled by his student Wushen. He taught an austere ascetic house-style, urging students to revive the dhuta practices of Shakyamuni and pre-Baizhang tradition and invoking Zhaozhou's thirty years of silence, Biandanshan's diet of acorns, Danxia's single cloth robe and Furong Kai's refusal of subscription books; his practice instruction combines huatou work with nianfo.

Northern Song Chan master, titled Foyin, of Zhihai monastery in the Eastern Capital (Kaifeng). A native of Tong'an in Quanzhou, surname Ye, he was a bright and widely-read Confucian student in youth; before he came of age he turned to the teaching of emptiness and left home under Huiru of Luyuan monastery. He travelled widely and clarified the mind-ground only in Yuanyou's assembly, becoming his heir. He first came forth at Wuzu, where his reputation grew, and was then summoned by edict to Zhihai; on his opening day Emperor Zhezong sent a palace envoy to offer incense.

Yuan-dynasty Chan master styled Gufeng, personal name Dewang, who taught at Baoning and at Jingci (the lamps head his heirs' section 淨慈德禪師法嗣). He tested the young Benjiong on his matching verses to the Liangshan Ten Oxen with 'where is the ox?', found him remarkable and made him his attendant; Benjiong later opened the dharma at Jueyan in Suzhou in 1366 offering incense as Gufeng's heir, and went on to head Lingyin.

Southern Song / Yuan Chan master styled Gufeng, resident in Fujian. The Xu chuandeng lu catalogue lists two dharma heirs under him, Wanshan Zhengning of Gushan and Yina Jie of Shuanglin. Wanshan came to him in Fujian after awakening under Wuming Xing at Shuangta; Gufeng put Zhaozhou's 'a dog has no buddha-nature' to him, which he could not answer for over half a year before penetrating it — and even then Gufeng said 'you have it, but you are not there yet.'

Song Chan master of Guifeng in Xinzhou, styled Hui'an, a native of Jianning; a dharma heir of Wuju Daoxing in the Yangqi branch of Linji. His sermons work a running joke on 'vexation': Bodhidharma was vexed nine years, Lotus Peak's hermit was too vexed to settle, Nanyue Si too vexed to come down the mountain, and Linji and Deshan wore out their own dregs. His heir Meng'an Yuancong, acclaimed his foremost student, went on to head Xuefeng and then Jingshan in 1197.

Song Chan master of Jianfu in Raozhou, a native of Jiangzhou, and a dharma heir of Dahui Zonggao. He followed Dahui from Yunmen in Jiangxi to Xiaoxi in southern Quanzhou; feeling passed over as others received Dahui's seal, he meant to leave, but Dahui told him 'just concentrate on your investigation — if you get something, I will know it before you open your mouth.' Goaded by Dahui's public jibe that 'Attendant Ben has practised for years and can only say I don't understand,' he threw himself into the 'no' of Zhaozhou's dog; one night near the third watch, dozing against a hall pillar, the word 'wu' fell from his lips and he suddenly awakened.

Five Dynasties Chan master of Jinfeng in Fuzhou (Jiangxi), titled Xuanming, a dharma heir of Caoshan Benji and thus a first-generation Caodong master. Known for flint answers: asked who the true host of Jinfeng is, 'the county seat is not far from here — don't be rash'; asked why he would not say, 'my mouth is like a plinth stone'; asked which of the thousand peaks is Jinfeng, he shaded his brow and peered.

Qing Chan master of Xingshan at Jiangshan (Zhongshan) in Jinling, styled Jie'an, personal name Chen; a native of Xiangtan, surname Li. Raised a Confucian, he was awakened to the illusoriness of worldly toil by the dynastic collapse of 1644-45, was tonsured by Buyun of Taohua shan, travelled to many teachers, and finally received transmission certification as an in-room true son of Hongjue (Muchen Daomin), after which he came forth at Xingshan in Jinling.

Northern Song Chan master of Jingtu at Miyan in Raozhou, a dharma heir of Huilin Yuanzhao Zongben in the Yunmen school. His one preserved address runs: 'The Way has no motion or stillness; dharmas follow conditions. Wherever you stand is real, and you are host wherever you turn — in heaven and earth it covers and bears, in sun and moon it shines, between ruler and minister it reforms customs, in the Buddhist house it sets compassion in motion. And on a patch-robed monk's part, what then?' After a pause: 'Words will not reach it — better discuss it under the trees.'

Northern Song Chan master of Qixian on Mt. Lu, a dharma heir of Tianyi Yihuai in the Yunmen school. Asked whether, beyond question-and-answer as mere gate-front teaching, there is anything further, he said 'there is' — 'clouds follow the dragon, wind follows the tiger'; when the monk pressed the image he cut him off: 'reciting other people's talk.'

Song Chan master of Liangshan in Dingzhou, in the Caodong line: a dharma heir of Liangshan Yan, himself an heir of Liangshan Yuanguan, placed at the tenth generation below Qingyuan. Asked 'when you brush away the dust and see the Buddha, what then?' he said 'don't let your eyes flower'; asked when he would become a buddha, 'don't press a free man into slavery.' His verse on Luzu facing the wall runs: 'Luzu's samadhi was the least effortful — the moment a monk came, he faced the wall. For one who knows mind and has reached the Way, it takes no raised eyebrow to be understood.'

Song Chan master of Falun on Mt. Nanyue, a dharma heir of Letan Hongying in the Huanglong branch of Linji. He is known for his 'four shouts' sermon: a shout — 'the lion roars'; a shout — 'the elephant king stretches'; a shout — 'a mad dog chases the clod'; a shout — 'the shrimp cannot leap out of the measure'; and then: 'of these four shouts, one is fit to be teacher to buddhas and ancestors — which?' To a student begging instruction he said 'did you hear the drum just now?' — 'I did.' — 'Then give me back my huatou.'

Five Dynasties Chan master of Piyun in Shaozhou, a dharma heir of Yunmen Wenyan and thus a first-generation Yunmen master. Asked 'what is the realm of Piyun?' he said 'in broad daylight there are no idlers here.' On Yunmen's riddle-graph — 'not quite the character yi, not quite the character ba' — he answered in verse: 'Not yi, not ba: the myriad forms are made clear right in this. Even if you cleverly expound a thousand marvels, it is neither a ditty nor a sutra.'

Song-dynasty Chan master of the Linji/Yangqi line, dharma-heir of Longmen Foyan Qingyuan. A native of Huzhou, surname Yu, he taught at the Daochang monastery in Anji (Huzhou) and was known by the style Zhengtang.
Northern Song Chan master of the Linji/Huanglong line who taught at Liangshan in Tanzhou (Hunan). Dharma-heir of Qingyuan Weixin, himself an heir of Huanglong Huitang Zuxin.

A Korean-born (高麗) monk of the Five Dynasties who travelled in Min and Yue and became a dharma-heir of Xuefeng Yicun. He taught at Longhua monastery in Hangzhou and was titled Zhenjue dashi (真覺大師); also known as Zhao buna (照布衲) and Qiyun heshang. Died 947, aged 78.

names: 杭州西興化度院師郁悟真
masters.notes: Five Dynasties Chan master from Quanzhou (Putian), dharma-heir of Xuefeng Yicun, from whom he received the mind-seal. His teaching flourished in the Hangzhou-Yue region and he settled at the Huadu cloister in Xixing. Titled Wuzhen.

Tang-dynasty master of the Northern School (北宗), dharma-heir of Yuquan Shenxiu. A native of Anlu, surname Cao; he first trained under Lang of Minfu cloister studying the Lotus and Vimalakirti sutras, then entered Shenxiu's room. Invited to Anguo cloister, he later moved to Wutai shan where he taught for over twenty years. Died 727, aged 81.

Southern Song Chan master known as Tudu (塗毒), dharma-heir of Yunyan Tianyou. A native of Tiantai, surname Chen, tonsured under Chuguang of Huguo monastery. He ended his career as abbot of Jingshan, where his disciples enshrined his whole body in a stupa on the eastern ridge. Died 1192, aged 76.

Twelfth-century Chan master of the Linji/Yangqi line, styled Kuoan, dharma-heir of Dasui (Nantang) Yuanjing. A native of Hechuan, surname Lu, he resided at Liangshan in Changde. He composed the celebrated Ten Ox-Herding Pictures with verses (十牛圖頌), the version that became standard in Chan and Zen. He had one dharma-heir, Xinxiang Yi of Chengdu.

Song Chan master of the Linji school, surname Fu, dharma-heir of Dawei Muzhe. After more than ten years living quietly in Linchuan he took up residence at Letan Baofeng in Longxing at the age of fifty-four, where students regularly numbered five thousand. He later headed Jiangshan in Jinling and Yuantong monastery in Jiujiang, returned to Letan, and died in 1132 at Hongfu monastery in Fujian, aged 71.

Five Dynasties master of the Lingshu cloister in Shaozhou, a native of Min (Minxian, Fujian). He first met Changqing Da'an and thereafter his teaching flourished south of the passes. The Liu rulers of Southern Han honoured him across generations, consulting him on unresolved matters; his answers proved so reliable that he was privately titled Zhisheng dashi (知聖大師).
Five Dynasties Chan master of Longji in Fuzhou (Jiangxi), dharma-heir of Luohan Guichen (Dizang). He trained under Guichen alongside Fayan Wenyi, with whom the lamp records pair him as a co-disciple.

Northern Song Chan master of Jinluan in Jingzhou, a native of Gutian in Fuzhou. He served as attendant to Ciming Chuyuan and became his dharma-heir - DILA records his alias simply as 'Attendant Shan' (善侍者). Later masters record calling on him for approval alongside Shexian Guixing of Yexian.

The 'Wine Immortal' (酒仙), a Northern Song eccentric master from Changzhou in Gusu (Suzhou), surname Lin, whose mother is said to have conceived him after dreaming she swallowed a great pearl. Dharma-heir of Longhua Yanqiu. Died 1009, aged 88.

Tang-dynasty master of Songshan, dharma-heir of the 'Stove-Breaker' monk (破竈墮), who was himself an heir of Songyue Hui'an. Known from a terse exchange on what makes a person who cultivates good: 'One who wears the cangue and drags chains.'

Late-Tang / Five Dynasties master in the Qingyuan Xingsi line, approved by Luoshan Daoxian. Surname, birthplace and dates are unknown. Renowned for vigorous and sharply inventive teaching that both elders and juniors held in awe. He served as head seat at Zhizhe monastery in Wuzhou and then lived on Mingzhao shan for over forty years. Blind in his left eye, he was known as the One-Eyed Dragon (獨眼龍).

Northern Song master of the Yunmen school at Qianming in Dongchuan, dharma-heir of Shuangquan Shikuan. Three dharma-heirs are recorded for him: Yaoshan Su of Lizhou, Xichan Chuibai, and Baotang Wuyue.

Ming-Qing Chan master of the Linji/Yangqi line, styled Yuanyun, also called Huishan and Bawong. A native of Taicang, Jiangsu, surname Wang. After the fall of the Ming he took tonsure and ordination at Huashan in Jinling under the elder Sanmei (三昧老人). He consulted Tiantong and Xuejiao, then awakened to the Yunmen staff koan under Jude Hongli at Lingyin, becoming his heir. He first withdrew to Lushan, then opened the teaching at Yunju for ten years, and later headed Jianfu, the Fourth Patriarch's monastery at Huangmei, Anguo, Hanxi, Huguo and Shushan. In 1667 he succeeded to Lingyin. Died 1672, aged 63. Author of the Chanmen duanlian shuo (禪門鍛鍊說), a celebrated manual on training a Chan assembly.

Northern Song master of the Yunmen school at Yunfeng in Tanzhou, titled Zudeng, a native of Nanyue, surname Chen. Dharma-heir of Fayun Ben. Remembered for the address beginning 'Let it rest, let it cease - ten thousand years in a single thought.'

Southern Song Chan master of the Linji/Yangqi line, styled Ye'an (野庵), resident at Shiting in Longxing prefecture. Dharma-heir of Dawei Shanguo. Remembered for his verse on Zhaozhou's 'wash your bowl' case: 'Have you finished your gruel yet? Zhaozhou had no taboos.'

Northern Song Chan master of the Linji/Huanglong line at Jiuxian in Longxing. A native of Langyuan in Shu (Sichuan), surname Chen, and a grandson of the Chancellor Chen Yaosou. Bright from childhood, he was ordained at twenty-four and studied in the lecture assemblies of Chengdu; the master Zhenjue Sheng, after debating with him, sent him travelling south. He left the gorges in the Yuanfeng era and toured the ancestral seats, finally entering Huanglong's room. Died 1120.

names: 襄州鹿門山第二世譚和尚志行大師
masters.notes: Tang-dynasty master, second-generation abbot of Lumen shan in Xiangzhou, titled Zhixing dashi and known as Reverend Tan (譚和尚). Dharma-heir of Lumen Chuzhen; DILA places him in the Caodong line.

Tang-dynasty master of the Hongzhou school, one of the fifty-six recorded dharma-heirs of Mazu Daoyi. He survives through a single exchange: asked 'What about when not a single thought arises?', he simply remained silent a long while, and the monk bowed.

Southern Song Chan master of the Linji/Yangqi line, surname Liu of Wuxing, eighteenth generation under Huineng. He left home at thirteen at Qizheng cloister in Deqing and grasped the sutras at a glance. Calling on Fozhao Deguang at Maoshan, he awakened on the wind-and-banner koan and was sealed with the verse 'Today I pass you a single thread; cutting nails and shearing iron, it raises up our school.' He later sat facing a wall for ten years below Miaogao peak on Lushan - whence the name Miaofeng - headed Huiyin and other monasteries, and finished at Lingyin in Hangzhou. The assembly affectionately called him 'Old Liu' (老劉). Died 1235, aged 84.

names: 明州天童佛朗湛然自性禪師
masters.notes: 自性 (secular surname Han, of Yunyang), Ming-dynasty Chan monk of the Linji Yangqi lineage. Tonsured under Huihai Zhi at Hongzhao Hermitage in Liyang; his awakening was catalyzed in dialogue with Jingchuan Caoan Yihuan, then sealed by Quanshi Zongle (Zongle, 1318-1390) at Tianjie Monastery in Nanjing, making him a dharma heir in the 天界泐 line. Emperor Taizu bestowed on him the honorific title 佛朗禪師 in Hongwu 15 (1382). He served successively as abbot of Puguang (his home temple), Changzhou Yongqing, Fuzhou Shushan (by provincial appointment), and finally — by imperial edict — Tiantong Jingde Monastery in Ningbo, hence his fullest style, 明州天童佛朗湛然自性禪師.

names: 湖州楊墳資福嵩庵正禪師
masters.notes: 湖州楊墳資福嵩庵正禪師, a native of Qianzhou surnamed Chen. Dharma-heir of 靈機行觀 (1616–1681), whom he succeeded ('繼席') as abbot of Zifu monastery at Yangfen, Huzhou. Fell mildly ill in the winter of a bingyin (丙寅) year; on the fifth day of the first month of the following year he bathed, changed robes, sat in meditation posture and died, aged 58, having been a monk 26 years; his stupa was built at Qianling.

names: 樂清雁山羅漢寺冶翁伯禪師
masters.notes: 樂清雁山羅漢寺冶翁伯禪師 (Chan Master Yeweng Bo of Luohan Monastery, Mt. Yandang, Yueqing). Late Ming/Qing Linji-school monk, dharma-heir of 古泉清 (Guquan Qing, abbot of 永嘉護國寺), who was in turn heir of 通奇/林野奇 (Tong Qi / Linye Qi, 1596-1652), a disciple of 密雲圓悟 (Miyun Yuanwu). Had at least one recorded dharma-heir of his own, 斯準衡 (per DILA).

The actual subject of the 道影讚 (portrait encomium) whose lay signatory 鄭溥元 was mistakenly recorded as the batch record (see Zheng Puyuan / 鄭溥元 above, _b:6). 即非如一, a Fujian (Fuqing) native, ordained under 西來灝 at Longshan, studied further under 石雨(明方) and 朝宗(通忍), took full ordination and dharma-transmission under 隱元隆琦 (Yinyuan Longqi) at Huangbo, and held the seat at 廣壽/雪峰崇聖. In 1657 he crossed to Nagasaki at Yinyuan's invitation and taught at 聖壽山/崇福寺, becoming a founding figure of Japan's Ōbaku lineage there. Author of 《即非禪師全錄》 20 fasc.

Chinese Chan master, dharma-heir of Shishuang Qingzhu (青原下第五世); governs his own 法嗣 heading over three named Silla-Korean disciples (瑞巖, 百巖/泊巖, 大嶺) -- a Chinese master with Korean heirs. Not to be confused with the bare toponym '谷山' that appears as a visiting interlocutor inside 潭州秀溪和尚's ~8th-century entry two generations earlier in the same fascicle (that citation is a separate, unresolved orphan).

Song monk, lay surname Hu, of Taizhou Linhai. Tonsured and ordained under 護國瑞禪師 (a distinct tonsure master — not to be conflated with his dharma teacher). Traveled widely, then went to Longmen and presented his understanding to Foyan Qingyuan; Foyan told him this was mere intellectual understanding, not true awakening, and set him to work in the kitchen, where he later broke through. Confirmed as Foyan's dharma heir.

masters.teacher: 隨州雙泉山師寬明教禪師 (Suizhou Shuangquan Shikuan)
masters.notes: Song monk of Shu (Sichuan). Left home, went to Suizhou Shuangquan Mountain, became dharma heir of Shikuan Chanshi (a third-generation descendant of Yunmen Wenyan). Later dwelt at Wuzu Mountain in Qizhou; late in life retired to Dayu, where he died leaning on his staff.
Qing-dynasty monk, disciple of Shigu Jingzi (石鼓淨滋).
Five Dynasties monk of the Huayan Cloister on Lumen Mountain in Xiangzhou, dharma heir of Caoshan Benji (曹山本寂) of Fuzhou.
Northern Song monk, dharma heir of Fenyang Shanzhao (汾陽太子禪院善昭禪師), later abbot at Shishuang.

masters.teacher: 吉安 / 鐵牛持定 / 靈雲定 (Tieniu Chiding)
masters.notes: Yuan-dynasty monk of Jishui, lay surname Liu, monk of the Prajna cloister in Yuzhang (Nanchang). Dharma heir of Jian, i.e. 鐵牛持定/靈雲定.
Five Dynasties monk, dharma heir of Yunmen Wenyan (韶州雲門山文偃禪師), abbot of Miaosheng cloister in Lu prefecture.

Northern Song Linji-Huanglong monk, lay surname Peng, of Pingxiang in Yuanzhou (Jiangxi). Traveled to Donglin Changzong's assembly at the Zhaojue hall; long without formal sanction, until he was shown the 'Niaoke blows the down' (鳥窠吹布毛) exchange and suddenly awakened. Changzong confirmed him and made him head of the assembly; when Changzong was summoned to Donglin, 應乾 succeeded him at the Baofeng cloister of Letan.

Northern Song monk, dharma heir of Dagui Zhenru Muzhe (大溈[真如]喆禪師). Self-styled 碧落道人 ('Man of the Kingfisher-Blue Void'); wrote the seven Buddha-names on his robe, earning the nickname '蘭布裩' (Lan of the cloth trousers). Died a martyr's death during the Jin invasion at the end of the Jianyan era, self-immolating rather than betray the Song, and yielding five-colored relics.

Tang monk, lay surname Chen of Changxi. Left home at Turtle Mountain; traveled widely, questioned Shishuang, then attained the dharma under Yantou Quanhuo (巖頭[全]奯禪師, 828-887). Prince Wang Shenzhi of Min invited him to reside at Luoshan in Fuzhou; titled 法寶禪師.

masters.teacher: 行鞏 (石林行鞏 / 淨慈鞏, A008205)
masters.notes: Linji-Yangqi monk of the Yuan, disciple of Jinci Shilin Xinggong. Left home at 14, studied under the Sichuanese monk Anshi, then trained under Xinggong at Chengtian. Opened his teaching at Tiantai Hanyan (1290), moved through Gusu Hanshan and Kunshan Dongchan, was summoned to Jingci in 1315 and later moved to Lingyin. Died 1327, posthumous title 'Mingzong Huiren Chanshi'. Author of the Liuhui Yulu.

Northern Song Yunmen-school monk, abbot of Jiufeng in Mingzhou (also given as Hangzhou Lin'an Jiufeng Jingtu). Dharma heir of Letan Huaicheng, 11th generation from Huineng. Wrote a petition urging Dajue Huailian to accept the abbacy of Ayuwang monastery. Dharma heir: Zujing Fayin.
Tang-dynasty monk, dharma heir of Yanguan Qi'an at Hangzhou. Attested in the Zutang ji and Jingde Chuandeng lu.
Northern Song Linji monk, abbot of Jingtu at Lin'an, Hangzhou. Dharma heir of Puti Guangyong.

Northern Song Yunmen-school monk, surname Wu, of Taizhou. Dharma heir of Tianyi Yihuai (993-1064), 12th generation from Huineng. Trained at Zisheng monastery, abbotted at Taiping and then Ruiyan. Six dharma heirs including Fuku Keying and Yuelin Tanzhen.
Dharma heir of Qingliang Wenyi (founder of the Fayan school) at Jinling. Abbot of Guizong at Lushan.
Dharma heir of Huilin Yuanzhao Zongben, abbot of Ganlu at Runzhou (also called 傳祖 Chuanzu, the 'patriarch's transmission').

masters.teacher: 贊元 (蔣山贊元/覺海贊元, A014470)
masters.notes: Northern Song Linji monk, abbot of Shimen in Quzhou. Recorded as one of nine dharma heirs of Jiangshan Zanyuan (four with recorded sayings: Xuedou Faya, Chengxi Yingyue, Shimen Ya, Guifeng Ziqiong).

Prominent Northern Song Yunmen-school monk, Ningbo Ayuwang (King Ashoka monastery) Dajue Huailian. Known for literary skill; studied under Huaicheng for over a decade. Later abbot of Dongjing Jingyin by imperial decree (1050), given title 'Dajue Chanshi'. Then invited to head Ayuwang for 20 years. Su Shi wrote his stupa inscription. Author of the 'Miaodao pian', which aimed to harmonize the Three Teachings.

Five Dynasties Min monk, surname Li, from Zhouzhou. Entered Min, trained under Yishan, silently transmitted the mind-source. Followed Changqing Huileng in his abbacy at Zhaoqing yuan, Quanzhou; when Huileng was summoned by King Wang Shenzhi to Changle, he succeeded him as abbot at Zhaoqing, given the title 'Fayin Dashi' by the Min king. Dates unrecorded.

Zhenzhou Changlu Yingfu, of the Jiang clan of Chuzhou (Anhui). Dharma heir of Tianyi Yihuai (992-1064), 11th generation after Huineng. Ordained under Chengtai at Baoning monastery in Jiangning, then studied under Tianyi Yihuai and inherited the Yunmen essentials. Held forth at Changlu with 25 recorded dharma heirs including Changlu Zongze (author of the Chanyuan Qinggui) and Xuedou Daorong.

Jizhou Heshan Chucai Chanzhi Chanshi, a native of Linjiang commandery. Dharma heir of Deshan (Huiyuan). Recorded exchanges on the coincidence of Buddha-decree and patriarch-decree, and on 'the phrase that transcends both ordinary and sage.'

masters.teacher: 子琦 / 開元子琦 (DILA A003639)
masters.notes: Sung-dynasty monk, lay surname Hu. Received mind-seal confirmation from Chan master Ziqi (d. ~1115). Dharma heir of Kaiyuan Ziqi, himself a dharma heir of Huanglong Huinan.

Founding patriarch of the Jingshan branch of the Niutou (Oxhead) school, Tang dynasty. Lay surname Zhu, of Kunshan. Originally a Confucian student; met Helin Xuansu who told him 'observing your spirit, you are truly a Dharma-vessel,' whereupon he was moved to awaken and was ordained. Settled at Jingshan in Hangzhou, attracting many students. Summoned to the capital in 768 (Dali 3) by Emperor Daizong, given the title 'National Teacher of the First Rank' (國一禪師). Later moved to the Pure Land Cloister of Longxing monastery. Disciples include Niaoke Daolin and Chongyun Huihui.

names: 福州安國弘瑫明真禪師
masters.notes: Chen-clan monk of Quanzhou. Studied under Xuefeng Yicun; a well-known exchange records Xuefeng grabbing hold of him and saying 'The whole universe is a gate of liberation — I grip your hand and pull, yet you will not enter,' to which Hongtan replied 'Reverend, you cannot blame Hongtan for that.' Later, at the invitation of the Min military governor, resided at Anguo monastery in Fuzhou and greatly propagated the teaching there.
A native of Jianning. Studied under Baizhang Daoheng ('Baizhang Heng Heshan') and attained realization; became abbot of Qixian monastery on Mt. Lu.

Ye-clan monk of Hangzhou's Longhua monastery. Ordained mid-Zhenming era (Liang), studied Vinaya deeply, then turned from lecturing to seek 'the firm dharma' after an awakening experience; traveled to Min and received the mind-transmission of Changqing (Huileng). Returning to Zhejiang, received by the Prince of Danqiu, resided at Liutong cloister; later summoned by the King of Southern Han (Qian clan) to Gongchen cloister, and finally returned to Longhua to gather students and teach.

names: 杭州中天竺空巖有禪師
masters.teacher: 荊叟如珏 / 徑山如珏 (DILA A021176)
masters.notes: Dharma heir of Jingshan Ru Jue (荊叟如珏). Recorded teaching-room utterance: 「黃金鑄就鐵真人」, with a verse by Donghai Yong.

names: 彭州大隨南堂元靜禪師
masters.notes: Southern Song Linji-Yangqi monk, lay surname Zhao, of Langzhong's Yushan. At ten, gravely ill, his parents vowed him to the monastic life on his recovery. Entered the order under Zongyi at Chengdu's Dacisi Baosheng cloister, ordained in Yuanyou 3 (1088). Studied and lectured for years, then went south; first called on Yong'an En on the 'three blows of Linji' koan, then studied under various teachers without full satisfaction; hearing of Wuzu Fayan's sharpness, sought him out and attained realization under his relentless questioning. Founded Nantang at Dasui shan in Pengzhou (hence 'Nantang Yuanjing/Daoxing'). Later abbot of Chengdu Zhaojue, Nengren, and Dasui monasteries. Author of the Nantang Xing Heshang Yuyao.

Lay surname Feng. Ordained young, studied the Lotus Sutra, Vijnaptimatratasiddhi and Awakening of Faith under a Mr. Bishang of Daliang; took full ordination at 38 under Duanheshang of Luoyang, then studied vinaya under Nanquan Hongjing. Went to Yuquan monastery in Jingzhou to study under Datong Shenxiu for six or seven years, mastering his method. In Kaiyuan 13 (725) entered Jing'ai monastery in Luoyang by imperial summons; in 727 followed the emperor to Chang'an and resided at Xingtang monastery, becoming the effective head of the Northern School after Shenxiu's death.

Hongzhou Letan Huaicheng Chanshi, dharma heir of Wuzu Shijie, 10th generation under Huineng. Called by all quarters 'Letan Cheng'. Huanglong Nan (Huinan, 1002-1069) studied under him longest of anyone. His pupils include Yubao Huailian (1010-1090) and Linyin Cijue.
Dharma heir of Chan master Huanglong Nan (Huinan). From Guixi in Xinzhou, lay surname Ying.

Surname Li, from Hanzhou; dharma heir of Yuanwu Keqin (1063-1135), 16th generation under Huineng. Studied Confucian classics young, later renounced lay life. Attained the essentials from Wuzu (i.e. via Yuanwu). Opened teaching at Dingzhou Deshan, later moved to Sushan, Daowu, and Dagui.

Surname Huai, from Qiantang; dharma heir of Yuantong Faxiu (1027-1090). Ordained at 15 under Xiyan, received dharma from Faxiu. Resided at Jiankang Baoning, Suzhou Huqiu, then Ersheng Lushan — nine abbacies in all.

No DILA authority record exists for him under any spelling tried (退庵空, 涼峰空, 凉峰). He survives only via mentions in his student Yinshan Can's (隱山璨) own record and yulu heading. Yinshan Can (Southern Song, Quanzhou, DILA A018328) is described as having 'succeeded to Liangfeng Kong, styled Tui'an — this Tui'an being his [dharma-]grandfather' (嗣涼峰空退庵，此庵乃其大父云), an unusual phrasing suggesting a generation-skip in the formal succession. A bibliographic catalog entry independently corroborates the relation with the same 嗣 verb.

masters.teacher: Beita Siguang 北塔思廣 (NOT in roster)
masters.notes: Surname Wang, from Danling in Meizhou. Ordained at Dali cloister in 1023. On pilgrimage met Beita [Siguang] and 'awakened the heart-essentials, attained the samadhi of ease'. Made a loincloth inscribed with the names of successive patriarchs, earning the epithet 'Hao of the inscribed loincloth'. Zhang Shangying sponsored his opening of teaching at Junzhou Dayang, later moved to Jingnan Yuquan. Zhang wrote his stupa inscription after death.

masters.teacher: Yuantong Kexian 圓通可僊 (NOT in roster)
masters.notes: Dharma heir of Chan master [Yuantong] Xian.

Early-Ming Linji-school abbot of Tianjie monastery in Nanjing (courtesy names 季潭/天界), Hongwu-era head of the national Buddhist registry, and the Hongwu Emperor's envoy to India. DILA A000581. Own teacher not researched in this fold; left null rather than guessed.
Abbot of Yongjia Huguo monastery (永嘉護國寺); dharma-heir of 林野通奇 (1596-1652), himself a disciple of 密雲圓悟. Teacher of the rescued orphan 冶翁伯.
Southern Song Linji-Yangqi master, abbot of Huazang in Changzhou; direct dharma-heir of Dahui Zonggao (大鑑下第十七世). Wrote a 1199 colophon for 《叢林盛事》. Teacher of the noteacher-rescued master 西山亮.
Yuan-dynasty Linji-Yangqi master (萬壽霖/竺田霖), dharma-heir of 天童止泓鑒. Teacher of the noteacher-rescued master 孤峰明德 (= 孤峰德旺 = 淨慈德).

The only Chinese emperor to claim Chan enlightenment. Compiled the Yuxuan yulu (1733), a 19-fascicle anthology of Chan recorded sayings. Authored Jianmo bianyi lu, banning Hanyue Fazang's works and settling the Miyun-Hanyue controversy in Miyun's favor. Lay Buddhist name Yuanming jushi. Reshaped Chan orthodoxy by imperial decree.
